I. Executive Summary
1. Overview
1.1. Summary of Regulatory Action
Bayer Healthcare Pharmaceuticals (hereafter referred to as the Applicant), submitted
NDA 219469 under the 505(b)(1) regulatory pathway, proposing to market the new molecular
entity (NME) elinzanetant for the treatment of moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms (VMS)
due to menopause.
A multidisciplinary review team has reviewed this application, and each discipline recommends
approval of this application. The signatory authority for this application concurs and
recommends approval for this indication.
Menopause is a natural process in a woman’s life that marks the decline of ovarian hormone
production and cessation of reproductive capacity. This process is associated with profound
physiological changes, resulting in symptoms such as VMS or hot flashes (HFs), and symptoms
of vulvovaginal atrophy (vaginal dryness, irritation, and pain with intercourse). Menopausal
symptoms, such as vasomotor symptoms, can negatively affect women’s daily activities and
quality of life (Whiteley et al. 2013a). In addition, menopausal symptoms can persist for long
periods in some individuals.
Vasomotor symptoms, also known as hot flashes or HFs, occur as a result of estrogen withdrawal
and represent a disorder of hypothalamic thermoregulation. The kisspeptin/neurokinin B
(NKB)/dynorphin (KNDy) neurons in the thermoregulatory center in the hypothalamus are
thought to be responsive to both estrogen and ambient temperature. In response to decreasing
estrogen levels, hypertrophy and activation of the KNDy neurons are thought to disrupt
thermoregulation and trigger VMS. Elinzanetant is a neurokinin 1 (NK1) and neurokinin 3
(NK3) receptor antagonist that blocks NK1,3 receptors on the KNDy neurons. The Applicant
hypothesizes that blockade of the KNDy neurons attenuates vasomotor symptoms associated
with menopause.
Substantial evidence of effectiveness (SEE) of elinzanetant for treatment of moderate to severe
vasomotor symptoms due to menopause was established with two adequate and well-controlled
studies. For full details, refer to Section 1.2.
The available clinical data show that elinzanetant is safe for its intended use. Common adverse
reactions include headache, fatigue, dizziness, somnolence, abdominal pain, rash, diarrhea, and
muscle spasm.
Central nervous system depressant effects and daytime impairment were seen, and patients
should refrain from driving or engaging in hazardous occupations or activities until the effects
have resolved. Hepatic transaminase elevations were seen in the clinical development program
and hepatic transaminases should be measured prior to initiating therapy and 3 months after
initiation. In addition, there will be enhanced pharmacovigilance for hepatic adverse events.
4
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
Animal studies suggest that elinzanetant may cause pregnancy loss or stillbirth. Females of
reproductive potential should have pregnancy excluded prior to initiating elinzanetant and should
use effective contraception for 2 weeks after stopping elinzanetant. In addition, animal studies
showed convulsions and there was one patient with a history of seizures who experienced a
seizure during the clinical program. The identified risks for elinzanetant can be adequately
mitigated through labeling and routine pharmacovigilance.
As described in Section 2.2, we conclude that the reduction in frequency and severity of hot
flashes observed with elinzanetant outweighs the risks when elinzanetant is used as
recommended in the approved labeling.

1.2. Conclusions on Substantial Evidence of
Effectiveness
We conclude that substantial evidence of effectiveness for elinzanetant 120 mg daily (taken as
(b) (4) for moderate to severe VMS in postmenopausal women has been
two 60 mg
demonstrated with two adequate and well-controlled studies (Study 21651 [OASIS 1] and Study
21652 [OASIS 2]).
A total of 796 postmenopausal women (396 in OASIS 1 and 400 in OASIS 2) aged 40 to 65
years who had a minimum of 50 moderate to severe HFs, including nighttime HFs, per week,
were enrolled in OASIS 1 and OASIS 2. Subjects were randomized to elinzanetant 120 mg or
placebo.
The primary efficacy endpoints in both studies were the mean change in frequency and in
severity of moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms from baseline to Weeks 4 and 12, including
day and night HFs measured using the Hot Flash Daily Diary (HFDD). In both studies,
elinzanetant showed a statistically significant and clinically meaningful reduction (≥2 hot flashes
over 24 hours) in the frequency of HFs from baseline to Weeks 4 and 12 compared to placebo.
Also, in both studies, there was a statistically significant reduction in the severity of HFs from
baseline to Weeks 4 and 12 compared to placebo.
Substantial evidence of effectiveness for elinzanetant 120 mg for the treatment of moderate to
severe VMS associated with menopause has been demonstrated based on the results of two Phase
3 studies (OASIS 1 and OASIS 2).

Conclusions and Reasons

Menopause is a natural and normal physiological process marking the decline of
reproductive capacity in females.
In the United States, nearly 63 million women are past the average age of
natural menopause of 51 years of age (50 years of age and older as of July 1,
2021) (United°States°Census°Bureau 2020).
Menopause is associated with profound physiological changes. Symptoms of
menopause, such as vasomotor symptoms (VMS) [hot flashes/hot flushes] and
vulvar and vaginal atrophy (VVA) symptoms (also referred to as genitourinary
syndrome of menopause or GSM) [vaginal dryness, vaginal irritation/itching, and
pain with sexual activity (dyspareunia)] can be debilitating with respect to a
woman’s ability to accomplish her normal activities, including sleep (Whiteley et
al. 2013a). However, menopause is not directly a life-threatening condition.
VMS are experienced by up to 80% of individuals during menopause (Gold et al.
2006). The prevalence of moderate to severe VMS associated with menopause
was 34% in the United States, 40% in Europe, and 16% in Japan (Nappi et al.
2021).
Hot flashes involve sudden sensations of heat in the upper body, particularly in
the head, neck, chest and upper back. These symptoms occur as episodes that
usually last 1 to 5 minutes and are characterized by perspiration, flushing, chills,
clamminess, anxiety and, on occasion, heart palpitations.
An individual’s experience can vary based on a combination of genetic
background, psychological and socio-economic factors and other health
conditions and/or treatments.
The duration of VMS from the time of symptom onset is typically 7.4 years and
symptoms commonly persist for nearly a decade (Freeman et al. 2011; Avis et
al. 2015).

2.2. Conclusions Regarding Benefit-Risk
Vasomotor symptoms are common during menopause and can negatively impact the quality of
life for women and work productivity (Blumel et al. 2011; Whiteley et al. 2013a; Whiteley et al.
2013b). Vasomotor symptoms are characterized by problems with sleep, mood, joint pain, back
pain, headaches, fatigue, loss of libido, mood swings and genitourinary problems (Nelson 2008;
Berecki-Gisolf et al. 2009; Joffe et al. 2010; Moilanen et al. 2010; Seritan et al. 2010; Mishra
and Kuh 2012; Whiteley et al. 2013a). In addition, menopausal symptoms can persist for long
periods in some individuals (Freeman et al. 2014).
While there are numerous hormone therapy products for the treatment of vasomotor symptoms
associated with menopause, there are only two nonhormonal options currently approved. Since
some women cannot take or choose not to take hormone therapy, it is desirable to have
additional nonhormonal treatments available to manage menopausal symptoms.
The efficacy of elinzanetant 120 mg orally once daily at bedtime was demonstrated in two
adequate and well-controlled Phase 3 studies (OASIS 1 and OASIS 2) in postmenopausal
women aged 40 to65 years with moderate to severe VMS. A total of 796 women (396 in
OASIS 1 and 400 in OASIS 2) who had a minimum of 50 moderate to severe HFs, including
nighttime HFs, per week, were enrolled in OASIS 1 and OASIS 2. Subjects were randomized to
elinzanetant 120 mg or placebo. In both studies, elinzanetant showed a statistically significant
and clinically meaningful reduction (≥2 hot flashes over 24 hours) in the frequency of HFs from
baseline to Weeks 4 and 12 compared to placebo. At 4 and 12 weeks, respectively, the difference
in the mean change from baseline in the frequency of HFs compared to placebo (least squares
[LS]-mean [SE]) was -3.29 (0.61) and -3.22 (0.81) in OASIS 1 and -3.04 (0.69) and -3.24 (0.69)
in OASIS 2. Also, in both studies, there was a statistically significant reduction in the severity of
HFs from baseline to Weeks 4 and 12 compared to placebo. At 4 and 12 weeks, respectively, the
difference in the mean change from baseline in severity of HFs compared to placebo ([LS]-mean
[SE]) was -0.33 (0.06) and -0.40 (0.07) in OASIS 1 and -0.22 (0.06) and -0.29 (0.08) in OASIS
2.
The available clinical data show that elinzanetant is safe for its intended use. The safety database
for elinzanetant for moderate to severe VMS was adequate. Dose adjustment to 60 mg daily is
recommended for patients taking concomitant moderate CYP34 inhibitors due to increased
elinzanetant exposure and the potential for associated increased adverse reactions. Common
adverse reactions include headache, fatigue, dizziness, somnolence, abdominal pain, rash,
diarrhea, and muscle spasms. Nervous system effects (i.e., somnolence, fatigue, vertigo,
dizziness, and presyncope) were seen. Given the central nervous system depressant effects and
daytime impairment, patients should refrain from driving or engaging in hazardous occupations
or activities until these effects have resolved. Hepatic transaminase elevations were seen in the
clinical development program and hepatic transaminases should be measured prior to initiating
therapy and 3 months after initiation. In addition, there will be enhanced pharmacovigilance for
hepatic adverse events. Animal studies suggest that elinzanetant may cause pregnancy loss or
stillbirth. Females of reproductive potential should have pregnancy excluded prior to initiating
elinzanetant and should use effective contraception for 2 weeks after stopping elinzanetant. In
addition, animal studies showed convulsions and there was one patient with a history of seizures
9

Based on review of the available efficacy and safety data, NDA 219469 for elinzanetant provides
substantial evidence of effectiveness and a favorable benefit-risk profile for the treatment of
moderate to severe VMS in postmenopausal women.

II. Interdisciplinary Assessment
3. Introduction
Menopause is a natural and normal physiological process marking the decline of reproductive
capacity in females. In the United States, nearly 63 million women are past the average age of
natural menopause of 51 years of age (50 years of age and older as of July 1, 2021)
(United°States°Census°Bureau 2020). Menopause is associated with profound physiological
changes. Symptoms of menopause, such as vasomotor symptoms (VMS; hot flashes/hot flushes)
and vulvar and vaginal atrophy symptoms (vaginal dryness, vaginal irritation/itching, and pain
with sexual activity [dyspareunia]) can be debilitating with respect to a woman’s ability to
accomplish her normal activities, including sleep (Whiteley et al. 2013a). However, menopause
is not directly a life-threatening condition. VMS are experienced by up to 80% of individuals
during menopause (Gold et al. 2006). The prevalence of moderate to severe VMS associated
with menopause was 34% in the United States, 40% in Europe, and 16% in Japan (Nappi et al.
2021).
Hot flashes involve sudden sensations of heat in the upper body, particularly in the head, neck,
chest, and upper back. These symptoms occur as episodes that usually last 1 to 5 minutes and are
characterized by perspiration, flushing, chills, clamminess, anxiety and, on occasion, heart
palpitations. The duration of VMS from the time of symptom onset is typically 7.4 years and
symptoms commonly persist for nearly a decade (Freeman et al. 2011; Avis et al. 2015). VMS
can impact several areas of life and can affect work, social activities, leisure activities, sleep,
mood, concentration, sexual activity, total energy level, and overall quality of life (Williams et
al. 2009).
In menopause, there is a decrease in estradiol levels due to decreased ovarian function, resulting
in increased gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) secretion from the hypothalamus leading
to increase in luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) concentrations
(Freeman et al. 2005). A group of neurons in the hypothalamus is an important regulator of
GnRH. These neurons coexpress kisspeptin, dynorphin as well as NKB and are known as the
kisspeptin/NKB/dynorphin neurons (KDNy neurons). The KDNy neurons in the hypothalamus
have been identified as playing a role in thermoregulation that is responsive to estrogen and
ambient temperature (Rance et al. 2013). In menopause, excessive KNDy neuron firing is
thought to disrupt baseline thermoregulation and trigger VMS. Elinzanetant acts as an antagonist
at NK1 and NK3 receptors, which are on KNDy neurons. Blocking these receptors is
hypothesized to decrease hot flushes experienced by women with moderate to severe VMS during
menopause.

Current Treatment Options
Women with mild symptoms of VMS (sensation of heat without sweating) typically do not
require pharmacologic therapy. In contrast, women with moderate to severe symptoms of VMS
may require pharmacologic therapy. The FDA has approved numerous postmenopausal hormone
therapy products, both estrogens alone (Table 3) for use in a woman without a uterus, and
estrogens plus progestogens products (Table 4 and Table 5) for use in a woman with a uterus, as
well as two nonhormonal products for the treatment of moderate to severe VMS (Table 6).
Hormone therapy has been the predominant treatment for moderate to severe VMS. Risks of
estrogen plus progesterone therapy include deep venous thrombosis, pulmonary emboli, stroke,
myocardial infarction, and breast cancer. Risks of estrogen-alone therapy include endometrial
cancer, stroke, and deep venous thrombosis. Although hormone therapy is effective, these
products are contraindicated in women who have breast cancer or a history of breast cancer,
venous thromboembolism (or a history of venous thromboembolism) or thrombophilia, and those
with a history of stroke or myocardial infarction. Currently, women who pursue treatment for
VMS and are unable to take hormone therapy may try Brisdelle (paroxetine) or Veozah
(fezolinetant), but additional options would be desirable.

VMS can profoundly impact women, and it is important to have additional therapeutic options.

3.2. Approach to the Clinical Review
The primary evidence of efficacy and safety of elinzanetant in postmenopausal women with hot
flashes is from three clinical studies: OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and OASIS 3. Two of these studies,
OASIS 1 and OASIS 2, were submitted as the primary evidence of efficacy of elinzanetant in
postmenopausal women. The primary assessment of safety was based on data from OASIS 1,
OASIS 2, and OASIS 3.
The clinical studies conducted to support the primary benefit-risk assessment of elinzanetant for
the treatment of moderate to severe hot flashes in postmenopausal women are summarized in
Table 7.
Determination of Efficacy
Clinical data from the first 12 weeks of two randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled
studies (OASIS 1 and OASIS 2) in postmenopausal women with moderate to severe hot flashes,
were submitted as the primary evidence of efficacy of elinzanetant. In each of these two studies,
after the first 12 weeks, women on placebo were switched over to elinzanetant and all women
were then treated with elinzanetant for a 14-week extension for up to 26 weeks total exposure. In
OASIS 1 and OASIS 2, a total of 796 postmenopausal women were randomized to receive
elinzanetant or placebo. Women who had at least 50 moderate to severe HFs, including nighttime
HFs, per week, were enrolled in OASIS 1 and OASIS 2. The primary efficacy endpoints in both
studies were the mean change in frequency and in severity of moderate to severe vasomotor
symptoms from baseline to Weeks 4 and 12, including day and night HFs measured using the
HFDD.
Determination of Safety
The primary safety evaluation is based on the 12-week placebo-controlled period of OASIS 1
and OASIS 2, in addition to a 52-week, randomized, placebo-controlled study (OASIS 3) in
postmenopausal women with hot flashes. OASIS 3 was a multicenter Phase 3 study with a
primary efficacy endpoint of mean change in frequency of moderate to severe vasomotor
symptoms from baseline to Week 12 and a long-term safety evaluation up to 52 weeks in 628
postmenopausal women. Additional data from Phase 1/2 studies were evaluated to support the
safety evaluation. See Section 7.3 for further details.
The assessment of AEs, laboratory evaluations, vital signs, and electrocardiograms (ECGs) was
performed based on descriptive summaries and tables provided by the Applicant and Clinical
Data Scientists from the FDA. Subject narratives were reviewed for death, treatment
discontinuation, serious adverse events (SAEs), and adverse event of special interest. Clinical
study data were independently analyzed using JMP and JMP Clinical as appropriate. All safety
assessments and conclusions were those of the clinical review team unless otherwise specified.
Key review issues that were identified during the review are addressed in greater detail in
Section 7.7 for safety. Overall, the submitted clinical studies were adequate for the safety and
efficacy evaluation of elinzanetant.

5. Pharmacologic Activity, Pharmacokinetics,
and Clinical Pharmacology
5.1. Nonclinical Assessment of Potential
Effectiveness
The nonclinical pharmacological data indicate that elinzanetant acts as an antagonist at NK1 and
NK3 receptors. These receptors on the KNDy neurons in the thermoregulatory center in the
hypothalamus are thought to be responsive to both estrogen and ambient temperature. The
activation of the KNDy neurons in response to declining estradiol levels during menopausal
transition is thought to contribute to the hot flashes or HFs experienced by women with moderate
to severe VMS during menopause.

19
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)

5.1.1. Pharmacology
Elinzanetant is a NME that acts as a noncompetitive antagonist of both the human NK1 and NK3
receptors (NK1R and NK3R, respectively). In binding assays, elinzanetant displayed high
affinity for human NK1R (pKi (negative base-10 logarithm of the inhibition constant) values of
8.71 to 10.15 [mean pKi of 9.43]) and NK3R (pKi values of 8.03 to 8.8[mean pKi of 8.42]).
Elinzanetant has ~10-fold lower affinity towards human NK3R compared to human NK1R.
Additionally, elinzanetant has higher affinity for human NK1R and NK3R receptors than for
human NK2 receptors (pKi values of approximately 6.0). In functional in vitro assays,
elinzanetant inhibited the activity of human NK1R and NK3R, with calculated pKB values of
9.02 to 9.1 for human NK1R and 8.17 to 8.5 for human NK3R. Ex vivo receptor occupancy
studies in human putamen showed that elinzanetant occupied NK1Rs in the human putamen in a
concentration-dependent manner with a pKi of 9.44.
Each of the principal metabolites of interest–M27, M30/34 and M18/21, which accounted for
6%, 11% and 5.5%, respectively, of total radioactivity in the human biotransformation clinical
Study CPMX 50130/B002427–showed high affinity and noncompetitive antagonistic activity at
the human NK1R and NK3R. The affinities and potencies of the metabolites at human NK1R
and NK3R are similar to those of elinzanetant.
In vivo pharmacodynamic (PD) activity of elinzanetant was investigated in a gerbil foot tapping
model of NK1 activity and in the guinea pig wet-dog shake model of NK3 activity. After oral
dosing with elinzanetant, there was reversal of foot tapping induced by the NK1R agonist
GR73632 in male gerbils (ID50 [dose resulting a 50% reduction in time spent foot
tapping]=1.36 mg/kg). Similarly, elinzanetant doses of 8.5 and 25.5 mg/kg significantly reversed
wet-dog shake behavior induced by the NK3R agonist senktide in the guinea pigs, indicating
central NK3R antagonist activity. While the Applicant did not conduct studies in animal models
to demonstrate the effects of elinzanetant in reducing HF-like symptoms, overall, the
pharmacology data support the Applicant’s therapeutic rationale for the use of elinzanetant to
modulate neuronal activity in the vasomotor center. Refer to Section 5.1.2 below.
Selectivity screens were performed to evaluate the potential for off-target binding for
elinzanetant and the three principal human metabolites of elinzanetant (M27, M30/34, and
M18/21).
Elinzanetant was >100-fold more selective for the human NK3R and >300-fold for the human
NK1R versus 88 other nontachykinin human receptors, enzymes, and transporters.
Refer to Section 13.2 for a full review of the pharmacological studies submitted by the
Applicant.
The pharmacologic class term for elinzanetant is NK1 and NK3 receptor antagonist.

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)

5.1.2. Mechanism of Action
NK1R and NK3R antagonists are thought to act by inhibiting the activity of KNDy neurons,
which project to the vasomotor center in the median pre-optic nucleus to modulate neuronal
activity involved in thermoregulation. This inhibition of KNDy neurons, which are thought to be
in a hyperactivated state because of estrogen decline in menopause, is proposed to result in
improvement of menopause-associated VMS (also called HFs).

Secretion, and the Vasomotor Area in the Hypothalamus

SP, substance P; WS, wavelet synapse

EPC
Neurokinin 1 (NK1) and neurokinin 3 (NK3) receptor antagonist
Mechanism of action Elinzanetant, as an NK1 and NK3 receptor antagonist, may decrease the activity
of KNDy (kisspeptin/neurokinin B [NKB]/ dynorphin) neurons, which can be in a
hyperactivated state due to declining estrogen levels in menopause. KNDy
neurons project into the vasomotor center in the median pre-optic nucleus and

Half-life
The half-life of elinzanetant is approximately 45 hours following once daily oral

Metabolic pathway(s) Elinzanetant is primarily metabolized by CYP3A4, producing three principal
metabolites M18/21, M27, and M30/34. Metabolite M30/34 is a major metabolite of
elinzanetant in human plasma representing 13.7% of total drug-related exposure,
whereas M27 and M18/21 each represents 7.6% and 4.9%, respectively.
Primary excretion
Following oral administration of elinzanetant, approximately 90% of the dose is
pathways (% dose) excreted in feces (50% unchanged) and less than 1% in urine.
Intrinsic Factors and Specific Populations
Body weight
Population PK analysis demonstrated that body mass (BMI 21.9 kg/m2 to
34.1 kg/m2) is unlikely to have a clinically meaningful impact on the exposure of
elinzanetant and its metabolites. No dosage adjustments are recommended based
on body mass or weight.
Age
Population PK analyses based on the PK data from eleven Phase 1 studies, one
Phase 2 study, and three Phase 3 studies demonstrated that age (range: 22 to 75
years) is unlikely to have a clinically meaningful impact on the exposure of
elinzanetant and its metabolites. No dosage adjustments are recommended in
patients based on age.
Renal impairment
Population pharmacokinetic analysis demonstrated that among subjects enrolled
in Phase 3 studies, subjects with mild (eGFR 60-90 mL/min, n=402) or moderate
(eGFR 30-60 mL/min, n=23) renal impairment did not have significantly higher
exposure of elinzanetant compared to those with normal renal function (n=586)
and no additional safety concerns were identified in subjects with mild or moderate

renal impairment. The dedicated renal impairment Study 21669 suggested that

Hepatic impairment Population pharmacokinetic analysis demonstrated that mild hepatic impairment
does not significantly affect the drug exposure (AUC) of elinzanetant in the Phase
3 study population. The effect of moderate hepatic impairment on the drug
exposure was not evaluated in the population pharmacokinetic analysis due to the
limited number of subjects with moderate hepatic impairment in the analysis
(N=1). The dedicated hepatic impairment study (Study 21668) indicated that
individuals with moderate hepatic impairment exhibited 2.3-fold increase in AUC
compared to healthy subjects. Consequently, no dose adjustment is necessary for
patients with mild hepatic impairment but elinzanetant is not recommended for
patients with moderate to severe hepatic impairment.

6. Efficacy (Evaluation of Benefit)
6.1. Assessment of Dose and Potential
Effectiveness
The clinical development program evaluated doses ranging from 1.5 mg to 300 mg. The free
base form of elinzanetant in a soft-gel capsule formulation was evaluated at doses between
25 mg and 160 mg once daily. The Applicant conducted a Phase 2 study, SWITCH-1 (also
known as Study 814-PM-02), to evaluate a four-fold range of elinzanetant doses – 40, 80, 120,
and 160 mg once daily over 12 weeks. SWITCH-1 was a Phase 2b, international, randomized,
double-blind, placebo-controlled, dose-finding study. Subjects were postmenopausal women
aged 40 to 65 years who were in good general health and reported an average of at least 8
moderate or severe hot flashes per day (including nighttime) over the last 5 days of recording in
the paper diary during screening. The primary efficacy outcomes were mean change in the
frequency and severity of moderate and severe hot flashes from baseline at Week 4 and
Week 12, respectively.
Following randomization, 47 subjects received placebo and 152 received elinzanetant. The
number of subjects randomized to different doses was not evenly distributed due to the adaptive
design of the study. After reviewing emerging efficacy and safety data during interim reviews, a
blinded data review committee decided to discontinue first the 80 mg group then the 40 mg
group, resulting in changes to the randomization ratio. Ultimately, of those randomized to
elinzanetant, 31 received the 40 mg dose, 17 received 80 mg, 52 received 120 mg, and 52
received 160 mg. Of the randomized subjects, 43 (91.5%) completed the treatment with placebo;
29 (93.5%), 14 (82.4%), 51 (98.1%) and 43 (82.7%) completed treatment with 40 mg, 80 mg,
120 mg and 160 mg elinzanetant, respectively.

The plasma concentrations achieved with the 120 mg dose are associated with full occupancy of
central NK1 receptors throughout a dose interval at steady state as demonstrated in a human
positron emission tomography (PET) study. Although it is not possible to assess NK3 receptor
occupancy directly, as a suitable NK3 PET ligand does not exist, the achieved concentrations are
also very likely to fully occupy central NK3 receptors.

6.2. Clinical Studies/Trials Intended To
Demonstrate Efficacy
6.2.1. Study Design, OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and OASIS 3
OASIS 1 and OASIS 2 were two randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, Phase 3,
international studies conducted in postmenopausal women aged 40 to 65 years with moderate to
severe VMS. Both studies were designed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of elinzanetant
120 mg for the treatment of moderate to severe VMS associated with menopause.
Both studies had virtually identical designs. In these studies, eligible subjects who met all the
enrollment criteria were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to receive either 120 mg of elinzanetant or a
matching placebo orally once daily. Randomization was stratified by region (North America and
the rest of the world).
Both studies included a wash-out period (if applicable), a screening period, and a 12-week
placebo-controlled treatment period where the subjects were randomized to receive either
elinzanetant 120 mg or placebo. After completing the first 12 weeks of treatment, subjects in the
placebo arm then received elinzanetant 120 mg for 14 weeks, and subjects who were in the
active arm continued to receive elinzanetant 120 mg for another 14 weeks. Following completion
of the 26-week treatment period (or early discontinuation), subjects were followed by a 4-week
safety follow-up period. Figure 2 below shows a schematic of OASIS 1 and OASIS 2 studies.
Figure 2. Schematic, OASIS 1 and OASIS 2

Source: Clinical study report for OASIS 1, p 21; clinical study report for OASIS 2, p19
Abbreviations: approx., approximately; ICF, informed consent form; Rand., randomization

OASIS 3 was a randomized, multi-center, multi-country, double-blind, placebo-controlled,
parallel-group, Phase 3 study conducted in postmenopausal women aged 40 to 65 years with
VMS. OASIS 3 was designed to provide long-term safety and supportive efficacy data.
Eligible subjects who met all the enrollment criteria in OASIS 3 were randomized in a 1:1 ratio
to receive either 120 mg of elinzanetant or a matching placebo orally once daily for 52 weeks.
Randomization was stratified by region (North America and the rest of the world).

6.2.2. Eligibility Criteria, OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and OASIS
3
OASIS 1 and OASIS 2 had identical eligibility criteria, with eligible subjects having a minimum
of 50 moderate to severe hot flashes (HFs, including nighttime episodes) per week at baseline. In
contrast, OASIS 3 had no required minimum episodes of moderate to severe hot flashes at
baseline. Also, unlike in OASIS 1 and OASIS 2, subjects in OASIS 3 were not required to have a
negative gynecologic ultrasound, endometrial biopsy, cervical cytology, or Electronic ColumbiaSuicide Severity Rating Scale (eC-SSRS) at screening. Otherwise, the three studies had the same
criteria for eligibility as outlined below.
Inclusion Criteria
(1) Females aged 40 to 65 years, inclusive, at signing of informed consent.
(2) Postmenopausal, defined as:
(a) at least 12 months of spontaneous amenorrhea prior to signing of informed consent, or
(b) at least 6 months of spontaneous amenorrhea prior to signing of informed consent with
serum FSH levels >40 mIU/mL and a serum estradiol concentration of <30 pg/mL, or
(c) at least 6 months after hysterectomy at signing of informed consent with serum FSH
levels >40 mIU/mL and a serum estradiol concentration of <30 pg/mL, or
(d) surgical bilateral oophorectomy with or without hysterectomy at least 6 weeks prior to
signing of informed consent.
(3) Moderate to severe HF associated with the menopause and seeking treatment for this
condition.
(4) Negative urine pregnancy test at Screening.
(5) In good general health, in the opinion of the investigator, based on the medical history,
physical examination, 12-lead ECG, bone mineral density (BMD), vital signs, gynecological
30
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)

ultrasound, endometrial biopsy, mammogram, clinical laboratory tests, eC-SSRS, and other
assessments completed during screening.
(6) Normal or clinically insignificant cervical cytology not requiring further follow-up:
(a) cervical cytology sample has to be obtained during screening, or
(b) A documented normal result has to be available from cervical cytology conducted within
12 months prior to signing of informed consent.
(c) HPV testing in subjects with ASCUS will be used as an adjunctive test automatically.
Subjects with ASCUS can be included if they are negative for high-risk HPV strains.
(d) HPV testing in subjects with “absence of endocervical/transformation zone component”

(8) Subject has a screening mammogram performed, unless she is able to provide a written

(e.g., tamoxifen, aromatase inhibitors, GnRH analogues) cannot be enrolled in this study.

(a) Treated hyperthyroidism with no abnormal increase of thyroid function laboratory
parameters and no relevant clinical signs for >6 months before signing of informed

(b) Treated hypothyroidism with normal thyroid function test results during screening and a

6.2.3. Clinical Endpoints, OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and
OASIS 3
Primary Efficacy Endpoints, OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and OASIS 3
In OASIS 1 and OASIS 2, the following four coprimary efficacy endpoints were assessed:


Mean change in the frequency of moderate to severe VMS from baseline to Week 4



Mean change in the frequency of moderate to severe VMS from baseline to Week 12



Mean change in the severity of moderate to severe VMS from baseline to Week 4



Mean change in the severity of moderate to severe VMS from baseline to Week 12

In OASIS 3, the primary endpoint was assessed as the mean change in the frequency of moderate
to severe VMS from baseline to Week 12. In this study, this endpoint was assessed to provide
supportive efficacy evidence.
Across the three studies, subjects recorded the number (frequency) and severity of each hot flash
twice daily (morning and evening) using a HFDD data at baseline, during the entire 26-week
treatment, and at the 4-week follow-up periods. See Section 16.5 for more details on the eDiary,
HFDD. Hot flash severity was graded as mild (a sensation of heat without sweating), moderate (a
sensation of heat with sweating, but able to continue activity), and severe (a sensation of heat
with sweating, causing cessation [stopping] of activity). See Section 16.5 for a copy of morning
and evening HFDD.
In all three OASIS studies, the calculations of frequency and severity data at baseline and at each
postbaseline visit are discussed below.
Baseline Frequency/Severity
The baseline frequency was calculated based on data from all available days during the 14 days
prior to start of treatment and is shown in Equation 1.

When no moderate or severe HF were reported for a particular day, the mean severity for that

Per protocol, at least 11 days need to be available for the derivation of the baseline frequency or
severity value. Otherwise, the baseline value was set as missing. Based on this rule, all subjects
in OASIS 1 had baseline frequency/severity scores, while one subject each in OASIS 2 and
OASIS 3 had missing baseline frequency/severity scores.

At the postbaseline visits, weekly frequency and severity values were calculated using available

When no HFs were reported for a particular day, the mean severity for that day was set to 0.
Per protocol, when data were missing for more than 2 days within a week, the frequency or
severity value for that week was set to missing.
6.2.3.1. Key Secondary Endpoints, OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and
OASIS 3
In OASIS 1 and OASIS 2, the Applicant defined the following three key secondary efficacy
endpoints. There was no key secondary endpoint defined in OASIS 3.


Mean change in frequency of moderate to severe HF from baseline to Week 1



Mean change in Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System Sleep
Disturbance Short Form 8b (PROMIS SD SF 8b) total T-score from baseline to Week 12



Mean change in Menopause Specific Quality of Life Scale (MENQOL) total score from
baseline to Week 12

34
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
During the 12-week placebo-controlled period, PROMIS SD SF 8b and MENQOL were
administered to subjects electronically per the following schedules:


PROMIS SD SF 8b: baseline, Weeks 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, and 12



MENQOL: baseline, Weeks 4, 8, and 12

For PROMIS SD SF 8b, subjects’ responses to eight items of the instrument (such as restless
sleep, satisfaction with sleep, refreshing sleep, difficulties sleeping, difficulties getting to sleep,
difficulties staying asleep, amount of sleep, and overall sleep quality) were scored on a 1 to 5
numeric rating scale and aggregated to derive total raw scores ranging from 8 to 40. These total
raw scores were then converted into T-scores using a look-up table for comparison with
population norms. A higher score indicates a higher level of sleep disturbance.
For MENQOL, subjects’ responses to the 29 items were scored individually on a scale indicating
whether the subject experienced the symptom (yes/no). If they select yes, they rate how bothered
they were by the symptom using a 6-point verbal descriptor scale. The items assess four domains
of symptoms and functioning: vasomotor symptoms, psychosocial functioning, physical
functioning, and sexual functioning. Domain scores are calculated as mean of single item
converted scores. The MENQOL total score was calculated as the mean of four domain mean
scores.
It is important to note that, as communicated to the Applicant in the end-of-phase 2 (EOP2) Final
Meeting Minutes dated December 17, 2020, results from the key secondary endpoints would not
be considered for labeling for the following considerations:
“Class Labeling” for an approved VMS indication will include efficacy findings for the four
primary VMS endpoints and the clinically meaningful reduction in hot flash frequency, and safety
(b) (4) are not
findings as appropriate. Outcomes of secondary endpoints
used to determine the effectiveness of drug product for a VMS indication and are not included in
labeling. NT-814 [elinzanetant] will receive labeling consistent with other drugs approved for the
same VMS indication.

Therefore, in this review, the analyses of these key secondary endpoints were considered for
exploratory use only.

6.2.4. Statistical Analysis Plan for Efficacy, OASIS 1,
OASIS 2, and OASIS 3
6.2.4.1. Analysis Populations, OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and OASIS
3
All efficacy analyses were conducted based on the full analysis set (FAS), which consisted of all
randomized subjects.
In OASIS 1, the FAS population consisted of 396 subjects (199 in elinzanetant 120 mg arm and
197 in placebo arm). Of these, 393 subjects received study medication (199 received elinzanetant
120 mg and 194 received matching placebo).
35
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
In OASIS 2, the FAS population consisted of 400 subjects (200 in elinzanetant 120 mg arm and
200 in placebo arm). All 400 subjects received study medication (201 received elinzanetant
120 mg and 199 received matching placebo).
In OASIS 3, the FAS consisted of 628 subjects (313 in elinzanetant 120 mg arm and 315 in
placebo arm). Of these, 627 subjects received study medication (313 received elinzanetant
120 mg arm and 314 received matching placebo).
6.2.4.2. Analysis of Coprimary Efficacy Endpoints, OASIS 1,
OASIS 2, and OASIS 3
The primary efficacy objective of OASIS 1 and OASIS 2 studies was to assess the superiority of
elinzanetant 120 mg to placebo in the four coprimary endpoints in postmenopausal women 40 to
65 years of age with moderate to severe VMS.
The prespecified primary analysis to evaluate the superiority of elinzanetant 120 mg to placebo
in the four coprimary efficacy endpoints was performed using MMRM analysis including all
randomized subjects, even if they stopped treatment temporarily or permanently, or took
prohibited medications, following a treatment policy strategy. The MMRM model included
treatment group, week (Weeks 1, 4, 8, and 12), and region (United States and the rest of the
world) as factors, baseline VMS as covariate, and the interaction effects of treatment by week
and baseline measurement by week. An unstructured covariance structure shared across
treatment groups was used to model the within-patient errors. The Kenward-Roger
approximation was used to estimate denominator degrees of freedom and to adjust standard
errors.
Based on the MMRM model, the LS estimates of the mean change from baseline and standard
error (SE) for each treatment arm at Weeks 1, 4, 8, and 12 as well as the LS estimates of the
treatment differences (elinzanetant-placebo), SE of the differences, associated 95% confidence
interval (CI), and p-value (one-sided) were reported.
The primary efficacy endpoint in OASIS 3 was assessed similarly to the primary analysis of the
coprimary efficacy endpoints in OASIS 1 and OASIS 2.
Type I Error Control (Plan for Multiplicity Adjustment)
In OASIS 1 and OASIS 2, superiority in each of the four coprimary endpoints were tested at a
one-sided significance level of 2.5%. Since superiority in all four coprimary endpoints within
each study must be established to claim study success, the study-wise Type I error rate was
controlled at a one-sided significance level of 2.5%. Similarly, since superiority in the single
primary endpoint in OASIS 3 must be established to claim study success, the study-wise Type I
error rate was also controlled at a one-sided significance level of 2.5%.
Handling of Missing Data
In the primary efficacy analyses in OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and OASIS 3, the Applicant imputed
nonmonotone (intermittent) and monotone missing data using Monte Carlo Markov Chain
multiple imputation (MI) method under a missing at random missing data mechanism.
36
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
Within each study, the Applicant created a total of 500 multiply imputed datasets using SEED
numbers 21651 in OASIS 1, 21652 in OASIS 2,
and 21653 in OASIS 3, respectively. After the completion of the imputation steps, each imputed
dataset was analyzed using the MMRM model as specified for the primary analysis of the four
coprimary endpoints. Then, the results from each multiply imputed dataset were combined using
the Rubin’s rule (Rubin 1987) to obtain an overall estimated treatment effect.
See Section 16.1 for a detailed description of the missing data handling in the statistical analysis
plan-specified primary analyses of (co)primary endpoints in OASIS 1, 2, and 3.
Given the minimal dropout rates and limited missing data within each study (Table 14), the
Applicant’s approach to handling missing data in the primary efficacy analysis appears
reasonable.
Sensitivity Analyses
To evaluate the robustness of the primary efficacy results, the Applicant performed the following
sensitivity analyses based on the FAS population under the treatment policy strategy.


Sensitivity analysis 1 (SA1): MMRM analysis without any missing data imputation. The
MMRM model used in SA1 was the same as those used in the primary analyses except that
SA1 used all data from Weeks 1 to 12 while the primary analyses used data only from
Weeks 1, 4, 8, and 12. This sensitivity analysis was conducted by the Applicant post hoc per
FDA’s request.



Sensitivity analysis 2 (SA2): A tipping point analysis was used to assess the sensitivity of the
main analysis results to violations of missing at random assumptions used in the primary
analyses. In the tipping point analysis, delta adjustments were applied only to the MI values
in the elinzanetant arm. For the two coprimary endpoints of VMS frequency, the adjustments
were applied with delta values from 1 to 10 with an increase of 1 in each successive tipping
point iteration. For the endpoints related to severity of hot flashes, the adjustments were
applied with delta values of 0.2 to 2 with an increase of 0.2 in each successive tipping point
iteration.

To further assess the robustness of the primary efficacy analysis based on the treatment policy
strategy, the Applicant reanalyzed the primary analysis using the following two supplementary
estimands:


In the first supplementary estimand, observed data after temporary treatment interruption and
permanent treatment discontinuation due to COVID-19, administrative and any other
treatment unrelated reasons, and intake of prohibited medications and permanent treatment
discontinuation with initiation of alternative VMS treatment, were censored and imputed by
the MMRM model.



In the second supplementary estimand, observed data after temporary treatment interruption
and permanent treatment discontinuation due to COVID-19, administrative and any other
treatment unrelated reasons were censored and imputed by the MMRM model whereas
observed data after intake of prohibited medications and permanent treatment discontinuation
37

Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
with initiation of alternative VMS treatment were censored and imputed by baseline data
(considered as treatment failure).
Subgroup Analyses
In OASIS 1 and OASIS 2, subgroup analyses of the four coprimary efficacy endpoints were
performed by geographic region (North America and the rest of the world), age group (40 to 49,
50 to 59, and 60 to 65 years), BMI group (<18.5, ≥18.5 to <25, ≥25 to <30, and ≥30 kg/m2), race
(Black or African American, White, Asian, American Indian or Alaskan Native, and Multiple),
ethnicity (Hispanic or Latino and Not Hispanic or Latino), and smoking history (Current,
Former, and Never smokers). Analyses within each subgroup were performed similarly to the
primary analysis for the coprimary endpoints.
Given that OASIS 3 was a supportive study, subgroup analysis of the primary endpoint was not
conducted in this study.
6.2.4.3. Analysis of Key Secondary Endpoints, OASIS 1,
OASIS 2, and OASIS 3
Three key secondary endpoints in OASIS 1 and OASIS 2 were analyzed similarly to the primary
analysis for the coprimary efficacy endpoints. For PROMIS SD SF 8b, the MMRM model used
data from Weeks 1, 4, 8, and 12. For MENQOL, the MMRM model used data from Weeks 4, 8,
and 12 since Week 1 data were not collected for MENQOL. In the analysis of PROMIS SD SF
8b total T-score and MENQOL total score, score-level missing data were handled by multiple
imputation.
There was no prespecified key secondary endpoints in OASIS 3.

6.2.5.3. Results for Analyses, OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and OASIS 3
6.2.5.3.1. Coprimary Endpoints OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and
OASIS 3
Primary Analyses of Coprimary Endpoints
The coprimary efficacy endpoints were analyzed using MMRM model. Results are summarized
in Table 18 for the frequency and Table 19 for severity of HFs.
Reduction in the Frequency of VSMs at Weeks 4 and 12
The mean frequency of moderate to severe HFs per day were balanced at baseline in both studies
(Table 18). In OASIS 1, subjects in the elinzanetant and placebo groups experienced a mean of
13 and 14 episodes of moderate to severe HFs per day. In OASIS 2, subjects in the elinzanetant
and placebo groups had a mean of 15 and 16 episodes of moderate to severe HFs, respectively.
The data from both OASIS 1 and OASIS 2 showed that subjects in the elinzanetant group had a
statistically significant reduction from baseline in the frequency of moderate to severe HFs per
day at Weeks 4 and 12 compared to those in the placebo group (all p<0.0001). At Week 4,
subjects in the elinzanetant group reported an average reduction from baseline of 8 (OASIS 1) to
9 (OASIS 2) episodes in moderate to severe HFs per day compared to an average reduction of 4
(OASIS 1) to 6 (OASIS 2) reported by subjects in the placebo group. Similarly, at Week 12,
subjects in the elinzanetant group reported an average reduction from baseline of 9 (OASIS 1) to
10 (OASIS 2) episodes in moderate to severe HFs per day compared to an average reduction of 5
(OASIS 1) to 6 (OASIS 2) episodes reported by those in the placebo group.
In addition to the statistical significance, both studies met the Division’s criteria of a clinically
meaningful reduction in the frequency of moderate to severe HFs of at least 2 episodes per day
(or 14 per week) above that demonstrated with placebo at Week 4 and maintained through

Reference ID: 5682958

Figure 4 and Figure 5 below show the mean changes from baseline in the frequencies of
moderate to severe HFs episodes over time in OASIS 1 and OASIS 2, respectively.
In both studies, subjects who received elinzanetant 120 mg had greater reductions in the mean
frequency of moderate to severe HFs compared to those given placebo during the 12-week
placebo-controlled treatment period. The effect was noticed as early as Week 1. During the
Week 12 to Week 26 crossover period, continued reduction in VMS frequency in both treatment
arms was observed. Subjects who were initially randomized to placebo but switched to
elinzanetant 120 mg during this 14-week placebo crossover period reported pronounced
improvement, further providing efficacy evidence for elinzanetant 120 mg. Additionally, in both
OASIS 1 and OASIS 2, the mean changes in the frequency of moderate to severe HFs increased
in both arms during the 4-week follow-up post-treatment period (i.e., during Week 26 to
Week 30). By Week 26, subjects who were initially randomized to active study drug had
received elinzanetant 120 mg for the full 26 weeks, whereas those originally assigned to placebo
had taken elinzanetant 120 mg for 14 consecutive weeks. Upon discontinuation of treatment,
both groups exhibited a similar degree of symptom recurrence, which further affirm the

The percentages of subjects who achieved a certain level of reduction in the frequency and
severity of HFs at Weeks 4 and 12 were also assessed in both OASIS 1 and OASIS 2. Figure 88,
Figure 89, Figure 90, and Figure 91 in Section 16.3 display the cumulative percent of subjects
who achieved a certain level of reduction in the frequency and severity of HFs by treatment
group. As shown, in both studies, and at both Week 4 and Week 12 timepoints, the cumulative
distribution function curves of the two groups clearly separate, indicating that more elinzanetanttreated subjects than placebo-treated subjects achieved a given level of reduction in the
frequency and severity of HFs at these timepoints. For example, in OASIS 1, more elinzanetanttreated subjects than placebo-treated subjects reported a mean of at least five fewer episodes of
moderate to severe HFs daily at Week 4 (68% versus 40%) and at Week 12 (74% versus 50%),
respectively. Corresponding results were seen in elinzanetant subjects compared to placebo
subjects in OASIS 2 at Week 4 (68% versus 45%) and at Week 12 (77% versus 55%),
respectively. The findings related to reduction in the severity of moderate to severe HFs were
similar. More elinzanetant-treated subjects than placebo-treated subjects achieved at least 1-unit
reduction per day in severity score at both timepoints in both studies (26% versus 5% at Week 4
and 40% versus 16% at Week 12 in OASIS 1; 30% versus 13% at Week 4 and 44% versus 22%
at Week 12 in OASIS 2).
In summary, the primary analyses of the four coprimary endpoints in both OASIS 1 and
OASIS 2 studies have shown that subjects treated with elinzanetant 120 mg had a statistically
significant reduction in the frequency and severity of VMS from baseline at Week 4 and
Week 12.

6.2.5.3.2. Sensitivity Analysis of Coprimary Endpoints
OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and OASIS 3
Two sensitivity analyses (SA1 and SA2) described in Section 6.2.4.2 were conducted for the four
coprimary efficacy endpoints (Table 216 and Table 217 in Section 16.2). Both sensitivity
analyses results showed the robustness of the primary efficacy results under varying model
specification (SA1) and missing data assumption (SA2). See Section 16.2 for the results from the
sensitivity analyses.
To further evaluate the robustness of the primary analyses results for the four coprimary
endpoints, several supporting analyses under different estimand strategies (e.g., composite
strategy for ICE of intake of prohibited medications and permanent treatment discontinuation
with alternative VMS treatment), different model specifications, and data handling strategies
were conducted. The various supporting analyses provided the same conclusion except for minor
numerical differences. The consistent findings across these analyses reinforce the reliability of
the primary analysis results.
6.2.5.3.3. Subgroup Analysis of Coprimary Endpoints
OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and OASIS 3
In OASIS 1 and OASIS 2, subgroup analyses for the four coprimary endpoints were performed
based on geographic region, age group, race, ethnicity, BMI, and smoking status. These analyses
were consistent with the primary analyses, demonstrating that elinzanetant 120 mg treatment
resulted in greater reduction in VMS frequency and severity at both Weeks 4 and 12 compared to
placebo within each subgroup category.
The results of subgroup analyses are presented in Figure 92 through Figure 99 in Section 16.4.
6.2.5.3.4. Key Secondary Endpoints OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and
OASIS 3
Table 21, Table 22, and Table 23 below show the results of the three key secondary endpoints as
described in Section 6.2.4.3. As shown in Table 21, in both studies, the reductions in the mean
frequency of moderate to severe HFs from baseline to Week 1 were statistically significantly
higher in the elinzanetant group than in the placebo group (p<0.0001 in OASIS 1 and p=0.0013
in OASIS 2). Similarly, the reductions (improvement) from baseline to Week 12 in the PROMIS
SD SF 8b total T-scores (Table 22) and in MENQOL total scores (Table 23) in both OASIS 1
and OASIS 2 were statistically significantly greater in the elinzanetant 120 mg group than in the
placebo group (all p<0.01). Since there was no multiplicity adjustment plan for testing these
secondary endpoints, p-values are intended for descriptive use only.

6.3. Key Efficacy Review Issues
The review team did not identify any substantive review issues related to efficacy. Substantial
evidence of efficacy was established based on OASIS 1 and OASIS 2. See Section 6.2.5.3.1
above for additional discussion.

7. Safety (Risk and Risk Management)
7.1. Potential Risks or Safety Concerns Based on
Nonclinical Data
The Applicant completed a comprehensive nonclinical program with elinzanetant and its major
metabolites to inform safety considerations for the clinical use of elinzanetant. The program
included pivotal, good laboratory practice (GLP)-compliant general toxicology studies in rats
and monkeys, reproductive and developmental toxicology studies in rats and rabbits, in vitro and
in vivo genotoxicity studies, and carcinogenicity studies in rats and transgenic mice. The main
clinically relevant nonclinical safety signals include: (i) central nervous system (CNS)-related
signals, including tremors and convulsions, (ii) skeletal muscle degeneration, (iii) malignant
adenocarcinoma of the uterus, the combination of malignant and benign endometrial tumors and
squamous cell carcinoma of the uterus, and lymphomas of the hematolymphoid system,
(iv) phototoxic signals, (v) gastrointestinal (GI)-related signals, and (vi) reproductive and
developmental toxicity signals. The potential for hepatotoxicity with elinzanetant, based on the
integrated assessment of liver-related signals detected in the nonclinical studies and a
comparative quantitative structure-activity relationship analysis of elinzanetant and the NK3R
inhibitor fezolinetant, is discussed at the end of this section.
A brief overview of the nonclinical pharmacology and pharmacokinetic (PK) data on
elinzanetant is described below. This is followed by integrated summary sections of all pertinent
findings and studies that identified potential risks or safety concerns. Biological plausibility of
certain findings, for example the CNS-related findings, is included. However, the underlying
51
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
plausible mechanism could not be determined for all findings based on the known pharmacology
and pharmacodynamics of elinzanetant and its metabolites. Full reviews of all the studies are in
Section 13.2 and in the nonclinical review in DARRTS (DARRTS°ID:°5623053 2025).

7.1.1. Pharmacology
Elinzanetant is an NK1R/NK3R antagonist. Inhibition of NK1R/NK3R on KNDy neurons can
decrease neuronal activity involved in thermoregulation, which is thought to contribute to the
VMS associated with menopause.
Elinzanetant has ~10-fold higher affinity to NK1R compared to NK3R, with mean pKi values of
9.43 and 8.42 for NK1R and NK3R, respectively. Elinzanetant has three principal metabolites,
M27, M30/34, and M18/21, which also act as noncompetitive antagonists at NK1R and NK3R.
In vitro selectivity assays including a wide range of receptors, ions channels, transporters, and
enzymes to identify potential off-target effects of elinzanetant yielded only a few notable
findings. Elinzanetant and its three principal metabolites may have the potential to inhibit
estrogen and progesterone receptors (ER and PR, respectively). Radioligand binding and
functional assays with elinzanetant produced equivocal results. In Study R-13674, elinzanetant
had no effect on radioligand binding to ER and PR, and in Study R-14344, elinzanetant (up to
30μM) had no effect on the activity of recombinant human PR-B. However, in Study 14343,
elinzanetant inhibited radiolabeled estradiol and progesterone binding to recombinant human
ERβ and to recombinant human PR-B, respectively; the half maximal inhibitory concentrations
(IC50s) were 22.5μM and 0.64μM, respectively. The metabolites M27, M30/M34 (major
metabolite), and M18/21 inhibited radiolabeled progesterone binding to recombinant human PRB with IC50s of 1.34μM, 1.20μM, and 1.69μM, respectively.
Elinzanetant did not generate major safety signals in a complete battery of safety pharmacology
studies (cardiovascular, respiratory, and CNS). Elinzanetant inhibited the activity of hERG
channels with an IC50 of approximately 31μM that provides multiples of exposure of 14X and
4,820X, based on the maximum plasma concentration (Cmax) and Cmax, unbound at the maximal
recommended human dose, respectively. Elinzanetant metabolites M27, M30/34, and M18/21
had no effect on hERG channel activity. In a cardiovascular study in Cynomolgus monkeys at a
single oral dose of 60 mg/kg, there was an increase in heart rate (by ~15%) and a decrease in
body temperature (by ~0.6°C), which were both reversible. At the no-observed-adverse-effect
level (NOAEL) of 20 mg/kg, there is a safety margin of ~4X (based on the Cmax, unbound at the
maximal recommended human dose). There were no remarkable findings in respiratory function
and CNS assessments in Sprague-Dawley rats up to the highest single-dose tested (100 mg/kg),
with a safety margin of ~23X (based on the Cmax, unbound at the maximal recommended human
dose).

7.1.2. Pharmacokinetics
PK studies in rats, monkeys, and dogs demonstrated that elinzanetant is absorbed following oral
administration, with its oral bioavailability being moderate in male and female rats (77% and
47%, respectively), and low in monkeys and dogs (19%).

52
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
Autoradiographic studies revealed that, following the oral administration of radiolabeled
elinzanetant to different species, radioactivity distributed to major organs, including the liver and
pigmented tissues (e.g., the uveal tract and the retina). In typical PK studies, elinzanetant was
also found to cross the blood brain barrier. In pregnant rats, the organ distribution of elinzanetant
was similar to that in nonpregnant rats. In addition, elinzanetant crossed the placenta, and
elinzanetant and its metabolites were detected in different fetal organs, including the brain.
Collectively, these findings suggest that the brain, the liver, pigmented tissues, and the
developing fetus can be important targets for elinzanetant-related effects.
Plasma protein binding was high across all preclinical species tested (99.5 to 99.9%) and higher
in humans (>99.9%) for elinzanetant and its principal metabolites (M27, M30/34 and M18/21).
As such, whenever appropriate for the nonclinical safety assessments, the extent of protein
binding is included in the calculations of safety and exposure margins. The nonclinical safety
assessment further considers the finding that in animals, as in humans, elinzanetant is
metabolized primarily by oxidation at the methyl-phenyl moiety and the morpholine ring mainly
to metabolites M27, M30/34 (a major human metabolite), and M18/21.

7.1.3. Integrated Summary of Potential Safety
Concern Based on Nonclinical Findings
CNS-Related Safety Signals
Convulsions were noted in two nonclinical studies – a 2-year carcinogenicity study (Study
B003186) conducted in female Sprague-Dawley rats (Envigo [formerly Harlan], United States)
and a 13-week repeat-dose toxicity study (Study R-13628) conducted in male and female SD rats
(Envigo, Netherlands). Table 24 summarizes the CNS-related findings from these studies. The
substrain of SD rats from Envigo is referred to as Harlan Sprague-Dawley (SD:Hsd). The
sources of the SD:Hsd rats are noted here for context as the discrepant findings between the
different studies could potentially be linked to the substrain of rats and their origins.
The CNS-related findings from Studies B003186 and R-13628 are summarized in Table 24 and
elaborated in the subsequent paragraphs.

In the 13-week repeat-dose toxicity study, male SD:Hsd rats (Netherlands) were treated with the
doses of 0, 25, 60, or 150 mg/kg (highest dose decreased to 87.5 after Day 9), BID (twice daily),
and female SD:Hsd rats (Netherlands) were treated with the dose of 0, 10, 25, or 50 mg/kg, BID.
Treatments were delivered by oral gavage for 13 weeks. Muscle spasms (lasting up to 3 minutes)
and tremors were noted around Day 24 after start of treatment and were followed by convulsions
(starting around treatment Day 34) in 2 out 16 females at 20 mg/kg/day, 3 out of 16 females at
50 mg/kg/day, and 3 out of 21 females at 100 mg/kg/day. Likewise, 1 out of 16 males in the
groups that received the low and mid doses (50 and 120 mg/kg/day, respectively) had tremors,
whole-body rigidity, spasm (lasting up to 1 to 3 minutes), stiff tail, and involuntary muscle
contractions (convulsions). Male rats treated with the highest tested dose (300/175 mg/kg/day)
died prematurely after presenting with reduced activity, hunched posture, abnormal gait,
piloerection, and prostration.
In the 2-year carcinogenicity study, female SD:Hsd rats (United States) were treated with the
oral doses of 0, 3.5, 10, 30, or 40 mg/kg, BID, for total doses of 0, 7, 20, 60, or 80 mg/kg/day,
over the course of 104 weeks. At doses ≥7 mg/kg/day, there was an increased incidence of
irregular respiration. At doses ≥60 mg/kg/day, there was an increased incidence of reduced
general activity, increased sensitivity to touch, vocalization, hunched posture, and convulsions
(Table 25). At doses ≥60 mg/kg/day, prodromal signs of convulsions (e.g., increased sensitivity
to touch and decreased activity) generally preceded detection of convulsions, which were first
noted around Days 162 and 106 after start of treatment with the doses of 60 mg/kg/day and
80 mg/kg/day, respectively.

Convulsions were not reported in another 13-week repeat-dose toxicity study (Study R-13596)
and a 26-week repeat-dose toxicity study (Study R-13894) conducted with male and female SD
rats. In the 13-week Study R-13596, SD rats were from Charles River (Canada) and were treated
with the oral doses of 0, 5, 25, or 100 mg/kg, once daily. The substrain of SD rats from Charles
River is referred to as SD:Crl. In the 26-week study, SD:Hsd rats were from Envigo (United
56
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
Kingdom); in this study, female rats were treated with the oral dose of 0, 10, 25, or 40 mg/kg,
BID, and male rats were treated with the oral dose of 0, 25, 60, or 90 mg/kg, BID. In both
studies, the treatments were delivered by oral gavage. As further discussed in Section 13, the
absence of convulsions in these studies could not be explained by insufficient systemic exposure
of the animals to elinzanetant.
It is unclear why convulsions were inconsistently observed across the different studies. It is
possible that the differential seizure susceptibility of different SD rat substrains (SD:Crl versus
SD:Hsd) and of SD:Hsd rats from different sources (United Kingdom, Netherlands, and the
United States) could have accounted for, or contributed to, the discrepant findings from the
toxicity studies in SD rats treated with elinzanetant. According to a study published by Langer
and collaborators, SD:Crl rats are less susceptible than SD:Hsd rats to developing seizures in
response to electrical stimulation of the basolateral amygdala (BLA). In addition, SD:Hsd rats
from the Netherlands are less susceptible than SD:Hsd rats from Germany to developing seizures
in response to BLA electrical stimulation (Langer et al. 2011).
Biological Plausibility of Elinzanetant-Induced Seizures in Rats
Considering the current knowledge that NK1R/NK3R activation increases neuronal excitability
(Stacey et al. 2002; Gallopin et al. 2006), it is unlikely that elinzanetant-induced inhibition of
NK1R/NK3R would lead to the development of convulsions.
The Applicant has reported that, at 10μM, the elinzanetant metabolite BAY 3462933 (M30/34)
inhibits by ~55% [3H]tert-butylbicycloorthobenzoate ([3H]TBOB) binding to gamma-amino
butyric acid type A (GABAA) receptors in Wistar rat brain membrane preparations (Study R14018). GABAA receptor antagonists (e.g., picrotoxin and bicuculline) are well known for their
proconvulsant effects (Sigel and Steinmann 2012). Considering that, in female rats treated with
the elinzanetant dose of 60 mg/kg/day, Cmax and AUC(0-24) of BAY 3462933 (M30/34) were
2.09μM and 46.8μM•h, respectively, on treatment Day 358, BAY 3462933 (M30/34)-induced
inhibition of GABAA receptors may contribute to the proconvulsant effects of elinzanetant in
rats.
Additionally, BAY 3462933 (M30/34) inhibits [3H]progesterone binding to PR-B with an
inhibition constant of 0.96μM. Two other metabolites of elinzanetant – BAY 3462932 (M27)
and BAY 346934 (M18/21) – also inhibit PR-B with Kis of 1.08μM and 1.35μM, respectively.
According to binding studies, interactions of elinzanetant with PR-B are equivocal (see
Secondary Pharmacology above). However, in one study, elinzanetant inhibited binding of
[3H]progesterone to PR-B ectopically expressed in insect Sf9 cells with an IC50 of 0.64μM. PR-B
inhibition by the elinzanetant metabolites (and, possibly, elinzanetant itself) may contribute to
the proconvulsant properties of elinzanetant because PR antagonists and null mutations of the
genes that encode PR-A and PR-B reportedly suppress the anticonvulsant effects of progesterone
(Lonsdale et al. 2006; Shiono et al. 2021).

Summary and Conclusion
Based on the totality of evidence, the CNS-related findings in the rat were determined to be
related to elinzanetant treatment. The mechanism of the CNS-related findings in elinzanetanttreated rats has not been determined; however, as discussed above, PR-B inhibition by the
elinzanetant metabolites (and, possibly, elinzanetant itself) and GABAA receptor inhibition by
the metabolite BAY 3462933 could contribute to the convulsions observed in elinzanetanttreated rats. These finding were discussed with internal neurotoxicology experts, and it was
determined that additional nonclinical studies were not needed at the time of this review to better
define safety margins for this safety signal. For details refer to nonclinical review in DARRTS
(DARRTS°ID:°5623053 2025).
Skeletal Muscle Degeneration
In the 13-week repeat-dose toxicity study (Study R-13628 [RH17GJ]) conducted in SD:Hsd rats
(Envigo, Netherlands), male rats (11/11) and female rats (3/10) that died prematurely following
treatment with the highest test doses of elinzanetant (300 mg/kg/day and 100 mg/kg/day,
respectively) presented with moderate to severe degeneration and necrosis of the skeletal
muscles in the leg, tongue, and/or larynx (Table 26). Muscle degeneration/necrosis was not noted
in elinzanetant-treated rats that presented with convulsions.

Skeletal muscle degeneration/necrosis correlated with increased transaminases, lactate

histopathological findings. As a note, rats with the skeletal muscle degeneration findings were
different from the rats that had CNS-related findings (as described above).
The finding of skeletal muscle degeneration was not observed in other repeat-dose toxicity
studies conducted in rats and other animal species. In addition, the finding was not reproduced in
a separate study that the Applicant designed and conducted specifically to investigate the
mechanistic basis of the finding.

Summary and Conclusion
Biological plausibility of elinzanetant to cause skeletal muscle degeneration/necrosis is unclear.
A mechanistic study that was conducted in male rats (Study R-13644) to mimic the effects
recorded in the 13-week repeat-dose toxicity study (Study R-13628 [RH17GJ]) failed to
reproduce the severe skeletal muscle degeneration. The most conservative multiple of exposure
for this finding derived from the 13-week repeat-dose study at 100 mg/kg/day in female rats is
16X the human therapeutic exposure on an area under the concentration-time curve (AUC) basis.
The clinical relevance of this skeletal muscle finding is unknown.
Genotoxicity and Carcinogenicity
In vitro and in vivo genotoxicity studies with elinzanetant and its three main metabolites (M27,
M30/34, and M18/21) showed negative results.
There were no neoplastic findings in the 26-week transgenic mice study (Study B003184).
Positive carcinogenicity findings were present in the 2-year rat study (Study B003186). Female
rats were treated orally with elinzanetant doses ranging from 7 to 80 mg/kg/day compared to
vehicle for 104 weeks. Elinzanetant dose dependently reduced body weight gain (body weights
were 9%, 9%,17%, and 19% lower at 7, 20, 60, 80 mg/kg/day, respectively, compared to control
at terminal sacrifice), but had no effect on overall survival. Elinzanetant treatment resulted in
neoplastic findings in the uterus and the hematolymphoid system as described in Table 27 below
along with safety margins based on clinical exposure.
There were no neoplastic findings in the 26-week transgenic mice study (Study B003184).
