Biological Plausibility of Elinzanetant-Induced Endometrial Carcinomas in Rats
The main metabolites of elinzanetant – BAY 3462932 (M27), BAY 3462933 (M30/34), and
BAY 346934 (M18/21) – inhibit [3H]progesterone binding to PR-B with Kis of 1.08μM,
0.96μM, and 1.35μM, respectively. Considering that Cmax and AUC(0-24) of BAY 3462933
(M30/34) were 2.09μM and 46.8μM•h, respectively, in female rats treated with the elinzanetant
dose of 60 mg/kg/day, it is possible that inhibition of PR-B by BAY 3462933 (M30/34)
contributes to the increased incidence of endometrial cancers in rats treated with elinzanetant
doses ≥60 mg/kg/day.
As mentioned in the subsections “Secondary Pharmacology” and “CNS-related signals” above,
elinzanetant produced equivocal signals in binding studies assessing its interactions with PRs. In
one study, elinzanetant inhibited [3H]progesterone binding to PR-B in a concentration dependent
manner, with an IC50 of ~0.64μM. It is, therefore, plausible that inhibition of PR-B by the parent
drug may also contribute to the increased incidence of endometrial cancers in elinzanetanttreated rats.
The primary mechanism of action of elinzanetant as an NK1R/NK3R antagonist may also be an
important factor contributing to its carcinogenic potential, particularly if treatment spans ages
when sex hormones are regularly cycling as it did in the 2-year carcinogenicity in female rats. In
this study, twice daily treatment of female rats with elinzanetant started at adolescence (~2
months of age) and continued through adulthood and reproductive senescence.
NK1R/NK3R inhibition in the hypothalamus can reduce the activity of KNDy neurons, which, in
turn, can reduce activity of GnRH-releasing neurons and, thereby, contribute to suppression of
the activity of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis. Findings consistent with
suppression of the HPG axis were reported in healthy premenopausal women treated with
elinzanetant in a randomized, single-blinded, placebo-controlled clinical study (Pawsey et al.
2021). According to this clinical study, oral treatment of premenopausal women with
elinzanetant (40, 80, or 120 mg) dose dependently reduced serum levels of luteinizing hormone
and induced a hormonal imbalance with relative estrogen dominance. While levels of estradiol
were reduced by the elinzanetant treatment, they remained within the therapeutic window of 30
60
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
to 50 pg/mL thought to be important to minimize vasomotor symptoms and bone loss. However,
levels of progesterone were sufficiently reduced to increase the duration of the luteal phase of the
cycle and prolong bleeding during the menstrual cycle (Pawsey et al. 2021).
Considering the findings of the clinical study by Pawsey et al., it is plausible that, in the 2-year
carcinogenicity study, the life-long elinzanetant treatment covering ages when sex hormones
were regularly cycling in the female rats caused a hormonal imbalance with relative estrogen
dominance. This could, in turn, have contributed to a reduction of the potential protective effect
of progesterone against development of endometrial adenocarcinomas in the rats.
Summary and Conclusion
In the 2-year carcinogenicity study in female rats, the highest noncarcinogenic dose of
elinzanetant was 20 mg/kg/day (7.5X the human therapeutic exposure on an AUC basis) and the
lowest dose found to be carcinogenic was 60 mg/kg/day (~29X the human therapeutic exposure
on an AUC basis). The neoplastic findings were observed in the uterus and the hematolymphoid
system of the female rat.
Phototoxicity
Elinzanetant has several characteristics that, per the FDA guidance for industry S10 Photosafety
Evaluation of Pharmaceuticals (January 2015), make it a potential phototoxicant. The following
nonclinical studies are documented in the nonclinical review in DARRTS
(DARRTS°ID:°5623053 2025) and in Section 13.2 of this review.


Elinzanetant absorbs photons in the UV spectrum (290 to 700 nm).
- One peak was detected at 321.4 nm with a calculated molar extinction coefficient of
3762.3 L•mol-1, which exceeds the threshold of 1000 L•mol-1 for phototoxicity (Study R13578).



Elinzanetant distributes to and accumulates in melanin-rich tissues (Study R-13624; Study R14368).



Elinzanetant is cytotoxic in the in vitro Balb/c 3T3 neutral red uptake phototoxicity assay,
with an IC50 of 0.845 µg/mL in presence of UV-A (Study R-13578).

Summary and Conclusion
Based on the in vitro phototoxicity assay, the most conservative multiple of exposure (MOE) for
phototoxicity was approximately 7-fold. The MOE should be interpreted with caution because
elinzanetant concentrations in human pigmented tissues are derived based on the distribution of
elinzanetant to rat pigmented tissues (eyes and skin) and no additional in vivo animal
photosensitivity studies have been conducted.
GI-Related Signals
GI-related signals were noted with elinzanetant treatment in repeat-dose toxicity studies in rats
and monkeys.

61
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
In rats treated orally with elinzanetant for 7 days (Study R-13586), histopathological findings of
mucosa degeneration along with regeneration of the gastric mucosa, isthmus regenerative
hypertrophy, and/or hyperplasia of the isthmus epithelium were observed at 300 mg/kg/day in
both male and female rats. Minimal multifocal degeneration/regeneration was also noted at
100 mg/kg/day in female rats. In a 13-week repeat-dose toxicity study with 4-week recovery
(Study R-13628), rats with decreased food consumption died prematurely (three males at
300 mg/kg/day and two females at 100 mg/kg/day) and had alterations in the large intestine
consisting of distended colon or cecum and/or hard content in the colon.
In monkeys, GI-related adverse effects consisted of findings of loose feces, decrease food
consumption, and excessive salivation starting at 60 mg/kg/day (10-fold the human therapeutic
exposure on an AUC basis) in a 7-day oral repeat dose study (Study R-13627). Ulceration in the
pyloric region of the stomach was seen in females at 100 mg/kg/day (2.4-fold the human
therapeutic exposure on an AUC basis). In a 4-week oral repeat-dose toxicity study (Study R13639), 2 monkeys (one male and one female) that were prematurely sacrificed treated with
60 mg/kg/day (4-fold the human therapeutic exposure on an AUC basis) had abnormal fecal
consistency (loose/watery) and reduction in food intake along with histopathological findings of
hemorrhage in the adventitia and in mucosa of multiple regions in the GI tract.
Similar findings were noted in the 13-week studies (Study R-13629 and Study R-13612) and the
39-week study (Study R-13895), with abnormal feces (liquid/soft) and/or diarrhea observed in
many animals across all dose groups (highest dose tested was 80 mg/kg/day) at various points
throughout the study. In the 13-week study, monkeys treated with once daily oral elinzanetant
doses ≥20 mg/kg/day (≥0.5-fold the human therapeutic exposure on an AUC basis) presented
with increased incidence of thin appearance and dehydration; these findings are indicative of GI
disturbances. In the 13-week study, monkeys treated with twice daily oral elinzanetant doses
≥30 mg/kg/day (≥0.2-fold the human therapeutic exposure on an AUC basis) presented with
diarrhea and doses ≥80 mg/kg/day (≥2.3-fold the human therapeutic exposure on an AUC basis)
presented with thin appearance. In the 39-week study, two female monkeys treated twice daily
with oral doses ≥60 mg/kg/day (2-fold the human therapeutic exposure on an AUC basis) and
male monkeys treated twice daily oral administration at ≥30 mg/kg/day (0.7-fold the human
therapeutic exposure on an AUC basis) had diarrhea that led to dehydration, weight loss, and
general ill-health.
Summary and Conclusion
The multiples of exposure for the GI effects in monkey is low, with observed findings starting at
the oral elinzanetant doses equivalent to 0.2-fold the human therapeutic exposure at the
maximum recommended human dose (MRHD).
Reproductive and Developmental Toxicity
In reproductive and developmental toxicity studies, elinzanetant administration prior to or during
pregnancy caused fetal harm in rats in the form of pre- and postimplantation loss, reduced litter
size or total litter loss, decrease in fetal body weight, and decrease in neonatal pup viability. A
summary of relevant findings is provided below; for additional details refer to Section 8.4 and
Section 13 of this review. In a fertility and early embryonic development study in rats, there was
62
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
an increase in the percentage of pre- and postimplantation embryo loss and decrease in fetal body
weights at 14-fold the human therapeutic exposure when rat dams were treated orally prior to
mating and through the early embryonic period.
In a pre- and postnatal developmental study in rats, a higher incidence of still born pups, an
increase in total litter loss, a decrease in pup viability between postnatal Days 0 and 4, and an
increase in the number of neonatal pups without milk in the stomach were observed in the midand high-dose groups, with maternal systemic exposures that were within the range of human
therapeutic exposure. Decreased maternal care was also a clinical observation in these treatment
groups. Whether the neonatal effects were due to decreased maternal care or other potential
elinzanetant-related effects on the offspring could not be definitively concluded from this study.
In an embryofetal development study in rabbits, maternal toxicity was noted in the form of
marked body weight loss and decreased food consumption at systemic exposures that were
within the range of human therapeutic exposure.
No teratogenicity was observed in the reproductive and developmental studies with elinzanetant
in rats or rabbits.
Biological Plausibility of Pregnancy Loss and Stillbirths in Elinzanetant-Treated Rats
The pregnancy losses and stillbirths noted in rats exposed to elinzanetant during gestation may
be related, at least in part, to NK1R/NK3R inhibition. As discussed in an earlier section,
NK1R/NK3R inhibition can reduce the activity of GnRH-releasing neurons in the hypothalamus
and, consequently, suppress the HPG axis. It is plausible that suppression of the HPG axis leads
to an imbalance of the sex hormones needed to sustain pregnancy. In fact, drugs that act as
GnRH receptor inhibitors (e.g., relugolix) are known to cause pregnancy loss and stillbirth in rats
(Sumitomo°Pharma 2021).
Summary and Conclusion
Based on findings from animal reproduction studies, elinzanetant may cause pregnancy loss or
stillbirth when administered during pregnancy. Fetal malformations were not observed in these
animal studies.
Potential for Liver Toxicity
In the pivotal chronic toxicity studies conducted by the Applicant, including a 26-week study in
SD rats (Study R-13894) and a 39-week study in monkeys (Study R-13895), elinzanetant
increased levels of the liver-associated enzymes ALT, AST, and ALP. Specifically, in male rats
treated orally with the dose of 180 mg/kg/day (90 mg/kg, BID), ALT increased by ~2 fold, and
in female rats treated orally with ≥50 mg/kg/day (≥25 mg/kg, BID), AST increased by ~2 fold. In
male and female monkeys treated orally with the dose of 40 and 30 mg/kg, BID, respectively,
ALT increased by ~1.8 fold (male monkeys) to ~3.6 fold (female monkeys). In these studies, the
increased enzyme activity was not associated with histopathological findings that are typically
indicative of adverse liver tissue damage.

63
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
Liver damage was reported in nonpivotal short-term studies in rats and monkeys. Specifically,
following a 7-day oral treatment with elinzanetant tosylate doses of 100 and 300 mg/kg/day, SD
rats presented with hepatocellular necrosis and lobular hepatocellular hypertrophy
(Study 13586). In addition, following a 4-day oral treatment with the elinzanetant dose of
300 mg/kg/day, monkeys (n=2; one male and one female) presented with hepatocellular
vacuolation and/or single-cell necrosis (Study 13580).
The discrepancy in the liver-associated histopathology findings between the chronic and shortterm studies is unclear. However, upregulation of certain cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes is
thought to contribute to drug-induced liver injury (Jaeschke et al. 2002) and the Applicant
reports that elinzanetant and its metabolites can cause concentration-dependent CYP induction.
Thus, the initial injury that develops following short-term treatment with elinzanetant could
result at least in part from upregulation of CYPs and could be subsequently resolved by
adaptative responses. In this context, hepatic adaptation to an initial drug-induced liver injury has
been reported with other drugs (Eakins et al. 2015).
Following a consult request from the OND/Drug-Induced Liver Injury (DILI) Team, the Center
for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER) Computational Toxicology Consultation Service
(CTCS) team conducted a quantitative structure-activity relationship [(Q)SAR] analysis to assess
whether the chemical structure of elinzanetant has structural features that could predict its
hepatotoxic potential. The team concluded that, based on their (Q)SAR analysis, elinzanetant is
predicted to be equivocal for the endpoints of liver damage and cholestasis, negative for liver
enzyme abnormalities, and positive for bile duct disorders and gall bladder disorders. Refer to
nonclinical review in DARRTS for details and internal memo from the CTCS team appended in
the review (DARRTS°ID:°5623053 2025).
Hypothetical Hepatotoxicity Predictions for Elinzanetant Considering Findings From
Fezolinetant
Fezolinetant is an NK3R antagonist approved under the brand name Veozah (NDA 216578;
approval date: May 12, 2023) for the treatment of moderate to severe VMS due to menopause
(see Section 7.2 below). In the preapproval clinical study database, elevations of hepatic
enzymes were seen but there were no cases meeting Hy’s law criteria or with elevated bilirubin
levels. The approved fezolinetant labeling thus included a warning for its potential to elevate
liver enzymes, and FDA recommended monitoring and follow-up of hepatic function and injury
in patients taking fezolinetant. After receiving postmarketing reports of serious hepatotoxicity in
patients taking fezolinetant, FDA revised labeling in 2024 to add a Boxed Warning for serious
hepatotoxicity that occurred within 40 days of starting treatment and recommended monthly
testing of hepatic function for the first three months of treatment and additional follow up testing
at 6 and 9 months after initiation of treatment.
In February 2025, Nuthi et al. published an article reporting that a reactive carbene metabolite
could contribute to the hepatotoxicity of fezolinetant. The authors hypothesized that the high
electrophilicity of a carbene metabolite that can be generated from the fezolinetant metabolite
referred to as fezo-acid, as illustrated in Figure 9, is likely to favor the carbene reaction with thiol
groups in the liver to produce thiol adducts that can be hepatotoxic (Nuthi et al. 2025).

Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
Figure 9. Generation of the Fezo-Carbene Metabolite by Decarboxylation of the Fezolinetant
Metabolite Fezo-Acid

Source: Reviewer-generated figure based on Nuthi et al. (2025)
The red circles highlight the carboxylic acid group in the fezo-acid structure and the neutral carbon atom with a valence of two and
two unshared valence electrons in the fezo-carbene structure.

The Nonclinical Team consulted with the CTCS team to determine if the mechanism
hypothesized in this paper could help further inform the (Q)SAR assessment to predict the
hepatotoxic potential for elinzanetant and its metabolites. The CTCS team’s overall conclusion
indicated that elinzanetant is unlikely to be converted into a carbene metabolite and is not
predicted to have a hepatotoxic potential comparable to that of fezolinetant. The following is a
summary of the CTCS assessment:


The elinzanetant acid metabolite M10 could hypothetically undergo decarboxylation to form
a carbene metabolite (Figure 10). However, per Nuthi et al. (2025), in part due to
stabilization of charges by resonance, decarboxylation would be more likely for
heteroaromatic rings (as the thiadiazole ring that has the -COOH group in fezo-acid) than for
a benzene ring (as the ring that has the -COOH group in the elinzanetant metabolite M10).
Without empirical evidence, it is difficult to predict whether decarboxylation of the benzene
group in the M10 metabolite can happen in vivo.

Figure 10. Hypothetical Carbene Metabolite Generated by Decarboxylation of the Elinzanetant
Metabolite M10

Source: Reviewer-generated figure
The red circles highlight the carboxylic acid group in the elinzanetant M10 metabolite and the neutral carbon atom with a valence of
two and two unshared valence electrons in the hypothetical carbene metabolite.



Both elinzanetant and fezolinetant have bi-aryl structural alerts (Figure 11). However, in part
because the dissimilar aromatic ring types between the two compounds cause the alerts to be
weighed differently for each molecule, the (Q)SAR models predict elinzanetant to be
negative and fezolinetant to be positive for liver enzyme abnormalities.



The presence of a methyl substituent (that could undergo enzymatic oxidative hydrolysis) in
the bi-aryl alert is not a requirement for a bi-aryl substructure to be identified as an alert by

65

Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
the hepatotox (Q)SAR models. Thus, the possibility of carbene generation is not a
requirement for bi-aryl substructures to be identified as structural alerts for hepatotoxicity.
Figure 11. (Q)SAR-Identified Structural Alerts in Fezolinetant and Elinzanetant

Source: figure modified by reviewer from the CTCS consult report issued on December 19, 2024
The blue circles highlight the bi-aryl substructures in the structural alerts (substructures in red font) in fezolinetant and elinzanetant.
The stars mark the methyl groups that could undergo enzymatic oxidative hydrolysis to carboxylic acids.
Abbreviation: (Q)SAR, quantitative structure-activity relationship



Additional (Q)SAR analysis on M10 or any other metabolites is unlikely to yield additional
useful information because the liver tox model training sets are largely populated with drug
substances with information from postmarket reporting and do not include many metabolites
or impurities.

Summary and Conclusion
There were no histopathological findings indicating hepatotoxicity in the pivotal, long-term
repeat-dose toxicity studies in rats and monkeys. The findings of hepatocellular necrosis and
lobular hepatocellular hypertrophy, hepatocellular vacuolation, and/or single-cell necrosis seen
in short-term toxicity studies at high doses have multiples of exposure of 21X (average of males
and females) in rats, 13X in male monkeys, and 2.7X in female monkeys as compared to the
human therapeutic exposure on an AUC basis. Considering the comparative (Q)SAR analysis by
the CTCS team, the likelihood of generation of a reactive carbene metabolite that can form
hepatotoxic thiol adducts is low for elinzanetant compared to fezolinetant due to their dissimilar
structures. Therefore, from the nonclinical perspective, the potential for hepatotoxicity with the
maximal recommended human dose of elinzanetant appears lower than with fezolinetant.

7.2. Potential Risks or Safety Concerns Based on
Drug Class or Other Drug-Specific Factors
Elinzanetant is a combined NK3/NK1 receptor antagonist. To date, there are no FDA-approved
products with a combined NK3/NK1 receptor antagonism profile. Fezolinetant (Veozah,
NDA 216578), an NK3 receptor antagonist only, is approved for the treatment of moderate to
severe VMS due to menopause and is known to cause rare but serious hepatotoxicity with a
relatively short latency period (within 2 months).
FDA has approved several NK1 related products, e.g., substance P/NK1 receptor antagonists, for
the prevention of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, including aprepitant (proprietary
name Emend, NDAs 021549 and 207865), fosaprepitant, Focinvez, and rolapitant (proprietary
name Varubi, NDS 206500). Additionally, netupitant/palonosetron (proprietary name Akynzeo,
NDA 205718) combines netupitant, a substance P/NK1 receptor antagonist and palonosetron, a
66
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
5-HT3 receptor antagonist, for the same indication. Safety issues noted in the labeling for these
drugs include drug-drug interactions arising from the inhibition of CYP3A4/CYP2D6, reduced
International Normalized Ratio or prothrombin time when coadministered with warfarin, and
reduced efficacy of hormonal contraceptives. For aprepitant, labeling recommends exercising
caution when administered in patients with severe hepatic impairment. Because these NK1
receptor antagonists are approved for use in cancer patients who are taking chemotherapy, not all
the safety concerns identified with these products may be relevant to the target population for
elinzanetant due to different risk-benefit considerations.
Of note, due to concerning findings from nonclinical reproductive toxicity studies (see
Section 7.1), use of elinzanetant is contraindicated in pregnancy and effective contraception is
recommended in perimenopausal women who may want to take elinzanetant to treat their VMS.
Hormonal contraceptives are metabolized by CYP enzymes. Because elinzanetant does not have
induction potential for any CYP enzymes, reduced efficacy of hormonal contraceptives is not
expected to be an issue in the indicated population.

7.3. Potential Risks or Safety Concerns Identified
Through Postmarket Experience
Not applicable. During this review, elinzanetant was approved for marketing in several countries,
including the United Kingdom and Canada. Given the recent approval, there is no postmarket
experience to report.

7.4. FDA Approach to the Safety Review
Section 3.2 provides a description and assessment of the clinical studies and whether the studies
submitted were fit for purpose.
The Phase 3 studies OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and OASIS 3 provide primary support for safety of
elinzanetant for the treatment of moderate to severe VMS due to menopause. Subjects taking
elinzanetant 120 mg/day in the SWITCH-1 study (a dose-finding Phase 2 study) also provided 12
weeks of safety information.
The safety data reviewed includes the final study reports submitted by the Applicant for each
OASIS study and their corresponding datasets (Study Data Tabulation Model and Analysis Data
Model), the 120-day safety update, the Applicant’s responses to information requests, and
literature references provided by the Applicant. The primary safety assessment examined adverse
events of special interest (AESIs), safety findings from each of the three OASIS studies and
overall safety profile from the pooled OASIS 1 and OASIS 2 using the Medical Dictionary for
Regulatory Activities (MedDRA) version 21.0. To assess severity, a 3-point grading scale was
used (mild, moderate, severe). The Applicant considered the following AEs to be of special
interest: events triggering close liver observation, somnolence or fatigue, phototoxicity, and
postmenopausal bleeding. Safety assessments included adverse events, including SAEs, AESIs,
AEs related to abuse potential, clinical safety laboratory assessments, including liver monitoring,
vital signs, and physical examinations (including weight, hip and waist circumference, and waist
to hip ratio). Additional assessments included mammograms, transvaginal ultrasound (TVU),
67
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
endometrial biopsy, sleepiness scale, suicidal ideation and behavior measured with eC-SSR, and
ECGs. Bone mineral density was measured in OASIS 3. In OASIS 1, 2, and 3, treatmentemergent adverse events (TEAEs) were defined as those that occurred or worsened on or after
the first dose of study drug up to 14 days after the last dose of study drug.
The clinical team reviewed the Applicant’s mapping of verbatim terms to MedDRA preferred
terms (PTs) for the events reported in the relevant clinical studies and found the Applicant’s
mapping strategy acceptable. The team also reviewed the definitions of TEAEs and AEs in the
relevant clinical studies and found them to be acceptable. The review team assessed the
narratives of all SAEs and discontinuations due to adverse events.
The clinical team identified the following key safety review issues: number of deaths, SAEs,
adverse events leading to discontinuation, TEAEs, and AESIs including abuse potential, bone
safety, hepatic safety, cardiac safety, nervous system disorders (including CNS depression
[somnolence/fatigue], vertigo/dizziness, syncope/presyncope/hypotension), fractures, driving
ability, breast safety, endometrial safety, seizures, and phototoxicity. The safety data will be
presented for the placebo-controlled Weeks 1 to 12 (OASIS 1 and 2) and 1 to 52 (OASIS 3). The
data from OASIS 1 and 2 is shown from the individual studies and from the pooled studies for
Weeks 1 to 12. It is reasonable to pool these studies as they have a very similar study design.
Data from OASIS 1 and 2 from Weeks 13 to 26 (when all subjects took elinzanetant) are not
presented in tables given limitations to these analyses as there is no control group during this
study period. The narratives of SAEs and discontinuations due to AEs were assessed for OASIS
1 and 2 from Weeks 13 to 26, when all subjects were on elinzanetant. The most robust long-term
safety data are from OASIS 3, which was placebo-controlled for 52 weeks. The Applicant also
provided an integrated analysis of safety, from studies 21686 (SWITCH-1), and OASIS 1, 2, and
3. The safety analysis set (SAF) was defined as all subjects who receive at least one dose of
study drug. Safety data, such as narratives from the entire clinical program, including the Phase 1
and 2 studies, are discussed as relevant to specific safety considerations, such as adverse events
of special interest.
When evaluating the individual results of OASIS studies, the rates of adverse events in placebo
versus treatment were compared with the number (percentage) of subjects who experienced an
AE along with the risk difference or the risk ratio (with 95% CI). The evaluation of pooled data
that includes variable duration of exposures to placebo and elinzanetant was carried out through
the exposure adjusted incidence rate for statistical analysis of adverse events, calculated diving
the number of subjects with event X by the total patient years. For OASIS 3, data are shown for
number (percentage) and exposure adjusted incidence rate.
The review team’s approach to the data presentation and analysis of the three clinical studies
consisted of review of the raw data presented by the Applicant in adsl.xpt and adae.xpt files, and
tabulation and statistical analysis of the raw data in collaboration with the FDA Clinical Data
Science Analysis Scientific Team. The Clinical Data Science Analysis Scientific Team
performed standard safety analyses including OND custom medical queries (OCMQs) to
determine safety signals, and additional analyses as requested by the clinical team.

The safety database was adequate for sufficient safety analysis of elinzanetant for the proposed

identify any major data quality or integrity issues that precluded performing a thorough safety
review. No major issues were identified with respect to coding of adverse events.

Demographic and Baseline Clinical Characteristics
The baseline demographic and clinical attributes of the safety population of clinical study
OASIS 3 are shown in Table 34. There were noted similarities in mean age of subjects, age
groups. race, ethnicity, and country of participation in the study and control groups (elinzanetant
and placebo). In OASIS 3, the treatment arms were well-balanced with regards to demographics
and other baseline characteristics, with no relevant differences in age, ethnicity, race, weight,
height, or BMI. Most women in the safety analysis set were White (77%) or Black or African
American (16.0%) and 11.2% of the women were Hispanic or Latino by ethnicity. The overall
mean (SD) age was 54.6 (4.6) years and 54.9 (5), for the elinzanetant and placebo groups
(respectively) and the overall mean (SD) BMI was 27.59 (4.68) kg/m2. The majority of women
never smoked. The most frequent medical history findings were obesity (28.5%), hypertension
(28.7%), and hysterectomy (22.5%).

Screening and Enrollment
Out of 1,524 screened subjects there were 896 screening failures, resulting in 628 randomized
subjects (Table 35). Subjects were randomized to elinzanetant 120 mg/d (n=313) or placebo
(n=315). The safety population consisted of 313 and 314 subjects in the elinzanetant and placebo
groups, respectively, with 453 individuals completing the study.

7.6.1.1. Overview of Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events
Summary, OASIS 1 and OASIS 2 (Weeks 1 to 12)
The total number and percentages of AEs for the safety population for OASIS 1 and OASIS 2,
and pooled data from OASIS 1 and OASIS 2, for Weeks 1 to 12 are presented in Table 37.

(0.8%) with SAEs. Similar trends were seen for AEs leading to discontinuation and AEs leading
to dose modification. The percentage of subjects with any AE was similar in the elinzanetant
(47.8%) and placebo (43.3%) arms. AEs were mainly mild or moderate.

7.6.1.3. Serious Adverse Events, OASIS 1 and 2 (Weeks 1 to
12)
Subjects with SAEs during Weeks 1 to 12 in OASIS 1 and OASIS 2 (and pooled data), are
shown in Table 38. In OASIS 1 and the pooled analyses, the percentage of subjects with SAEs
was slightly higher in the elinzanetant groups versus the placebo groups. In OASIS 2, the
percentage of subjects with SAEs was the same in the elinzanetant and placebo groups (0.5%).
The SAEs were spread over various system organ classes, without a clear pattern. Analyses by
OND custom medical query (OCMQ) (narrow) (Table 39) were similar to the analysis by PT and
did not reveal any other safety concerns.

The following subjects in the elinzanetant arm had SAEs during OASIS 1 and OASIS 2
(including the period after 12 weeks when subjects on placebo switched to elinzanetant (the
placebo-elinzanetant arm)). SAEs related to AEs of special interest (including seizure and
syncope) are also described in this section. Of the 20 subjects with SAEs, the seizure event was
probably related to elinzanetant. For the accident and syncope SAEs, it is unclear if they were
related to elinzanetant based on limited information or lack of other factors suggesting causality
(such as dechallenge/rechallenge information).
OASIS 1
There were 13 subjects with SAEs while taking elinzanetant:


4 subjects randomized to elinzanetant during Weeks 1 to 12 (diverticulitis, pulmonary
embolism and pneumonia (same subject), syncope, and arthrodesis)



9 subjects in the placebo-elinzanetant arm during Weeks 13 to 26 after switching to
elinzanetant (pyelonephritis, cholelithiasis (two subjects), otitis externa, bunion operation,
abdominal pain, accident, mammoplasty, and tibia fracture).

In addition, one subject had a post-treatment SAE of adenocarcinoma of the colon about 3 weeks
after the last dose of elinzanetant.
Descriptions of the SAEs are included below:
(b) (6) was a 46-year-old woman randomized to the placebo-elinzanetant
(1) Subject

investigator considered this event to be severe in intensity and not related to elinzanetant.
The subject was treated with antibiotics and recovered. The review team agrees with the
assessment that this SAE does not appear related to elinzanetant.
(b) (6) was a 55-year-old woman who was randomized to the placebo(2) Subject
elinzanetant arm. She developed an SAE of cholelithiasis 66 days after starting elinzanetant.
The investigator considered this event to be moderate in intensity and not related to study
intervention. The subject was hospitalized, drug was interrupted, and she recovered. The
review team agrees with the assessment that this SAE does not appear related to elinzanetant.

this SAE does appear related to elinzanetant.

OASIS 2
There were six subjects with SAEs while taking elinzanetant:


Two subjects randomized to elinzanetant (one DVT/PE during the first 12 weeks, and one



dose of elinzanetant.

related to elinzanetant. She received ketorolac and the last recorded outcome was

found to have been randomized by mistake and should have been a screen failure. The
subject’s value of TSH and free T4 were abnormal during the screening visit and met
exclusion criterion #6. The review team agrees with the assessment that the SAE does not
appear related to elinzanetant.
(b) (6) was a 46-year-old woman randomized to elinzanetant who
(6) Subject
developed an SAE of a urinary tract infection (which also led to discontinuation). The SAE
occurred 179 days after starting elinzanetant and was of severe intensity and deemed not
related to elinzanetant, which the review team agrees with. The subject discontinued due to
the AE.

LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
7.6.1.4. Adverse Events Leading to Discontinuation, OASIS 1
and OASIS 2 (Weeks 1 to 12)
Table 40 displays subjects with adverse events leading to treatment discontinuation by system
organ class and PT (Weeks 1 to 12). In the pooled data from OASIS 1 and OASIS 2,
discontinuations occurred in more subjects in the elinzanetant group [30 subjects (7.5%)]
compared to the placebo group [17 subjects (4.3%]).
For the OASIS 1 and OASIS 2 studies, the largest imbalance of AEs leading to discontinuation
was for fatigue. In the pooled analyses, a higher percentage of subjects in the elinzanetant group
(2%) compared to the placebo group (0%) discontinued due to fatigue. Refer to Section 7.6.3.6
for further discussion of fatigue as an AESI. AEs leading to discontinuation in the system organ
class (SOC) psychiatric disorders occurred in a higher percentage of the elinzanetant group
(1.2%) compared to the placebo group (0.5%). However, this imbalance did not appear to be
driven by any specific PTs and there was some overlap in similar PTs observed in the placebo
group and the elinzanetant group (such as depressed mood, dysphoria, depressive symptoms, and
depression). Given similarities in the PTs, the depression OCMQ (narrow) was evaluated (Table
41). In the pooled data, the elinzanetant and placebo groups had the same percentage of subjects
with depression OCMQ (narrow) (0.5%). This OCMQ was made up of the following PTs:
depressed mood (0.2% elinzanetant versus 0% placebo), dysphoria (0.2% elinzanetant versus 0%
placebo), depression (0% elinzanetant versus 0.3% placebo), and depressive symptom (0%
elinzanetant versus 0.3% placebo). There were no notable imbalances in AEs leading to
discontinuation between the elinzanetant group and the placebo group, other than fatigue in the
analyses by PT and OCMQ (narrow).

Table 42 displays common adverse events occurring at ≥2% frequency in the safety population,

looking at the individual studies with adverse events occurring in at least 2% of subjects (Table
43), the types and percentages of adverse events were similar. Analyses by OCMQ (narrow) did
not reveal any other safety considerations.

OCMQ Analyses
Additional OCMQ (narrow) analyses were performed for fatigue, headache, gastroesophageal
reflux disease, somnolence, and dizziness. See Section 7.6.3.6 for discussion of fatigue,
somnolence, and dizziness. Additional safety analyses for headache and gastroesophageal reflux
disease are provided below.
Headache
The headache OCMQ (narrow) was made up of the following PTs: headache, migraine, sinus
headache, and tension headache, all of which occurred in a higher percentage of subjects in the
elinzanetant group compared to the placebo group (Table 44). All the events were mild to
moderate severity and none were serious. In the elinzanetant group (pooled data), 1.8% of
subjects on elinzanetant compared to 1% of subjects on placebo discontinued due to headache.
Headache will be included in the United States Prescribing Information (USPI).

Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease
Gastroesophageal reflux was reported by a higher percentage of subjects in the pooled (OASIS 1
and OASIS 2) elinzanetant group (1.2%) compared to the placebo group (0.5%) (Table 45). All
the events were mild to moderate severity, except two were severe. None were serious. In the
elinzanetant group (pooled data), two subjects (0.5%) on elinzanetant compared to no subjects on
placebo discontinued due to gastroesophageal reflux.
Details of the two subjects who discontinued are included below:




(b) (6) discontinued 1 day after starting elinzanetant due to severe
Subject
gastroesophageal reflux disease. She had a history of gastroesophageal reflux disease, and the
event resolved after discontinuation. The investigator considered the adverse event related to
elinzanetant, and the review team agrees with this assessment, but notes the short latency
between starting elinzanetant and the AE.
(b) (6) discontinued 4 days after starting elinzanetant due to
Subject
gastroesophageal reflux disease that was moderate in intensity. The investigator considered
the adverse event related to elinzanetant, and the review team agrees with this assessment.

As described in Section 7.1.3, there were GI-related findings in the nonclinical studies. In rats
there were histopathological findings in rats of mucosa degeneration along with regeneration of
the gastric mucosa, isthmus regenerative hypertrophy, and hyperplasia of the isthmus epithelium.
In monkeys, there were histopathological findings of hemorrhage in the adventitia and in the
mucosa of multiple regions in the GI tract. See Section 7.6.2 for additional discussion of GIrelated adverse events in OASIS 3.
7.6.1.6. Laboratory Studies, OASIS 1 and OASIS 2 (Weeks 1
to 12)
In OASIS 1 and OASIS 2, no relevant trend was observed for any laboratory parameter based on
descriptive summary statistics. None of the hematology, general chemistry, coagulation,
hormone, vitamin, and urinalysis parameters displayed substantial changes over time and no
differences between treatment arms were observed (see clinical study report [CSR] PH 42782,
Section 8.3.5 and CSR PH 42784, Section 8.3.5). There was a slight increase of sex hormonebinding globulin in the elinzanetant group compared to the placebo group. As noted in
Section 7.1.3, there was skeletal muscle degeneration noted in the nonclinical studies, but no
elevations in creatine kinase were noted in OASIS 1 or OASIS 2. See Table 46 for selected
analytes. See Section 7.6.3.3 for discussion of laboratory studies associated with hepatic safety.

7.6.1.7. Vital Signs, OASIS 1 and OASIS 2 (Weeks 1 to 12)
There were no clinically meaningful changes in vital sign measurements during OASIS 1 and
OASIS 2. Median and interquartile range of systolic blood pressure, diastolic blood pressure, and
pulse, over time by treatment arm depicted no differences for any parameters over the study.
There were no differences between the elinzanetant and placebo groups regarding percentage of
subjects with maximum systolic blood pressure, maximum diastolic blood pressure, or
hypotension levels. Figure 13 and Figure 14 show heart rate findings according to treatment arm
through the duration of treatment for OASIS 1 and OASIS 2, respectively. Similar findings were
seen for diastolic blood pressure (Figure 15 and Figure 16) and systolic blood pressure (Figure
17 and Figure 18). See Section 7.6.3.6 for additional discussion of hypotension and syncope.

7.6.2. Safety Results, OASIS 3
7.6.2.1. Overview of Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events
Summary, OASIS 3
An overview of adverse events in OASIS 3 is shown in Table 48. The percentage of subjects
with SAEs was higher in the elinzanetant group (4.2%) compared to the placebo group (1.9%).
The overall number of SAEs was relatively low, and none of the events were assessed as related
to the study drug by the investigator. There were no reported deaths. The percentage of AEs
leading to permanent discontinuation was higher in the elinzanetant group (12.5%) compared to
the placebo group (4.1%).
The percentage of any AE was higher in the elinzanetant group (70%) compared to the placebo
group (61.1%). In the elinzanetant group, 62.6% of these events were mild or moderate,
compared to 54% in the placebo group.
No new trends were found when evaluating the data by exposure adjusted incidence rates (Table
48).

7.6.2.3. Serious Adverse Events, OASIS 3
Serious adverse events were analyzed by system organ class and PT (Table 49). The percentage
of subjects with SAEs was higher in the elinzanetant group (4.2%) versus the placebo group
(1.9%). The overall number of SAEs was relatively low, and none of the events were assessed as
related to the study drug by the investigator. All events were reported as single PTs and
distributed over several system organ classes without a pattern. Similar trends were seen
evaluating the data by exposure adjusted incidence rates.

SAEs, it was difficult to assign causality of two of them (syncope and peripheral vertigo);
however, there are factors that suggest these SAEs were not secondary to elinzanetant. These
SAEs of special interest are also discussed in Section 7.6.3.6 and Section 7.7.5.
(b) (6) had an SAE of blood glucose increase of severe intensity that
(1) Subject

participation in the study. The review team agrees with the investigator that the SAE does not
appear to be related to elinzanetant.
(b) (6) was a 57-year-old woman who was an unrestrained driver in a car
(2) Subject

combined with acetaminophen), and gabapentin, all of which could be associated with CNS

7.6.2.4. Adverse Events Leading to Discontinuation, OASIS 3
The percentage of subjects with AEs leading to permanent study discontinuation was higher in
the elinzanetant group (12.5%) compared to the placebo group (4.1%) (risk difference 8.3%, CI:
4.1, 12.8).
Notable imbalances included:
(1) Gastrointestinal disorders SOC occurred in a higher percentage of subjects in the elinzanetant
group (2.9%) compared to placebo (1.6%). A variety of PTs occurred at a higher percentage
in the elinzanetant group, including abdominal pain upper, gastroesophageal reflux disease,
abdominal pain, abdominal pain lower, and diarrhea.
(2) General disorders SOC occurred in a higher percentage of subjects in the elinzanetant group
(1.6%) compared to placebo (0%) based on an imbalance in fatigue.
(3) Nervous system disorders SOC (including headache, dizziness, amnesia, lethargy, multiple
sclerosis, and somnolence) occurred in a higher percentage of subjects in the elinzanetant
arm (2.9%) compared to placebo (0.3%).
(4) Psychiatric disorders SOC occurred in a higher percentage of subjects in the elinzanetant
group (2.9%) versus placebo (0.3%). A variety of PTs were included in this category, such as
depressed mood, depression, anxiety, apathy, nervousness, suicidal ideation, and insomnia,
albeit in small numbers.
(5) Skin and subcutaneous tissue disorders SOC occurred in a higher percentage of subjects in
the elinzanetant group (1.3%) compared to placebo (0%). A variety of PTs were included in
this category, such as rash, alopecia, dry skin, and photosensitivity reaction.
By PT, the most frequently reported AEs leading to discontinuation were fatigue, headache,
abdominal pain upper, and depressed mood, which occurred in 1.6%, 1.3%, 1%, and 1% of the
elinzanetant group, respectively, compared to 0% of the placebo group.
Refer to Section 7.6.3.6 for further discussion of nervous system disorders (fatigue, somnolence,
dizziness/vertigo) as adverse events of special interest.

LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
Table 52 presents data for subjects with adverse events leading to treatment discontinuation by
system organ class and OCMQ (narrow). The results were similar to those seen analyzed by PTs.
The most frequent events by OCMQ comparing elinzanetant versus placebo were:
(1) Abdominal pain (gastrointestinal disorder SOC), five subjects (1.6%) versus zero;
(2) Fatigue (general disorders SOC), six subjects (1.9%) versus zero;
(3) Headache (nervous system SOC), four subjects (1.3%) versus zero; and
(4) Depression (psychiatric disorders SOC), five subjects (1.6%) versus zero.
For further discussion of fatigue, please see Section 7.6.3.6. The results for abdominal pain,
fatigue, headache, and depression are discussed below.
Abdominal Pain
The gastrointestinal disorder OCMQ (narrow) was made up of the following preferred terms:
abdominal pain, dyspepsia, diarrhea, and nausea. All these AEs were more common in the
elinzanetant arm than the placebo arm, except for nausea (which occurred in the same percentage
of subjects in the elinzanetant and placebo arms). Abdominal pain will be included in the USPI.
Depression
The depression OCMQ was made up of the following PTs: depressed mood and depression, both
of which occurred in a higher percentage of subjects in the elinzanetant arm. AEs in the
depression OCMQ leading to discontinuation were reported by a higher percentage of subjects in
the elinzanetant group (1.6%) compared to the placebo group (0.0%) (Table 51). Of the five
subjects with AEs related to depression, two were moderate, two were severe, and one was mild.
None were serious.
Details of the subjects who discontinued due to depression are included below:
(b) (6) was a 53-year-old woman who developed two AEs leading to
(1) Subject
discontinuation: depression and weight increased. The increased weight occurred 96 days
after starting elinzanetant. The investigator considered this event to be moderate in intensity
and related to study intervention. Then, 165 days after starting elinzanetant, the subject
developed severe depression and stopped elinzanetant. The investigator considered this event
to be severe in intensity and related to study intervention.
(b) (6) was a 57-year-old woman who developed an AE of depression
(2) Subject
leading to discontinuation 98 days after starting elinzanetant. The investigator considered this
event to be mild in intensity and not related to study intervention. The subject received
medications for her depression.
(b) (6) was a 62-year-old woman who developed an AE of depressed
(3) Subject
mood 6 days after starting elinzanetant and leading to treatment discontinuation. The subject
had a history of depression. The investigator considered the AE to be moderate in intensity
and related to elinzanetant.

(1) Subject

In OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and OASIS 3, suicidal ideation and behavior was monitored by the
eC-SSRS, In OASIS 3, 47 subjects (15%) in the elinzanetant arm and 40 subjects (12.7%) in the
placebo arm reported a history of previous suicidal ideation or behavior at baseline. Four
subjects, all of whom were in the elinzanetant arm, had experienced suicidal ideation within the
past 6 months before the baseline visit. During treatment, the number of subjects reporting
suicidal ideation was low in both treatment arms (ranged from 2 to 5 subjects per arm at all
timepoints measured). No suicidal behavior was reported by any subject during treatment.

experienced AEs leading to discontinuation of treatment during the 52-week study period. AEs
leading to discontinuation were increased in elinzanetant from the onset of the study, with
relative stability after 120 days of treatment.

Additional OCMQ (narrow) analyses were performed for fatigue, dizziness, somnolence, study
agent abuse potential, rash, and diarrhea. An assessment of fatigue, dizziness, and somnolence is
included in Section 7.6.3. The results for study agent abuse potential, rash, and diarrhea are
discussed below.
Study Agent Abuse Potential
The study agent abuse potential OCMQ (narrow) was made up of only one PT: somnolence,
which occurred in a higher percentage of subjects in the elinzanetant group (5.1%) compared to
the placebo group (1.3%). See Section 7.6.3.6 for further discussion of somnolence.

The rash OCMQ (narrow) was made up of the following PTs: acne, dermatitis, rash, and
urticaria, all of which occurred in a higher percentage of subjects in the elinzanetant group
compared to the placebo group, except for urticaria, which occurred in an equal percentage of
subjects in both groups (0.6%) (Table 55). There was one AE of rash that was not initially

safety considerations not previously identified. The reviewers performed an in-depth analysis of
potential cases of syncope which is further discussed in Section 7.6.3.

7.6.3. Adverse Events of Special Interest
For the clinical program, the adverse events of special interest included abuse potential, bone
safety, hepatic safety, endometrial safety, cardiac safety, nervous system disorders, fractures,
driving ability, and breast safety.
7.6.3.1. Abuse Potential
The Controlled Substance Staff evaluated abuse-related preclinical and clinical data submitted by
the Applicant.
The Controlled Substance Staff concluded that elinzanetant appears to be selective for NK1 and
NK3 receptors and does not bind with significant affinity to receptor subtypes or targets
associated with abuse potential. In nonclinical assessments, elinzanetant was not selfadministered by nonhuman primates, suggesting a lack of reinforcing effects and negligible
potential for abuse. In nonclinical assessments of physical dependence in nonhuman primates,
elinzanetant did not produce a withdrawal syndrome upon discontinuation after 30 days of
administration. Elinzanetant did not function as discriminative stimulus in trained nonhuman
primates, further supporting its low abuse potential.
In clinical studies, elinzanetant showed no significant abuse potential or risk of physical
dependence, as potential abuse-related adverse events were mostly limited to somnolence and
dizziness, were self-resolving, and lacked euphoria or other effects attractive to recreational drug
users, aligning with nonclinical data.
These data suggest elinzanetant has no, or negligible, potential for abuse.

Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)

LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
7.6.3.2. Bone Safety
In OASIS 3, the effect of elinzanetant on BMD was assessed by dual-energy X-ray
absorptiometry in 343 women. At baseline, the mean BMD values of the lumbar spine, total hip,
and femoral neck were similar in both groups. At Week 52, the mean BMD values numerically
decreased at all anatomical sites in both groups. At Week 52, the mean BMD values numerically
decreased by <0.01% to 0.7% at all anatomical sites in the elinzanetant treatment group
compared to decreases of 1.2% to 1.4% in the placebo group. In both groups, the mean
percentage changes in BMD were within the expected age-related loss per year.
7.6.3.3. Hepatic Safety (Drug-Induced Liver Injury)
Elinzanetant inhibits NK1 and NK3 receptors. The clinical program included monitoring for
drug induced liver injury as nonclinical data suggested hepatoxicity risk and there were elevated
liver enzymes seen in Phase 1 and Phase 2 studies. In May 2023, fezolinetant, another oral NK3
inhibitor, was approved under NDA 216578 for the same indication as elinzanetant. At the time
of approval, fezolinetant’s labeling had a Warning and Precaution for hepatic transaminase
elevation, which was updated with a Boxed Warning based on postmarket cases of DILI leading
to jaundice. Given these considerations, hepatic safety was an adverse event of special interest in
the elinzanetant program.
Hepatic Safety: Laboratory Data (OASIS, 1, OASIS 2, and OASIS 3)
In the Phase 2b and three Phase 3 studies, there were no cases meeting aminotransferase and
total bilirubin criteria for Hy’s law.
In OASIS 1, there was a slightly higher percentage of subjects in the elinzanetant group (1%)
with ALT >3xULN compared to the placebo group (0.5%) (Table 59). In OASIS 3, this
difference was slightly larger (Table 61). This difference did not persist at the ALT >5xULN cutoff and was not seen in OASIS 2 (Table 60).

LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
In summary, the DILI team determined that:
While the nonclinical data (in vitro and animal) supports a hepatotoxicity risk, for the Phase 2b
and three Phase 3 studies, there were no clinically significant events of hepatotoxicity with
elinzanetant. There were two cases of liver injury that were attributable to elinzanetant. There
were no cases meeting Hy’s law. There were slightly higher proportion of subjects with
ALT >3xULN in the elinzanetant 120 mg arm than that in the placebo arm during the doubleblind, placebo-controlled treatment period in OASIS 3 and OASIS 1, but not OASIS 2. The liver
injury signal was described as weak, but the number of women exposed is still low relative to the
number of women who may be treated postmarket. Thus, liver injuries of clinical significance
could still arise in postmarket, similar to what was seen for fezolinetant. Furthermore, the risk
tolerance for fatal or life-threating liver injury for both elinzanetant and fezolinetant is low due to
the targeted disease, which has substantial morbidity but low risk of mortality. Also, more
substantial liver injury may have been mitigated by the scheduled liver blood test monitoring and
EOT. The two probable cases of DILI had liver injury as elinzanetant was stopped per protocol
EOT, not because of liver enzyme elevations.
7.6.3.4. Endometrial Safety
As noted in Section 7.1, there were positive carcinogenicity findings in the 2-year rat study.
These findings included malignant lymphoma, malignant adenocarcinoma of the uterus,
malignant and benign endometrial tumors, and malignant squamous cell carcinoma of the uterus.
The highest noncarcinogenic dose of elinzanetant was 20 mg/kg/day (7.5X the human
therapeutic exposure on an AUC basis) and the lowest dose found to be carcinogenic was
60 mg/kg/day (~29X the human therapeutic exposure on an AUC basis).
There were no neoplastic findings in the 26-week transgenic mice study, and the in vitro and in
vivo genotoxicity studies with elinzanetant and its three main metabolites showed negative
results.
Given the neoplastic findings that were observed in the uterus and the hematolymphoid system
of the female rat, FDA performed an extensive evaluation of the clinical data related to
malignancy and endometrial safety.
In OASIS 3, the percentage of subjects with AEs in the SOC neoplasms benign, malignant, and
unspecified was higher for the elinzanetant group (five subjects, 1.6%) than the placebo group
(two subjects, 0.6%). However, the PTs were generally for single terms that did not raise specific
concerns of a pattern that would be suggestive of a malignancy signal (PTs for elinzanetant
group: melanocytic nevus (2), fibroadenoma of breast, hypergammaglobulinemia benign
monoclonal, invasive ductal breast cancer, and squamous cell carcinoma of skin).
Endometrial safety was assessed in OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and OASIS 3 by TVU and endometrial
biopsies according to FDA draft guidance for industry Estrogen and Estrogen/Progestin Drug
Products to Treat Vasomotor Symptoms and Vulvar and Vaginal Atrophy Symptoms —
Recommendations for Clinical Evaluation (January 2003).
In OASIS 3, out of the 170 women with an intact uterus who completed one year of treatment
with elinzanetant 120 mg, biopsy samples could be obtained from 140 women providing 116

Overall, 609 EOT endometrial biopsies were obtained from women receiving elinzanetant

pathologies in any if these cases.

one year was below the FDA-specified background incidence rate of ≤1% with an upper bound
of the one-sided 95% CI below 4%. However, review of endometrial safety revealed minimal
discrepancies among pathologists such as atrophic versus inactive endometrium, and a handful of
cases of disordered proliferative endometrium.

7.6.3.5. Cardiac Safety
The cardiac safety of elinzanetant including effects on the QT interval has been investigated by
means of standard 12-lead ECG and continuous 12-lead Holter ECG in various Phase 1 studies
in healthy volunteers, as well as in Phase 2a and 2b studies in women with VMS. Doses in these
studies were up to elinzanetant 600 mg. The highest clinically observed geometric mean plasma
concentration in these studies were up to approximately 5-fold higher than the geometric mean
steady-state exposure of the planned therapeutic dose of 120 mg as obtained in Phase 3 studies.
According to the Applicant, based on the study results there is no indication of a QTc interval
prolongation or other relevant cardiac safety risk by elinzanetant after single oral administration
of elinzanetant at doses up to 5 times the maximum recommended dose. Evaluations also showed
no relationship between elinzanetant plasma concentration and QTc interval. This assessment is
supported by the absence of relevant findings in the nonclinical cardiac safety studies.
The data were reviewed by the Interdisciplinary Review Team for Cardiac Studies. In summary,
elinzanetant did not prolong the QTcF interval in the QTc assessment of PK/ECG data from
Study 21670. However, due to the limitations of the clinical study and the nonclinical assays, this
QTc assessment does not sufficiently characterize QTc effects of elinzanetant at the anticipated
high clinical exposure scenario which is in patients coadministered with strong CYP3A4
inhibitors. The labeling will indicate that patients should avoid concomitant use with strong
CYP3A4 inhibitors.
Among subjects in OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and OASIS 3, there was an imbalance in adverse events
in the cardiovascular system organ class with more events in the elinzanetant group compared to
the placebo group. In OASIS 3, 1.9% of subjects in the elinzanetant versus 0.6% of subjects in
the placebo group had treatment-emergent AEs in the SOC cardiac disorders. The cardiac
disorders SOC was made up of single terms (elinzanetant group: acute myocardial infarction and
sinus tachycardia), except for palpitations which occurred in a higher percentage of subjects in
the elinzanetant arm (1.6%) compared to the placebo arm (0%). All the AEs of palpitations were
mild or moderate.
7.6.3.6. Nervous System Disorders
In OASIS 3, adverse events in the SOC nervous system disorders occurred in a greater
percentage of subjects in the elinzanetant group (22%) compared to the placebo group (11.8%).
Adverse events of interest included somnolence, fatigue, vertigo/dizziness, syncope, and
hypotension/orthostatic hypotension. While it is possible for hypotension/orthostatic hypotension
to be secondary to CNS or cardiac/vascular causes, it was considered in the context of nervous
system disorders given the imbalances in other nervous system disorders. In addition, it is
possible for syncope to be secondary to multiple etiologies, such as cardiovascular or metabolic
causes.
Upon Agency request, the Applicant provided groupings (based on MedDRA labeling grouping)
for adverse events of special interest as outlined in Table 65. In each study phase (Table 66),

Somnolence/Fatigue
Somnolence and fatigue were considered an adverse event of special interest in the development
program given that clinical data suggested an increased risk of somnolence and fatigue following
elinzanetant exposure. In the clinical development program, women took the study drug at
bedtime and were instructed neither to drive nor operate machinery if they experienced
somnolence or fatigue.
In the SAF, pooled safety population, (up to Week 12) somnolence or fatigue occurred in a
higher percentage of subjects treated with elinzanetant (7.0%) compared to placebo (2.3%).
When using broader MedDRA PTs (somnolence, hypersomnia, asthenia, decreased activity,
fatigue, fatigue management, mental fatigue, physical deconditioning, and sluggishness) the
imbalance was larger (elinzanetant arm: 8.6% compared to placebo: 2%). None of the AEs of
somnolence or fatigue were serious.
In the SAF, pooled safety population, more subjects in the elinzanetant discontinued due to an
AE of somnolence or fatigue (1.8%) compared to the placebo group (0%). The majority of
events occurred during the first two weeks of treatment, were mild or moderate and resolved. No
difference in the incidence rates (100 person-years) in accidents and injuries, Standard Medical
Dictionary for Regulatory Activities Query (SMQ), were seen for the elinzanetant and placebo
groups.
In OASIS 1 and OASIS 2, the fatigue OCMQ (narrow), was made up of the following PTs:
asthenia, fatigue, and lethargy, all of which occurred in a higher percentage of subjects in the
elinzanetant group compared to the placebo group (Table 68). All the events were mild to
moderate in severity and none were serious. In the elinzanetant group (pooled data), 2% of
subjects discontinued due to fatigue compared to no subjects in the placebo group. In OASIS 3,
the fatigue OCMQ (narrow) was made up of the same PTs, all of which occurred in a higher
percentage of subjects in the elinzanetant group compared to the placebo group (Table 69). A
similar percentage of subjects discontinued due to fatigue in OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and OASIS 3.

elinzanetant group compared to the placebo group (Table 71). A similar percentage of
elinzanetant-treated subjects discontinued due to somnolence in OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and OASIS
3 (0 to -0.6%).

Given the findings in the clinical program, somnolence and fatigue will be included in the USPI.
Dizziness/Vertigo
In OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and OASIS 3, AEs of dizziness occurred more frequently in subjects in
the elinzanetant group compared to the placebo group. In OASIS 3, dizziness occurred in 2.2%
of the elinzanetant group compared to 1.0% of the placebo group.
In OASIS 1 and OASIS 2, the dizziness OCMQ (narrow) was made up of the following PTs:
balance disorder, dizziness, and vertigo (Table 72). In the pooled OASIS 1 and OASIS 2 studies,
more subjects in the elinzanetant arm had dizziness OCMQ (narrow) AEs (3.2%) than the
placebo arm (1.5%). In OASIS 3, the dizziness OCMQ (narrow) was made up of the following
PTs: balance disorder, dizziness, presyncope, vertigo, vertigo CNS origin, vertigo positional, and
vestibular neuronitis, all of which occurred in a higher percentage of subjects in the elinzanetant
group compared to the placebo group, except for presyncope (Table 73). All the events were
mild to moderate severity, except one event that was severe. In the elinzanetant group, 1% of
subjects discontinued due to dizziness compared to 0% in the placebo group.

In the Phase 2/3 clinical studies, three subjects in the elinzanetant arm (0.3%) compared to no
cases in the placebo arm experienced syncope. None of the subjects reported syncope
experienced accident, injury, fall or concussion. There was a total of five cases of syncope in the
entire clinical development program and the narratives are included below:

electrocardiogram, and head CT, were normal. The investigator did not think the SAE was
related to elinzanetant use. The review team notes that the etiology of syncope is unclear.

Accidental Injury Associated With Nervous System Disorders
The safety data were evaluated to assess whether nervous system disorders (including CNS
depression [somnolence or fatigue], vertigo/dizziness, or hypotension/syncope) were associated
with accidental injuries (such as fractures, accidents, or falls). At the Agency’s request, the
Applicant assessed all PTs under the MedDRA SMQ accidents and injuries in subjects with
nervous system disorders. There were eight subjects with an AE assigned to both “SMQ
accidents and injuries” and “AE CNS depression including somnolence or fatigue,
vertigo/dizziness, or hypotension/syncope” (Table 80). Of these eight subjects, two subjects had
an injury event on the same day as the nervous system disorder AE. One subject
(b) (6) had a mild muscle strain and mild vertigo on the same day.
(Subject
(b) (6)
Relevant medical history included Meniere’s disease. Another subject (Subject
(b)
(6)
[
in the CSR]) had fatigue and a thermal burn on the same day. In the remaining six subjects,
there did not appear to be an association between the injury/accident and the nervous system
disorder AE. The review team agrees with the Applicant’s conclusion that there did not appear to
be a clinically relevant association between CNS depressive effects, vertigo/dizziness, and/or
hypotension/syncope with accidents or injuries in the submitted data. However, there are
inherent limitations to the data given that it is challenging to assess AEs and vital signs before an
accident given that these events were not anticipated.

Fractures
A total of 25 subjects in pooled studies OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and OASIS 3 reported 30 events of
fractures, including two events of tooth fractures. There were five cases suggestive of fragility
fractures, while the remaining cases appeared to be secondary to major trauma (such as a motor
(b) (6) ), all the events were assessed as
vehicle accident). Except for one tibial fracture (SID
nonserious and unrelated to study drug. Most were mild to moderate intensity, and none led to
permanent drug discontinuation. During the placebo-controlled period (Week 1 to 12), out of 713
subjects in the elinzanetant group, 5 (0.7%) reported fracture events compared to 4 (0.6%) out of
713 subjects in the placebo arm. Many of the narratives specifically noted that there were no
other symptoms, injury or relevant central nervous system adverse events, which is important to
consider given that elinzanetant is associated with CNS events, such as fatigue and somnolence.
7.6.3.7. Dedicated Driving Ability Study
To further investigate the potential safety risk of somnolence and fatigue, the Applicant
conducted a dedicated driving ability study with elinzanetant. These data were reviewed by the
Division of Pharmacometrics. The results of the study and the assessment are summarized
below.
The driving ability study with elinzanetant was performed in healthy women (mean age 52.1
years). This study was conducted in a single center based on randomized, double-blind, placeboand active-controlled, 4-fold crossover design with oral administration of multiple doses (over 5
subsequent days to achieve steady state) of elinzanetant 120 mg (intended therapeutic dose),
elinzanetant 240 mg, placebo, or zopiclone 7.5 mg as positive control (on Days 1 and 5 only) per
treatment period. There were 61, 63, 62, and 61 subjects per group, respectively. The
240 mg/day dose was selected as supratherapeutic dose as it covers a potential maximum
exposure increase of elinzanetant that could occur when it is administered with a weak CYP3A4
inhibitor as a comedication. The predicted steady-state plasma concentrations have been
investigated in healthy subjects.
The study duration of 5 days was chosen because study state concentrations would be achieved
after 5 days of once daily dosing. Each treatment period was separated by a 7- to 14-day washout
period, which was assessed to be adequate.
Study interventions were administered in the evening via oral administration together with
240 mL of noncarbonated water at room temperature. Driving simulator assessments were
performed the next morning, approximately 9 to 10 hours after dosing. This timing was chosen
to reflect the recommended intake time of elinzanetant according to the intended label and to
investigate potential residual driving impairment and cognitive effects which might pose a risk
for patients. Blood samples for PK analysis were collected predose on Days 1 and 6- and 8.5hours postdose on Days 2 and 6.
The simulated driving performance was measured using standard deviation of lateral position
(SDLP) in the CRCDS-MiniSim™ 9 to 10 hours after dosing. SDLP data was analyzed using a
mixed model with fixed effects for sequence, period, and treatment, with repeated periods for
subjects. Noninferiority testing was applied, with a noninferiority margin of 4.4 cm. Additional

measures of simulated driving performance in the CRCDS-MiniSim™ included lane exceedance,
