7.7. Key Safety Review Issues
7.7.1. Hepatic Transaminase Elevation
Issue
There is nonclinical evidence for hepatotoxicity risk in short-term toxicity studies, and there is a
risk of hepatotoxicity with another drug that inhibits NK3 (fezolinetant).
Background
Elinzanetant, is an oral, small molecule that inhibits NK1 and NK3 receptors. The clinical
program included liver safety monitoring and there were two liver injury cases attributable to
elinzanetant. The cases of DILI were hepatocellular and relatively modest in severity and
recovered fully. While there were minimal imbalances in hepatic transaminases across the
clinical development program, there were some imbalances in ALT elevations >3xULN on the
elinzanetant arm compared to the placebo arm in OASIS 1 and OASIS 3.
Assessment
Although we did not identify a clinically significant hepatotoxicity risk with elinzanetant, there
were cases of DILI and elevations in liver function tests. Also, postapproval, the drug will be
used by patients with additional comorbidities and with less frequent monitoring. The number of
subjects exposed in the clinical studies is relatively low compared to the potential postmarket
use. Thus, clinically significant liver injuries could arise postmarketing, similar to what was seen
with another NK3 inhibitor for the same indication (fezolinetant). It is important to alert patients
and prescribers to this risk and to outline measures to take to monitor for hepatoxicity and
evaluate patients prior to starting the medication.

166
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
Conclusion
Hepatic transaminase elevations are a risk with elinzanetant. To mitigate this risk, the labeling
will include a Warning and Precaution to indicate that:


Providers conduct:
- Baseline bloodwork for hepatic function and injury prior to initiation of elinzanetant. Do
not start elinzanetant if serum transaminase concentration is equal to or exceeds two
times the ULN or if total bilirubin is equal to or exceeds two times the ULN
- Follow-up blood work of hepatic transaminase concentrations 3 months after initiation
- Unscheduled liver biochemical tests if new onset symptoms occur (new onset fatigue,
decreased appetite, nausea, vomiting, pruritus, jaundice, pale feces, dark urine, or
abdominal pain) suggestive of acute liver injury occur during elinzanetant treatment



Not recommended for use in patients with moderate to severe cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B or C)



Providers advise patients to discontinue elinzanetant immediately and seek medical attention
including hepatic laboratory tests if they experience signs or symptoms that may suggest
liver injury.

In addition, the Applicant will report postmarket cases of acute liver injury as AESIs to ensure
their timely reporting and follow-up to the Agency. This enhanced pharmacovigilance (ePV)
program will consist of (1) expeditious reports of AEs of interest beyond minimum reporting
requirements, and (2) a summary and assessment of AEs of interest at a frequency defined by
FDA.

7.7.2. Risk of Pregnancy Loss
Issue
Based on findings from animal reproduction studies, elinzanetant may cause pregnancy loss or
stillbirth when administered during pregnancy.
Background
In reproductive and developmental toxicity studies, elinzanetant administration prior to or during
pregnancy caused fetal harm in rats in the form of pre- and postimplantation loss, reduced litter
size or total litter loss, decrease in fetal body weight, and decrease in neonatal pup viability. In a
fertility and early embryonic development study in rats, there was an increase in the percentage
of pre- and postimplantation embryo loss and decrease in fetal body weights at 14-fold the
human therapeutic exposure when rat dams were treated orally prior to mating and through the
early embryonic period.
In a pre- and postnatal developmental study in rats, a higher incidence of still born pups, an
increase in total litter loss, a decrease in pup viability between postnatal Days 0 and 4, and an
increase in the number of neonatal pups without milk in the stomach were observed in the midand high-dose groups, with maternal systemic exposures that were within the range of human
167
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
therapeutic exposure. Decreased maternal care was also a clinical observation in these treatment
groups. Whether the neonatal effects were due to decreased maternal care or other potential
elinzanetant-related effects on the offspring could not be definitively concluded from this study.
In an embryofetal development study in rabbits, maternal toxicity was noted in the form of
marked body weight loss and decreased food consumption at systemic exposures that were
within the range of human therapeutic exposure.
No teratogenicity was observed in the reproductive and developmental studies with elinzanetant
in rats or rabbits.
These nonclinical data indicate that elinzanetant may cause pregnancy loss or stillbirth when
administered during pregnancy.
Elinzanetant is indicated for the treatment of moderate to severe VMS due to menopause.
Despite its intended use in menopausal women, there is a need to address the potential risks for
females of reproductive potential who might inadvertently use the drug.
Assessment
Given the risk of pregnancy loss or still birth based on data from animal studies, elinzanetant is
contraindicated during pregnancy.
Conclusion
To mitigate the risk of pregnancy loss or still birth due to exposure to elinzanetant during
pregnancy, the labeling will include:
(1) A contraindication for use in pregnancy
(2) A Warning and Precaution with instructions to:
(a) exclude pregnancy in females of reproductive potential prior to initiating elinzanetant,
and
(b) advise females of reproductive potential to use effective contraception during treatment
with elinzanetant and for 2 weeks after stopping elinzanetant
These measures aim to prevent potential exposure to elinzanetant during pregnancy, thereby
reducing the risk of pregnancy loss or stillbirth in case of accidental use by pregnant women or
women who may become pregnant. Importantly, elinzanetant is intended for you in woman
experience symptoms associated with menopause.

7.7.3. Endometrial Tumor Abnormality
Issue
Based on findings from a 2-year carcinogenicity study in female rats, there was an increase in
incidence of endometrial adenocarcinoma and the combination of malignant and benign
endometrial tumors and squamous cell carcinoma of the uterus.
168
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
Background
In a 2-year carcinogenicity study in female rats, oral doses of elinzanetant ≥60 mg/kg/day (29fold the total AUC(0-24) at the human therapeutic dose) increased the incidence of endometrial
adenocarcinoma, the combination of malignant and benign endometrial tumors and squamous
cell carcinoma of the uterus, and lymphomas of the hematolymphoid system. These effects were
not observed at a dose representing 7-fold the total AUC(0-24) at the human therapeutic dose.
In a 26-week carcinogenicity study in rasH2 transgenic mice, there was no evidence of drugrelated carcinogenicity at 85 or 70 mg/kg/day in males or females, respectively.
Elinzanetant showed no genotoxic potential in bacterial mutation assay (Ames test), mouse
lymphoma assay, and in vivo bone marrow micronucleus test in rats. Additionally, the principal
human metabolites of elinzanetant were negative for genotoxicity in vitro in the Ames and
micronucleus test.
In terms of clinical safety data, endometrial safety was assessed in OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and
OASIS 3 by TVU and endometrial biopsies according to FDA draft guidance for industry
Estrogen and Estrogen/Progestin Drug Products to Treat Vasomotor Symptoms and Vulvar and
Vaginal Atrophy Symptoms — Recommendations for Clinical Evaluation (January 2003).
Overall, 609 women underwent end-of treatment-endometrial biopsies in OASIS 1, OASIS 2,
and OASIS 3. A total of 477 women received elinzanetant 120 mg had endometrial biopsies.
Among these, 140 received elinzanetant for up to 52 weeks, 162 received elinzanetant for up to
26 weeks, and 175 received elinzanetant for up to 14 weeks. Three cases of endometrial
hyperplasia (one with and two without atypia), and a case of endometrial glandular hyperplastic
polyp (without atypia), were identified upon examination of individual pathologists’ readings.
Overall, the incidence of endometrial abnormality in all three OASIS studies combined was
0.8% (4 out of 477).
Assessment
In a 2-year carcinogenicity study in female rats, there was a statistically significant and doserelated increase in the incidence of endometrial adenocarcinoma and the combination of
malignant and benign endometrial tumors and squamous cell carcinoma of the uterus. However,
this finding was at exposures much higher than the clinical dose (29 times the recommended
clinical dose), and the clinical significance of these nonclinical findings is unknown. Further,
there were no concerning findings in other nonclinical carcinogenicity assessments. Transvaginal
ultrasounds and endometrial biopsy data up to 52 weeks from the clinical safety did not reveal a
rate of endometrial abnormality above the background rate in this population (1%).
The review team considered whether the carcinogenicity information warranted inclusion of the
concern for endometrial safety as a Warning and Precaution in labeling. The review team also
considered whether additional safety mitigation measures, such as a postmarketing requirement
or ePV would better characterize the endometrial safety risk. Given that the clinical significance
of the nonclinical findings is unknown and that the rate of endometrial abnormalities in women
who received elinzanetant was in line with expected background rate, it was determined that a

169
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
Warning was not necessary and that postmarketing requirement or ePV are not needed to further
characterize the risk endometrial abnormality.
Conclusion
In light of the within background rate of endometrial abnormalities in the Phase 3 database with
up to 52 weeks of surveillance, the clinical significance of nonclinical findings of endometrial
malignancies, at an exposure 29 times the recommended clinical dose, is unknown. The
nonclinical findings and clinical endometrial abnormalities will be communicated in
Sections 13.1 and 14.2 of labeling, respectively. Enhanced surveillance postmarket is not
necessary.

7.7.4. Seizures
Issue
Convulsions were observed in nonclinical studies conducted in male and female rats.
Background
Given the nonclinical observations related to convulsions, the clinical data were reviewed for
safety signals related to seizures/convulsions. In OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and OASIS 3, there were
seven women with a medical history of epilepsy or seizure (four in the elinzanetant group and
three in the placebo group). In OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and OASIS 3, there was one case of
generalized tonic-clonic seizure. An Information Request was sent to the Applicant, and they
responded on March 10, 2025, with additional details of the case and seizures in the clinical
program. The subject was a 58-year-old woman who had a history of generalized tonic-clonic
seizures greater than 30 years ago. She had been treated with various medications, and in (b) (6)
treatment (most likely Zarontin [ethosuximide] and Tegretol [carbamazepine]) was discontinued
(b) (6) , 46 days after staring
since she was doing well and had been seizure free. On
elinzanetant, she had two seizures at home and did not initially seek medical care. She then had a
third seizure on the same day and went to the hospital. The generalized tonic-clonic seizure was
felt to be related to study intervention and of mild intensity. The event was considered serious as
it required or prolonged hospitalization. She was treated for the seizure, discontinued study
medication, and withdrew from the study. She was noted to have recovered.
There was another case of a potential seizure during the clinical development program.
(b) (6) was a 56-year-old woman who had an SAE of syncope 55 days after
Subject
starting elinzanetant. The drug was interrupted and then the subject was able to complete the
study per protocol. The cause of the syncope was unclear. She reported that she felt disoriented
and passed out while in her car. She was admitted to the hospital and experienced slurred speech,
blurred vision, and elevated blood pressure and heart rate. It was noted that she may have had a
seizure and would require additional follow-up. Seizures were not included in her medical
history. Records noted that she had left-sided facial numbness, tremors, confusion, and
hypomagnesemia. Diagnostic evaluations included angiogram, chest X-ray, computerized
tomogram head, electrocardiogram, and magnetic resonance imaging of the head. The
investigator considered the SAE not related to the study medication, which is supported by the
observation that the subject was able to restart elinzanetant and complete the study.

LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
There were no additional cases of seizures detected in any other Phase 3 clinical studies. There
was no specific inquiry into seizure history at enrollment and no specific exclusion criterion for

criterion “In good general health…”. In addition, the list of prohibited medications may have

There was only one definitive serious adverse event of seizure. However, it is notable that the

communicated in labeling as a Warning and Precaution. Since only one case occurred and a lack
of clarity if patients with a history of seizure disorder are at increased risk of recurrence, there
will not be a specific contraindication to the use of elinzanetant in patients with a history of
seizure disorder.

7.7.5. Nervous System Effects
Issue
Increased nervous system disorders (including fatigue, somnolence, and dizziness/vertigo) were
observed in subjects treated with elinzanetant in the clinical development program.
Background
Adverse events in the SOC nervous system disorders occurred in a greater percentage of subjects
in the elinzanetant group (22%) compared to the placebo group (11.8%) in OASIS 3. An indepth analysis was performed of adverse events of interest including somnolence, fatigue,
vertigo/dizziness, syncope, and hypotension/orthostatic hypotension.
Assessment
In the SAF, pooled safety population, (up to Week 12) somnolence or fatigue occurred in a
higher percentage of subjects treated with elinzanetant (7.0%) compared to placebo (2.3%).
None of the AEs of somnolence or fatigue were serious. More subjects in the elinzanetant
discontinued due to an AE of somnolence or fatigue (1.8%) compared to the placebo group (0%).
The majority of events occurred during the first two weeks of treatment and were mild or
moderate and resolved. No difference in the incidence rates (100 person-years) in accidents and
injuries (SMQ) was seen for the elinzanetant and placebo groups.

171
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
Similar trends were seen for AEs of dizziness. In OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and OASIS 3, AEs of
dizziness occurred more frequently in subjects in the elinzanetant group compared to the placebo
group. In OASIS 3, dizziness occurred in 2.2% of the elinzanetant group compared to 1.0% of
the placebo group. The majority of these events were mild or moderate. In OASIS 3, in the
elinzanetant group, 1% of subjects discontinued due to dizziness compared to 0% in the placebo
group. The two subjects who developed dizziness leading to discontinuation developed the
dizziness on Day 11 to 12. There was also one subject in OASIS 3 with an SAE of dizziness (PT
vertigo) who reported peripheral vertigo 58 days after starting elinzanetant. The SAE was of
severe intensity. The investigator did not think it was related to elinzanetant. The subject
continued treatment and the SAE resolved.
The Applicant conducted a driving study that suggested that next day driving performance is
impaired in some subjects taking single and repeat dose of elinzanetant 120 mg and 240 mg.
There was one notable event of hypotension in a healthy volunteer, however it was unclear if it
was secondary to a vasovagal event or elinzanetant. There were small imbalances related to
decreased blood pressure in the clinical development program, but not clinically significant
findings. Given that hypotension and syncope could be secondary to vascular etiologies and
given the lack of significant clinical findings, they will not be described in the product labeling at
this time.
Conclusion
The label will mention that there is a potential for next-day residual effects in some patients
taking elinzanetant 120 mg. The labeling will include a Warning and Precaution of CNS
Depressant Effects and Daytime Impairment. The Warning and Precaution will describe the
nervous system effects (including somnolence, fatigue, vertigo, dizziness, and presyncope). In
addition, patients will be advised to take elinzanetant at bedtime. Dizziness, fatigue, and
somnolence will be mentioned in Section 6 of the labeling.

7.7.6. Photosensitivity
Issue
In vitro studies suggest a potential risk of photosensitivity reactions with elinzanetant.
Background
An in vitro study demonstrated that elinzanetant has some potential for photosensitization. While
studies of photosensitivity in animals were not conducted, there is evidence that elinzanetant
distributes to and accumulates in melanin-containing tissues in the rats. Based on the in vitro
phototoxicity assay, the most conservative MOE for phototoxicity was approximately 7-fold.
The MOE should be interpreted with caution because elinzanetant concentrations in human
pigmented tissues are derived based on the distribution of elinzanetant to rat pigmented tissues
(eyes and skin) and no additional in vivo animal photosensitivity studies have been conducted.
Photosensitivity is a reaction that occurs when a drug causes the skin to become more sensitive
to ultraviolet (UV) light or visible light, leading to skin reactions upon exposure to sunlight or
172
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
other light sources. Understanding the risk and characteristics of phototoxicity is important for
patient safety and appropriate use of elinzanetant.
In OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and OASIS 3, five subjects developed phototoxicity reactions. Four out
of five subjects did not have a history of photosensitivity. One subject had a previous sunexposure reaction.
Three cases occurred in OASIS 1:
(b) (6) was a 52-year-old woman who developed phototoxicity reaction 1
(1) Subject
day after starting elinzanetant. The AE was mild in severity and recovered/resolved.
(b) (6) was a 52-year-old woman who developed a phototoxicity
(2) Subject

(b) (6) was a 58-year-old woman who developed a photosensitivity
(3) Subject
reaction 120 days after starting elinzanetant. The AE was of moderate intensity and
considered related to elinzanetant.

Two cases occurred in OASIS 3:
(b) (6) was a 60-year-old woman who developed an AE of phototoxicity
(1) Subject
reaction 290 days after starting elinzanetant that led to discontinuation. The event was
moderate in intensity and considered related to study intervention. The event resolved after
stopping the medication.
(b) (6) was a 59-year-old woman who developed a photosensitivity
(2) Subject
reaction 157 days after starting elinzanetant. The event was mild and considered not related
to study treatment. Given the risk of photosensitivity observed in the clinical program, the
review team would consider this AE related to elinzanetant. The subject was able to continue
participation in the study and discontinued the study later due to subject decision.

Assessment
An in vitro study demonstrated that elinzanetant has some potential for photosensitization. While
the MOE for phototoxicity is approximately 7-fold, this must be interpreted with caution because
elinzanetant concentrations in human pigmented tissues are derived based on the distribution of
elinzanetant to rat pigmented tissues (eyes and skin) and no additional in vivo animal
photosensitivity studies have been conducted.
In the clinical program, the photosensitivity events occurred over a wide range of times from
initial exposure to elinzanetant. However, this does not rule out a photosensitivity reaction, since
the reaction is dependent on exposure to sunlight, which would not be controlled over the clinical
study. While the frequency of photosensitivity reactions was low in the clinical program, it is
important to communicate the risk to patients so that it can be mitigated.

8. Therapeutic Individualization
8.1. Intrinsic Factors
Elinzanetant is also referred to as GSK1144814, BAY 3427080, and NT-814.
Renal Impairment
The effects of renal impairment on the pharmacokinetics of elinzanetant were assessed (Study
21669) following a single 120 mg dose (2 x 60 mg soft gel capsules) in male and female subjects
with varying degrees of renal function: mild (estimated glomerular filtration rate [eGFR] 60 to
90 mL/min), moderate (eGFR 30 to 59 mL/min), and severe (eGFR <30 mL/min), as compared
to those with normal renal function (≥90 mL/min). For elinzanetant, individuals with mild renal
impairment exhibited a 1.61-fold increase in AUC and a 1.86-fold increase in Cmax compared to
healthy subjects. In those with moderate renal impairment, the AUC and Cmax increased by 1.73fold and 1.84-fold, respectively. Notably, individuals with severe renal impairment showed a
1.12-fold increase in AUC and a 1.2-fold increase in Cmax compared to healthy subjects. For
metabolites (M18/21, M27, and M30/34), the extent of exposure increase in individuals with
mild, moderate, and severe renal impairment to those with normal renal function was less than
that for elinzanetant (see Section 14.2.3.1).
Population PK analysis showed that mild (n=402) or moderate (n=23) renal impairment does not
significantly affect the drug exposure (AUC) of elinzanetant in the Phase 3 study population (see
Section 14.5). The safety evaluation by the clinical review team did not identify additional safety
concerns for subjects with mild or moderate renal impairment who participated in the Phase 2
(SWITCH-1) and Phase 3 (OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and OASIS 3) clinical studies. Therefore, dose
adjustment of elinzanetant for patients with mild or moderate renal impairment is not warranted.
Study 21669 demonstrated that severe renal impairment did not result in a significant change in
elinzanetant exposure (1.12-fold) and the extent of Cmax increase in subjects with severe renal
impairment (1.56-fold) is less than that in subjects with mild to moderate renal impairment (1.84
to 1.86-fold). Considering that renal clearance plays a minimal role in the elimination of
elinzanetant (less than 1% of the dose is excreted in urine), the review team recommends no dose
adjustment for patients with severe renal impairment as well. Elinzanetant is not recommended
for patients with end-stage renal disease because the impact of end-stage renal disease on the
pharmacokinetics of elinzanetant has not been evaluated.

174
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
Hepatic Impairment
A dedicated hepatic impairment study (Study 21668) was conducted to evaluate the
pharmacokinetics, safety, and tolerability of elinzanetant in subjects with impaired hepatic
function, categorized as Child-Pugh A (mild) or Child-Pugh B (moderate), in comparison to
matched controls with normal hepatic function. Elinzanetant total maximum concentration at
steady state (Cmax,ss) increased by 1.16-fold in subjects with mild hepatic impairment (90%CI:
[0.81; 1.67]) and by 2.32-fold in subjects with moderate hepatic impairment (90%CI: [1.61;
3.34]). Similarly, AUC over 24 hours at steady state (AUCss) increased by 1.45-fold in subjects
with mild hepatic impairment (90%CI: [1.04; 2.04]) and by 2.34-fold in subjects with moderate
hepatic impairment (90%CI: [1.67; 3.28]). The total exposure of the metabolites M18/M21,
M27, and M30/34 (Cmax,ss and AUCss]) did not exhibit significant changes (<2-fold) in subjects
with mild or moderate hepatic impairment (refer to Section 14.2.3.2; Table 154, Table 155, and
Table 156).
A population PK analysis revealed that mild hepatic impairment does not significantly affect the
drug exposure (AUC) of elinzanetant in the Phase 3 study population (refer to Section 14.5). The
safety evaluation by the clinical review team did not identify additional safety concerns for
subjects with mild hepatic impairment who participated in the Phase 2 (SWITCH-1) and Phase 3
(OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and OASIS 3) clinical studies. Therefore, no dose adjustment of
elinzanetant is recommended for patients with mild hepatic impairment.
Individuals with moderate hepatic impairment, as assessed in the dedicated study, exhibited a
2.32-fold increase in AUC compared to healthy subjects. Additionally, the Phase 2 and 3 clinical
studies did not include subjects with moderate or severe hepatic impairment and, thus, the impact
of moderate or severe hepatic impairment on the safety of elinzanetant remains unknown.
Therefore, elinzanetant is not recommended for patients with moderate or severe hepatic
impairment.
Subgroup Analyses by Race, Age, and Geriatric Use
Race
The population PK analysis demonstrates that race is not a significant covariate and there was no
significant difference in elinzanetant exposure (AUC) between Black and non-Black subjects in
the OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and OASIS 3 studies (refer to Section 14.5).
Age
Clinical pharmacology studies with elinzanetant included subjects with an age range of 18 to 75
years. There were no apparent age-related differences in the safety and tolerability of
elinzanetant.
Geriatric Use
There have not been sufficient numbers of geriatric women involved in clinical studies utilizing
elinzanetant to determine whether those over 65 years of age differ from younger women in their
response to elinzanetant.

8.2. Extrinsic Factors
Food Effect
Study 21678 assessed the effect of a high-fat breakfast (800 to 1000 kcal, with 500 to 600 kcal
derived from fat and 250 kcal from carbohydrates) on the bioavailability of elinzanetant
following 40, 80, 120, and 160 mg once-daily (QD) administration. Under fed conditions, Cmax
of elinzanetant was reduced by approximately 70%, and AUC(0-24) by 30 to 40% compared to the
fasted state. Additionally, the median time to maximum concentration (Tmax) was approximately
doubled in the fed state. These effects were consistent across the dosage range of 40 to 160 mg
QD.
Despite the exposure reduction due to food intake, the clinical pharmacology review team
concluded that the exposure change was clinically insignificant. This assessment was based on
the outcomes from Phase 3 clinical studies (OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and OASIS 3) and the Phase 2b
(SWITCH-1) study, where elinzanetant 120 mg was administered before bedtime regardless of
food intake. These clinical studies demonstrated a statistically significant and clinically
meaningful reduction in both the frequency and severity of hot flashes in patients with VMS
(refer to Section 6). Therefore, elinzanetant can be administered with or without food at bedtime.
Drug Interactions
Effect of Other Drugs on Elinzanetant
Elinzanetant is primarily metabolized by CYP3A4 and is a substrate of P-glycoprotein (P-gp)
(refer to Section 14.1.2).
CYP3A4 Inhibitors
Strong CYP3A4 and P-gp Inhibitors
The effect of multiple doses of the strong CYP3A4 and P-gp inhibitor, itraconazole 200 mg
(2x100 mg capsules), on pharmacokinetics of a single dose of elinzanetant 40 mg was assessed
in Study 21679. Study results showed that elinzanetant Cmax increased by 3.3-fold and AUCinf
increased by 6.32-fold following concomitant use with itraconazole. These data indicate that
elinzanetant is a sensitive substrate of CYP3A4 and/or P-gp. The increased exposure of
elinzanetant by strong CYP3A4 and/or P-gp inhibitors may increase the risk of elinzanetantassociated adverse events. Therefore, concomitant use of elinzanetant with strong CYP3A4 or
P-gp inhibitors is not recommended.
Moderate CYP3A4 Inhibitors
A physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) model was employed to predict the
concentration-time profiles of elinzanetant when coadministered with the moderate CYP3A4
inhibitor erythromycin and the weak CYP3A inhibitor cimetidine.

Therefore, the review team requested the Applicant to conduct additional PBPK simulations to
explore the option of managing this drug-drug interaction (DDI) by reducing the dose of
elinzanetant by half (i.e., from 120 mg QD to 60 mg QD) for subjects who have concomitant use
of moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors. The simulation results suggest that the dose reduction to 60 mg
QD would reduce the systemic exposure of elinzanetant to a level that is slightly higher (i.e.,
39% for steady state AUC) than elinzanetant 120 mg QD alone (Figure 35). The 39% increase in
AUC ss resulting from elinzanetant 60 mg QD in subjects with concomitant use of moderate
CYP3A inhibitors compared to subjects taking elinzanetant 120 mg QD alone is not considered
clinically significant. Therefore, the review team recommends reducing the dose of elinzanetant
from 120 mg QD to 60 mg QD for patients with the concomitant use of moderate CYP3A4
inhibitors.

based on the Phase 2b study results, elinzanetant 120 mg QD was selected for safety and efficacy
evaluation in the Phase 3 studies OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and OASIS 3.

CYP3A4 inducers, constituting 0.5% of total PK data observations. However, only one subject
used a moderate CYP3A4 inducer throughout the entire treatment period. The limited number of
PK observations in subjects using moderate CYP3A4 inducers concurrently did not meet the
requirement of at least 10% categorical covariate inclusion in popPK analysis. Consequently, the

Proton Pump Inhibitor Esomeprazole
Elinzanetant is a lipophilic base showing a strong pH-dependent solubility. Elinzanetant is
slightly soluble as a protonated cation under acidic conditions whereas the neutral base is
insoluble at neutral pH. Therefore, a DDI study with the proton pump inhibitor esomeprazole

Effects of Elinzanetant on Other Drugs
Inhibition Potential
The in vitro study showed that elinzanetant and its metabolite M27, M30/34, and M18/21 had no
significant inhibitory effect on the enzyme activity of human CYP isoforms 1A1, 1A2, 2A6,
2B6, 2C8, 2C9, 2C19, 2D6, 2E1 or 2J2. However, elinzanetant and its metabolites showed
inhibitory effect on CYP3A4. Therefore, the effect of elinzanetant on the pharmacokinetics of
midazolam (MDZ), a sensitive CYP3A4 substrate, was evaluated in vivo following single-dose
administration (Table 86) and multiple dosing (Study 21674, Figure 37) of elinzanetant and
following single- and multiple-dose administration of elinzanetant in Study 21840 (Figure 37)
(see Section 14.2.4.2, Section 14.2.4.8, and Section 14.2.4.3, respectively).
In Study 21667, coadministration of MDZ 1 mg with a single dose of elinzanetant 120 mg
resulted in 14% increase in Cmax and 45% increase in the AUC of MDZ. These findings suggest
that elinzanetant is a weak inhibitor of CYP3A4 (Table 86). In Study 21840, the effect of
elinzanetant on the pharmacokinetics of MDZ was investigated after a single dose of elinzanetant
120 mg and following repeated once daily oral administration of elinzanetant 120 mg over 14
days. Following a single dose of elinzanetant, a Cmax increase of 15%, and an AUC increase of
50% was observed. Following multiple doses of elinzanetant, an increase of Cmax by 49%, and an
increase of AUC by 80% was observed for midazolam, confirming that elinzanetant is a weak
inhibitor (<2-fold) of CYP3A4 after repeated dosing (Figure 37). Since the study results
demonstrated that the concomitant use of elinzanetant increases the exposure of CYP3A4
substrates, this may elevate the risk of adverse reactions associated with these substrates.
Therefore, the clinical pharmacology review team recommends avoiding concomitant use of
CYP3A4 substrates.
In vitro studies revealed that elinzanetant and its metabolites M27, M30/34, and M18/21 had
inhibitory effect on the activity of human uridine diphosphate glucuronosyltransferase 1A1
(UGT1A1) enzyme. By applying the mechanistic-static model described in the FDA guidance
for industry M12 Drug Interaction Studies (August 2024), no risk for clinically relevant DDIs
due to UGT1A1 inhibition by elinzanetant or its metabolites M27, M30/34, or M18/21 was
identified.
In vitro studies have demonstrated that elinzanetant and its metabolites M18/21, M27, and
M30/34 exhibit inhibitory activity against P-gp. However, clinical DDI Study 22081, which
involved the coadministration of dabigatran (DBG) etexilate and elinzanetant, revealed no
clinically significant inhibition of P-gp. In another study, Study 22004, following a single dose
administration of 20 mg tamoxifen (a P-gp substrate) together with multiple once daily doses of
120 mg elinzanetant, the effect of elinzanetant on the pharmacokinetics of tamoxifen and its
principal metabolites (N-desmethyltamoxifen, 4-hydroxytamoxifen, and endoxifen) were
investigated. The study results (Figure 37) showed that there were no clinically relevant changes

181
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
in the pharmacokinetics of tamoxifen and its metabolites. Therefore, no tamoxifen dose
adjustments are needed when elinzanetant is taken concomitantly.
In vitro analyses also indicated that elinzanetant and its metabolites inhibit breast cancer
resistance protein (BCRP) and elinzanetant possesses possible inhibitory potential for organic
anion transporting polypeptide (OATP) 1B1, and OATP1B3. Nevertheless, the results of the
dedicated clinical DDI Study 21666 did not identify clinically significant change in the exposure
of rosuvastatin (a sensitive substrate of BCRP, OATP1B1/1B3 and organic anion transporter
[OAT] 3) when rosuvastatin was administered either simultaneously with elinzanetant or 3 hours
after elinzanetant (Figure 37).
Clinical DDI studies were not conducted to assess elinzanetant and its metabolites M18/21, M27,
and M30/34 as inhibitors of OAT1, OAT3, organic cation transporter (OCT) 1, OCT2, multidrug
and toxin extrusion protein 2 splice variant K (MATE2K), or multidrug resistance-associated
protein 2 (MRP2) since in vitro data indicated no inhibitory effect on these transporters.
Moreover, the risk of clinically relevant inhibition of the multidrug and toxin extrusion protein 1
(MATE1) and bile salt export pump (BSEP) by elinzanetant and its metabolites is low based on
FDA’s guidance.
Induction Potential
In vitro studies using human hepatocyte demonstrated that elinzanetant and its metabolites
(M18/21, M27, and M30/34) did not induce CYP1A2. Similarly, elinzanetant and its metabolite
M30/34 did not induce CYP3A4 enzyme activity level. However, metabolites M18/21 and M27
exhibited slight induction of CYP3A4. Furthermore, elinzanetant and its metabolites M18/21,
M27, and M30/34 induced the coregulated CYP isoforms CYP2B6 and CYP2C19. Despite the
observed slight induction potential for certain CYP enzyme isoforms in vitro, per M12 Drug
Interaction Studies guidance (August 2024), elinzanetant and its metabolites M18/21, M27,
M30/34 have low induction potential on CYP enzymes in vivo. In addition, clinical studies
21667 and 21840 revealed no clinically relevant induction of CYP3A4 activity after multiple
dosing with elinzanetant (Figure 37).

8.3. Plans for Pediatric Drug Development
The elinzanetant clinical development program was undertaken to address an indication which is
applicable only to postmenopausal women. Therefore, no pediatric studies or assessments of
effects on growth were conducted for elinzanetant. In accordance with the Pediatric Research
Equity Act, Bayer requested a full waiver from the requirement to submit data adequate to assess
the safety and efficacy of the elinzanetant in all relevant pediatric subpopulations in accordance
with 21 CFR 314.55(c)(2)(ii).
Under IND 129492, the Applicant submitted an Initial Pediatric Study Plan on January 6, 2021,
and a Request for Full Waiver of Pediatric Studies on January 8, 2021. The Pediatric Review
Committee met on March 16, 2021, and agreed with issuing a full waiver for pediatric studies
because necessary studies are impossible or highly impracticable as the number of subjects
would be too small. On April 25, 2021, FDA issued an Agreed Initial Pediatric Study Plan letter
stating FDA’s agreement with the Applicant’s plan to request a full waiver of pediatric studies.
The Pediatric Review Committee reviewed and agreed with this waiver on June 17, 2025.

8.4. Pregnancy, Lactation, and Females/Males of
Reproductive Potential
Use of elinzanetant is contraindicated in pregnancy. Based on nonclinical findings, exposure to
elinzanetant may cause pregnancy loss or stillbirth when administered during pregnancy. Before
starting treatment with elinzanetant, pregnancy should be ruled out. If pregnancy occurs during
use of elinzanetant, treatment should be withdrawn. In addition, because postmenopausal status
is a typically retrospective diagnosis and it may be difficult for perimenopausal women to know
whether they are postmenopausal with certainty, women who are of child-bearing potential
should use effective methods of contraception during treatment with elinzanetant.
Regarding the risk of lactation, there are no data on the presence of elinzanetant or its
metabolites in human milk, the effects on the breastfed child, or the effects on milk production.
Animal Data
Nonclinical findings from developmental and reproductive toxicology studies conducted in rats
and rabbits were used in support of the drug’s labeling. Main nonclinical data supporting
labeling on fertility, pregnancy, and lactation are listed in Table 87. The reproductive and

Human Data
Pregnancy
No human pregnancies occurred during the development program for elinzanetant. Notably,
elinzanetant is intended for symptoms due to menopause.
Lactation
There are no data on the presence of elinzanetant or its metabolites in human milk, the effects on
the breastfed child, or the effects on milk production. Elinzanetant is present in animal milk.
When a drug is present in animal milk, it is likely that the drug will be present in human milk.
Females and Males of Reproductive Potential
Based on findings from animal reproduction studies, elinzanetant may cause pregnancy loss or
stillbirth but not fetal malformations when administered during pregnancy. For women of
reproductive potential, providers should exclude pregnancy before initiating treatment with
elinzanetant and perform pregnancy testing if pregnancy is suspected during treatment with
elinzanetant, and discontinue treatment if pregnancy is confirmed. Pregnancy should be
prevented in women of reproductive potential by using effective contraception during and for 2
weeks after stopping treatment because elinzanetant can cause pregnancy loss or stillbirth.

9. Product Quality
Drug Substance
Elinzanetant is a selective, nonhormonal NK1 and NK3 receptor antagonist. Elinzanetant has not
been previously approved or marketed as a drug in the United States and therefore, it is classified
as an NME.

III. Additional Analyses and Information
12. Summary of Regulatory History
NeRRE acquired NT-814 from GlaxoSmthKline (GSK) in 2012. On April 4, 2016, FDA
provided written responses to a pre-IND meeting request submitted by NeRRe Therapeutics Ltd.
(NeRRe) for NT-814 (later renamed elinzanetant). From a CMC perspective, the information on
drug substance and drug product appeared adequate to open an IND. Similarly, the
pharmacology/toxicology studies appeared adequate to open an IND, pending final review of the
study reports. In terms of the clinical study design, FDA did not agree with the proposed Phase
2a proof-of-concept study design. FDA recommended that the Applicant open the IND with a
stand-alone Phase 1, dose-escalating, PK/bioavailability study in postmenopausal women. FDA
expressed concerns about the proposed starting dose of (b) (4) mg once daily, citing cardiovascular
adverse events (including atrial fibrillation, ventricular tachycardia, syncope, and orthostatic
hypotension) observed at lower doses in previous studies. The Agency recommended starting at
50 mg with dose escalation by 50 mg increments up to 150 mg. Following completion of the
stand-alone PK/bioavailability study, FDA recommended the Applicant submit the results for
review and submit a protocol for a Phase 2 proof-of-concept study that could identify the lowest
effective dose to be studied in Phase 3. There was also discussion of the overall clinical
development program, and FDA emphasized the recommendations in the FDA draft guidance for
industry Estrogen and Estrogen/Progestin Drug Products to Treat Vasomotor Symptoms and
Vulvar and Vaginal Atrophy Symptoms – Recommendations for Clinical Evaluation (January
2003). Specific considerations included the anticipated study population for an indication of the
treatment of moderate to severe VMS due to menopause, and the FDA recommended four
coprimary endpoints: mean change in frequency and severity of moderate to severe vasomotor
symptoms from baseline to Weeks 4 and 12.
The investigational new drug application (IND 129492) was initially submitted by NeRRe on
June 6, 2016, and was allowed to proceed. On August 14, 2020, NeRRe submitted a special
protocol assessment (SPA) request for a 104-week Sprague Dawley rat carcinogenicity protocol.
The Agency denied the request on September 1, 2020, because it was an incomplete submission.
A SPA was resubmitted for a carcinogenicity protocol on September 4, 2020. The Executive
Carcinogenicity Assessment Committee agreed with the protocol and provided comments and
recommendations to the Applicant on October 21, 2020.
Bayer acquired NT-814 from NeRRe in September 2020.
On November 17, 2020, an EOP2 Type B meeting was held via teleconference (meeting minutes
dated December 17, 2020). The purpose of the meeting was to discuss the findings of the Phase
2b dose-finding study (SWITCH-1) and the Phase 3 clinical program. During this meeting, FDA
disagreed with Bayer's proposed single 120 mg dose for Phase 3 studies, noting that in
SWITCH-1, the 120 mg dose failed to meet all four coprimary endpoints, specifically lacking
statistical significance for severity reduction at Weeks 4 and 12 despite showing significant
frequency reduction. FDA recommended conducting dose-ranging Phase 3 studies including
both effective and ineffective doses. Bayer noted that with the planned sample size in the Phase 3

13.2.1. Pharmacology
13.2.1.1. Primary Pharmacology
Elinzanetant is an NME that acts as a noncompetitive antagonist of both NK1R and NK3R.
In binding assays, elinzanetant displayed high affinity for human NK1R (pKi values of 8.71 to
10.15 [mean pKi of 9.43]) and NK3R (pKi values of 8.03 to 8.8 [mean pKi of 8.42]).
Elinzanetant has ~10-fold lower affinity towards human NK3R compared to human NK1R.
Additionally, elinzanetant has higher affinity for human NK1R and NK3R than for human NK2
receptors (pKi values of approximately 6.0). In functional in vitro assays, elinzanetant inhibited
the activity of human NK1R and NK3R, with calculated pKB values of 9.02 to 9.1 for human
NK1R and 8.17 to 8.5 for human NK3R.
Drug Activity Related to Proposed Indication
In the context of VMS due to menopause, NK1R and NK3R antagonists are thought to act by
inhibiting the activity of KNDy neurons, which project to the vasomotor center in the median
preoptic nucleus to modulate neuronal activity involved in thermoregulation. This inhibition of
KNDy neurons, which are thought to be in a hyperactivated state because of estrogen decline in
menopause, is proposed to result in improvement of menopause-associated VMS (Figure 1).
KNDy neurons also synapse onto hypothalamic neurons that secrete GnRH, and, by suppressing
the activity of NK1R/NK3R in KNDy neurons, elinzanetant may suppress hypothalamic GnRH
secretion and, consequently, reduce the release of gonadotropins (LH and FSH) from the
pituitary (Figure 1). Although the relationship between gonadotropin levels and VMS is poorly
understood, studies have reported synchrony between hot flushes and LH secretion (Sassarini
and Anderson 2024). It is unknown whether suppression of gonadotropin levels contributes to
the effectiveness of elinzanetant to mitigate menopause-associated VMS.

Ex Vivo and In Vivo Receptor Occupancy Studies
Ex vivo receptor occupancy studies showed that elinzanetant occupied NK1Rs in the human
putamen in a concentration-dependent manner with a pKi of 9.44 (Study R-13876).
The PET study in baboon following a single intravenous (IV) dose demonstrated a dosedependent brain NK1R occupancy with an estimated half-maximal effective concentration
(EC50) of 9.93 ng/mL (Study R-13885).
Elinzanetant (HCl form) was found to penetrate the gerbil brain (dorsal striatum and cingulate
cortex) following single oral dosing (1, 3, 10, and 30 mg/kg) and occupy both NK1R and NK3R.
At 10 minutes after a single oral dose of 1 mg/kg, NK1R occupancy (~72%) was greater than
NK3R occupancy (~31%). Daily dosing (4 to 5 days) did not result in elinzanetant accumulation
in brain and blood and did not increase NK1R/NK3R occupancy (Study R-13860).
Ex vivo autoradiography in guinea pig brain was used to determine the effect of haloperidol (D2
antagonist) on elinzanetant exposure and receptor occupancy. Treatment of guinea pigs with
haloperidol had no significant effect on NK1R occupancy by elinzanetant, and mean NK1R
occupancy was >97% at all doses tested (30 mg/kg and 100 mg/kg). Mean NK3R occupancy by
elinzanetant at 30 and 100 mg/kg was 37% and 78% in vehicle-treated guinea pigs, respectively,
and 74% and 85% in haloperidol-treated guinea pigs, respectively. The apparently higher NK3R
occupancy in guinea pigs treated with haloperidol at the lower dose of elinzanetant correlated
with higher exposure of the haloperidol-treated animals to elinzanetant. The data suggest that
NK1R/NK3R occupancy by elinzanetant was not affected by the dopamine D2 receptor
antagonist haloperidol (Study R-13880).
In Vivo Primary Pharmacodynamic Studies
The Applicant investigated the in vivo pharmacodynamic activity of elinzanetant in a gerbil foot
tapping model of NK1R activity and in the guinea pig wet-dog shake model of NK3R activity.
Oral dosing of male gerbils with elinzanetant dose dependently reduced foot tapping induced by
the NK1R agonist GR73632 (ID50 [dose resulting a 50% reduction in time spent foot tapping]
=1.36 mg/kg). Similarly, elinzanetant doses of 8.5 and 25.5 mg/kg significantly reduced the wetdog shake behavior induced by the NK3R agonist senktide in the guinea pigs. Both findings
indicate a central NK3R antagonist activity of elinzanetant.
As noted earlier in Section 5, the Applicant did not conduct in vivo animal studies to
demonstrate elinzanetant effects in reducing hot flash-like signs.

13.2.2. Pharmacokinetics and Toxicokinetics
Absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion of elinzanetant were assessed in whole-body
autoradiography studies rats and nonradiolabeled assays in rats, monkeys, and dogs. The key
findings are noted below.
Absorption


Oral bioavailability was moderate in male and female rats (77% and 47%) and low in
monkeys and dogs (19%).



Clearance differed between species. It was low in rats with differential clearance between
male and female rats. Significant accumulation of elinzanetant was observed over the dose
range tested in female rats, but not in male rats.



High clearance of elinzanetant in dogs was associated with its low oral bioavailability in this
species. Therefore, monkeys (also with low bioavailability of 19% but moderate clearance

200
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
compared to dog) were chosen as the second nonclinical species for chronic toxicity studies
besides rats.


No notable accumulation was observed in monkeys after repeat dosing.

Distribution


In rat whole-body autoradiography studies, radioactivity showed high distribution in majority
of the tissues.
– Highest levels were noted in liver, kidney, adrenal gland, abdominal and brown fat,
bulbo-urethral gland, pancreas, lacrimal glands, harderian gland and mucous gland; brain
had lower levels which did not change with time (no accumulation).
– After 35 days, radioactivity was noted in brown fat, uveal tract/retina, spleen. and adrenal
cortex (Study R-13624).


The Applicant notes uveal tract/retina concentration indicates some long-term
association of drug-related material with melanin.



The Applicant conducted an in vitro phototoxicity study, which is discussed under
special toxicology studies (see Section 13.2.3).



The potential for elinzanetant to accumulate in melanin-rich tissues of the eyes and
skin and be phototoxic in humans cannot be ruled out and is also discussed in
Section 7.



In pregnant rats, the organ distribution of elinzanetant was similar to nonpregnant rats. Fetal
and associated tissue concentrations were generally much lower than maternal blood, except
for amnion, placenta, and brain. The AUC(0-tlast) ratio of placenta/maternal blood was 1.3,
fetus average/amniotic fluid was 18.3, and fetal brain/maternal brain was 2.4 (Study R14360).



Plasma protein binding was high across all preclinical species tested (99.5 to 99.9%) and
higher in human (>99.9%) for elinzanetant as well as the principal metabolites (M27,
M30/34, and M18/21). No concentration dependence of the unbound fraction (fu) of
elinzanetant was observed. These are summarized in Table 96.

Effects of Elinzanetant and its Metabolites on Transporters
The interaction of elinzanetant with various transporters was investigated in in vitro studies.
Elinzanetant as a Substrate


Elinzanetant is classified as a substrate of P-gp, a transporter that removes substances from
cells. IV coadministration of elinzanetant with elacridar (GF120918A) [a nonspecific
inhibitor of P-gp efflux transporters] to rats increased by ~5X the elinzanetant brain:blood
ratio and by ~2.5X the systemic exposure to elinzanetant (Study R-13621).



Elinzanetant is not a substrate of the bidirectional transporter BRCP, the uptake transporters
human OATP1A2 and human OATP2B1, and the MRP4 efflux transporters.



Elinzanetant is not a substrate of the OATP1B1, OATP1B3, OATP1A2 and OATP2B1
uptake transporters.

Elinzanetant and its Metabolites as an Inhibitor


Elinzanetant inhibited MATE1-, BSEP-, and OCT1-mediated metformin transport as well as
OAT3-, OATP1B1-, OATP1B3-mediated transport. Elinzanetant is an inhibitor of BCRP
with an IC50 value of 7.4μM (Study R-13631, Study R-13686, Study B002205, Study R13635).



OATP1B1 was inhibited by elinzanetant with an IC50 value of 0.7μM (Study R-13633).



Elinzanetant inhibited the transport of digoxin via human P-gp in vitro with an IC50 of
14±6μM (corresponding to 9.6 μg/mL as free base) (Study R-13634).



BAY 3427080 (elinzanetant), BAY 3462932 (M27), BAY 3462933 (M30/34), and BAY
3462934 inhibited OATP1B1 with IC50 values of 0.69μM, 0.59μM, 0.38μM and 1.21μM,
respectively (Study B002050).



BAY 3427080 (elinzanetant), BAY 3462932 (M27), BAY 3462933 (M30/34), and BAY
3462934 (M18/21) inhibited OATP1B3 with IC50 values of 0.25μM, 0.21μM, 0.19μM and
0.27μM, respectively (Study B002050).



Elinzanetant, BAY 3462932 (M27), BAY 3462933 (M30/34), and BAY 3462934 (M18/21)
inhibited human P-gp with IC50 values of 0.22μM, 1.51μM, 0.09μM and 2.94μM,
respectively (Study B002191).



Elinzanetant and the metabolites inhibited BCRP, with IC50 values of 0.08μM (elinzanetant),
0.48μM (M27) , 0.17μM (M30/34) and 1.38μM (M18/21) (Study B002163).



Using nonspecific binding of elinzanetant to OAT1, OAT3, OCT1, OCT2, MATE1, or
MATE2K, the Applicant predicted no in vivo DDI (Study R-14407).



BAY 3427080 (elinzanetant), M27, M30/34, M22 directly inhibited UGT1A1 in the uridine
diphosphate glucuronosyltransferases (UGTs) with IC50 values of 2.6μM., 0.46μM, 1.8μM
and 2.6μM, respectively (Study B002074).

Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)



Elinzanetant, BAY 3469432 (M27), BAY 3469433 (M30/34) and BAY 3469434 (M18/21)
were classified as inhibitors of BSEP with IC50 values of 2.13μM, 5.91μM, 9.20μM and
16.7μM, respectively (Study B002085).

13.2.3. Toxicology
13.2.3.1. General Toxicology (Pivotal Studies)
Single-dose and repeat-dose toxicity studies with elinzanetant and metabolite M27, a
disproportionate human metabolite, were conducted in rat and monkey. The key findings from
all pivotal repeat-dose toxicity studies are described in Table 101 below. The GLP status of each
study is also noted. For calculation of nonclinical safety or exposure margins, the clinical
exposure at the MRHD of AUC(0-24)=8572 μg.h/L (from the clinical study number CPM50130
[report number B002427]) was used for comparison unless otherwise noted.
Section 7 provides the nonclinical integrated summary for potential nonclinical signals of clinical
concern observed in these studies.
For summary of all general toxicity studies refer to the nonclinical review in DARRTS
(DARRTS°ID:°5623053 2025).

LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
Repeat-Dose Toxicity Studies in Rat
Study No./Design
(NOAEL and Safety
Margin*)
Study Findings
FDA Analysis
 Skeletal muscle findings:
The Applicant does not provide any mechanistic basis for the findings of skeletal muscle degeneration and
necrosis, but concludes that the findings, along with the CNS findings observed in this study, cannot be ruled out
as treatment related. A follow up mechanistic study [R-13644 [QL24QG] failed to reproduce the results seen in
this study. The findings from this study related to skeletal muscle necrosis is included in the integrated summary
in Section 7 of this review.
 CNS findings (tremors and convulsions):
The Lowest Observed Adverse Effect Level (LOAEL) for these safety signals were 20 and 50 mg/kg/day in
female and male rats, respectively. A NOAEL was not established. Exposure [AUC(0-24)] data are available only
for treatment Days 1 and 91, whereas convulsions were first noted around treatment Day 34 in female and male.
Using the linear regression of the available AUC(0-24), it was estimated that exposures generated by the LOAELs
on the first day when convulsions were noted are ~4-fold higher than the clinical exposure generated by the
MRHD. The CNS-related effects of convulsions were observed in this study and in the 2-year carcinogenicity
study in female rats. The integrated summary for this finding is included in Section 7 of this review. For details on
exposure margin estimation for the CNS effects, refer to Section 13.2.5.
 Liver findings:
Increased liver weight accompanied by minimal hepatocellular atrophy was seen in this study. A nonpivotal 7day study with elinzanetant (study R-13586) also noted liver toxicity characterized by hepatocyte necrosis. The
liver findings are included in the integrated summary in Section 7 of this review.

Study No./Design

Study Findings
Histopathology:
 Lung: Dose-related incidence of macrophage infiltrations in the alveoli was noted in both sexes, without
increase in severity. Minimal infiltrates were noted in M and F @ 50 and 20 mg/kg/day respectively (low dose),
and also @ higher dose groups.
 Kidney: Tubular basophilia, hyaline casts and cortical scars were seen in males (no dose response),
correlated with the increase relative kidney weights and kidney macroscopic observations. Additionally, the
alterations of plasma electrolyte concentrations and markers of glomerular filtration rate suggest mild kidney
toxicity.
 Adrenal: Minimal hypertrophy of the adrenal cortex noted in 5/12 males and 4/12 females @ the high dose in
M and F.
 Thymus: Dose-related decrease in thymus weight in males was consistent with the dose-related increase in
incidence and severity of the atrophy in the thymus in F (minimal severity, increased incidence with dose) and
M (minimal to moderate severity, increased severity and incidence with dose).
 Liver: No histopathological findings in the liver. Mild dose-related liver-related effects in M, manifested by
elevated ALT and AST activity, higher bilirubin and a dose-related reduction in cholesterol concentration.
These changes were not accompanied by correlating histopathology and were considered adaptive rather
than toxicological.
Toxicokinetics:
 No accumulation occurred in M; however, notable accumulation was observed in F at all doses (2.4- to 3.0fold) after 26 weeks of dosing. At the comparable dose for M and F (50 mg/kg/day), exposure in F was notably
higher than in males and this difference was more pronounced with repeated administration.

FDA Analysis
 No tremors, convulsions, or other CNS-related safety signals were noted in the present study. This contrasts
with the findings of CNS-related safety signals (including rigidity, tremors, and convulsions) noted in rats were

 The absence of CNS-related safety signals in the present study could not be accounted for by insufficient

were first noted in rats when systemic exposures reached ~35.1 μg.h/mL and ~150 μg.h/mL, respectively
which are considerably lower than exposures measured in the present study [see Section 7 and
Section 13.2.5 for a discussion of the apparently discrepant findings].

LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
Study No./ Design
(NOAEL and Safety
Margin*)

Study Findings
Organ weight:
 Increase liver weight (relative to body or brain weight) in both M and F @ 40 mg/kg BID, with no corresponding
microscopic changes in the liver.
 In M, dose-dependent decrease in epididymides and testes mean weight. The male animals were found to have
varying degrees of sexual maturity that may have influenced organ weight differences (i.e., 2 controls were
sexually mature, whereas all treated males were immature).
FDA Analysis
NK1R/NK3R inhibition in KNDy neurons in the hypothalamus reduces the activity of hypothalamic neurons that
secrete gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH). The reduced GnRH release suppresses the release of
gonadotropins (luteinizing hormone [LH] and follicular stimulating hormone [FSH]) from the anterior pituitary gland. A
reduction of the LH and FSH levels due to elinzanetant-induced inhibition of NK1R/NK3R could explain the dosedependent reduction of the mean weight of epididymides and testes.
Histopathology:
 No test article-related changes in microscopic findings.
Toxicokinetics:
 High interanimal variability and some overlap in exposure between doses.
Mean exposure in M was higher than in F on both Days 1 and 91 @ 15 mg/kg BID whereas on Day 1 the mean
exposure in F @ 30 mg/kg BID was higher than in M.

Study Findings
Histopathology:
 Liver: Sinusoid compression in liver, presenting as narrowing of the sinusoidal space in M and @ 40 mg/kg, BID
and F @ 30 mg/kg BID.
 Large Intestine: Minimal inflammatory cell infiltrate was present in the mucosa of the cecum or colon of F @
40 mg/kg, BID.
 Ovaries: Corpora lutea and/or follicular activity was absent in the ovaries of F @ 30 and 40 mg/kg, BID, correlating
with a reduction in ovary weight. These changes are consistent with an observed lack of menstrual cycling;
however, menstrual status was not monitored for females during the in-life phase of this study. These findings are
consistent with the expected pharmacological effects of elinzanetant.
Toxicokinetics:
 High inter animal variability was noted, which may impact dose proportionality, dose accumulation and gender
differences and therefore evaluations should be interpreted with caution. Of note, 1 F @ 60 mg/kg/day female (No.
470) showed notably higher systemic exposure than other females of the same group, likely causing higher AUC
compared to M at that dose.
 Excluding the 1 F @ 60 mg/kg/day (No. 470), systemic exposure (Cmax and AUC) increased in a dose proportional
manner from 30 to 60 mg/kg/day in both males and females.
 Exposure was notably higher (2.5X) in M @ 80 mg/kg/day on Day 1 compared to Week 39.
 Metabolites M27, M22, M18/21, and M30/34 systemic exposures were measured in this study. Refer to the
nonclinical review in DARRTS (DARRTS°ID:°5623053 2025) for details.

13.2.3.3. Carcinogenicity
The nonclinical integrated summary for the rat carcinogenicity findings as a potential nonclinical
signal of clinical concern is described in Section 7. Also refer to the carcinogenicity review in
DARRTS dated February 4, 2025 (DARRTS°ID:°5523839 2025) and FDA’s statistical review in
DARRTS dated December 12, 2024 (DARRTS°ID:°5494197 2024). A brief summary of both
studies is noted below.
13.2.3.3.1. Carcinogenicity Study in Rat (104-Week;
B003186)
The rat carcinogenicity study was conducted in female Sprague Dawley rat (Envigo, IN, United
States) at 0, 7, 20, 60, 80 mg/kg/day [0, 3.5, 10, 30, 40 mg/kg BID] via oral gavage. The overall
study conduct was considered adequate.
Key Study Findings


Oral treatment of female Sprague Dawley rats with elinzanetant doses ranging from 7 to
80 mg/kg/day compared to vehicle for 104 weeks dose-dependently reduced body weight
gain but had no effect on overall survival.



Elizabethan treatment resulted in neoplastic findings. The effects were statistically significant
with respect to the dose-response relationships and pairwise group comparisons with the
vehicle control. The neoplastic findings are noted below and in Table 116:
– Malignant lymphoma in the hematolymphoid system at 80 mg/kg/day.
– Malignant endometrial adenocarcinoma of the uterus at ≥60 mg/kg/day.
– Combined malignant and benign endometrial tumors at ≥60 mg/kg/day.
– Combined malignant and benign endometrial tumors and malignant squamous cell
carcinoma of the uterus at ≥60 mg/kg/day.



The oral dose of 20 mg/kg/day was the highest test dose not associated with carcinogenic
signals in female rats. Based on AUCs, the clinical exposure margins (safety margin)
provided by the highest noncarcinogenic dose to the MRHD is 7.5X for elinzanetant.



The oral dose of 60 mg/kg/day was the lowest test dose associated with carcinogenic signals
in female rats. Based on AUCs, the clinical exposure margin provided by this dose to the
MRHD is 29X for elinzanetant.
13.2.3.3.2. Carcinogenicity Study in Transgenic Mice (26Week; B003184)

The mouse carcinogenicity study was conducted in male and female transgenic ras H2 mice at 0,
10, 30, 85 mg/kg/day in males (0, 5, 15, 42.5 mg/kg BID) and at 0, 10, 20, 70 mg/kg/day in
females (0, 5, 10, 35 mg/kg BID) via oral gavage. N-methyl-N-nitrosourea single intraperitoneal
dose on Day 1 as used as the positive control. The overall study was considered adequate.
Key Study Findings


Elinzanetant did not affect the overall survival and induced no adverse clinical signs up to the
high dose of 85 mg/kg/day in males and 70 mg/kg/day in females.



Oral treatment with elinzanetant doses ranging from 10 to 85 mg/kg/day in males and 10 to
70 mg/kg/day in females compared to vehicle for 26 weeks resulted in no statistically
significant neoplastic findings.
13.2.3.4. Reproductive and Developmental Toxicity

A full battery of reproductive and developmental toxicity studies was conducted in rats and
rabbits. The studies are summarized below. Also refer to Section 8 for details on findings from
these studies used to support labeling.

for 22 days before cohabitation with untreated males and Days 1 to 14 during cohabitation with
untreated males and on postcoital Days 0 to 6. The major study findings are noted in Table 117:

13.2.5. Multiples of Exposure for Convulsions
CNS-related safety signals, including convulsions, were noted in the 13-week repeat-dose
toxicity Study R-13628 conducted in male and female rats and in the 2-year carcinogenicity
study conducted in female rats Study B003186. As discussed in this section, multiples of
exposure at the time convulsions induced by elinzanetant were first noticed in these studies were
estimated based on extrapolated AUC(0-24) for each study as compared to the exposure of
8572 μg•h/L generated by the MRHD.
In the 13-week repeat-dose toxicity Study R-13628, convulsions were observed at all tested
doses (≥20 mg/kg/day in female rats and ≥50 mg/kg/day in male rats) and were first noted
around treatment Day 34. In the carcinogenicity Study B003186, which was conducted in female
rats only, the incidence of convulsions was markedly higher in rats treated with elinzanetant
doses ≥60 mg/kg/day compared with vehicle. In this study, convulsions in rats treated with the
doses of 60 and 80 mg/kg/day were first noted around treatment Days 162 and 106, respectively.
For female rats, the oral LOAELs for convulsions were 20 mg/kg/day in the 13-week study and
60 mg/kg/day in the carcinogenicity study.
In the 13-week repeat-dose toxicity Study R-13628, exposures (AUC(0-24)) were measured on
treatment Days 1 and 91. Using the linear regression of the time-dependent increase in AUC(0-24)
Figure 41, the AUC(0-24) generated in female rats treated with the LOAEL (20 mg/kg/day) when
convulsions were first observed (treatment Day 34) was estimated to be approximately
35111 μg•h/L. Using the same approach, the AUC(0-24) generated in male rats treated with the
LOAEL (50 mg/kg/day) on treatment Day 34 was estimated to be approximately 31930 μg•h/L.
Within the study, elinzanetant exposures capable of inducing convulsions were relatively
consistent between sexes and were ~4-fold higher than the clinical exposure of 8572 μg•h/L
generated by the MRHD of elinzanetant (120 mg/day) in women.

In the 2-year carcinogenicity study, exposures were assessed on treatment Days 1, 176, and 358.
Using the linear regression of the time-dependent increase in AUC0-24 at the oral LOAEL for
convulsions in this study (60 mg/kg/day) (Figure 41), systemic exposure was estimated to be
~149399 μg•h/L at the time when convulsions were first noted in elinzanetant-treated female rats
(treatment Day 162). Using the same approach, the AUC(0-24) generated in female rats treated for
2 years with the elinzanetant dose of 80 mg/kg (Figure 42) was estimated to be ~150076 μg•h/L
at the time convulsions were first noted at this dose (treatment Day 106).
Thus, within the 2-year carcinogenicity study, exposures needed to induce convulsions in female
rats were relatively consistent between doses and were ~17-fold higher than the clinical exposure
of 8572 μg•h/L generated by the MRHD of elinzanetant (120 mg/day) in women.

Considering the estimated AUC(0-24) generated by the LOAELs in the 13-week toxicity study and
the carcinogenicity study and the exposure of 8572 μg•h/L generated by the MRHD, multiples of
exposure for convulsions were estimated to be ~4X and ~17X the MRHD, respectively.
Convulsions were not observed in the 26-week repeat-dose toxicity Study R-13894 in which
male and female rats were treated twice daily with elinzanetant doses ranging from 50 to
180 mg/kg/day and 20 to 80 mg/kg/day, respectively. However, the apparently inconsistent CNS
effects could not be fully accounted for by insufficient systemic exposures. As noted above, at
the time when convulsions were first noted, systemic exposures generated by the oral LOAELs
were ~35111 μg•h/L in female rats in the 13-week study and ~149399 μg•h/L in female rats in
the 2-year carcinogenicity study. In the 26-week study, systemic exposures were as high as
311000 μg•h/L in female rats treated twice daily with the oral dose of 80 mg/kg/day. Considering
the time-dependent increase in AUC(0-24) observed in females treated with the dose of
80 mg/kg/day in the 26-week study, AUC(0-24)s in these animals exceeded 149399 μg•h/L after
treatment Day 42. Yet, convulsions were not observed throughout the entire duration of the 26week study (182 days).
The studies differed with respect to the SD rat substrains and their sources. Specifically, the SD
rats used in the 13-week study, the 2-year carcinogenicity, and the 26-week studies were from
the same substrain (SD:Hsd). However, they were sourced from Envigo, United States, Envigo,
Netherlands, and Envigo, United Kingdom, respectively. Convulsions were also not observed in
the 13-week repeat-dose toxicity study R-13596 in which rats were treated once daily for 13
weeks with elinzanetant doses generating exposures as high as 56700 μg•h/L in male rats and

242
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
135000 μg•h/L in female rats. The substrain of rats used in the 13-week study R-13596 was
SD:Crl, and the animals were sourced from Charles River, Canada.
Although not conclusively established, the apparently discrepant findings could be related to
differential seizure susceptibility of the rat substrains from difference sources. According to a
published study (Langer et al. 2011), SD:Crl rats are less susceptible than SD:Hsd rats to
developing seizures in response to electrical stimulation of the BLA. In addition, SD:Hsd rats
from the Netherlands are less susceptible than SD:Hsd rats from Germany to developing seizures
in response to BLA electrical stimulation.

13.3. Excipients, Impurities and Degradation
Products
The excipients and their amounts in the elinzanetant drug product are acceptable from the
nonclinical perspective. The drug substance and drug product impurity release specification and
shelf-life specification are set either as per the ICH guidance for industry Q3A(R) Impurities in
New Drug Substances (June 2008) and the ICH guidance for industry Q3B(R2) Impurities in
New Drug Products (August 2006) or qualified based on Permissible Daily Exposure/Total Daily
Intake (PDE/TDI) calculation utilizing NOAEL derived from nonclinical studies. Overall, the
specifications are acceptable from nonclinical perspective.

13.3.1. Excipients
The elinzanetant drug product has no novel excipients for the oral route of administration. Table
129 lists the maximal daily exposures (MDEs) to the excipients considering the maximal
recommended human dose of 120 mg elinzanetant.

The maximal daily doses of two excipients (glyceryl monocaprylocaprate and glyceryl
monooleate) exceed the maximal daily exposures (MDEs) in previously approved oral drug
products per the FDA Inactive Ingredient Report (IIR) (Table 129).

Glyceryl Monooleate
Api et al. (2021) reported that the oral NOAEL for glyceryl monooleate in a repeat-dose toxicity
study in rats was 1,000 mg/kg/day (the highest test dose). In this GLP-compliant, combined
repeat-dose and reproductive study, Sprague Dawley rats were administered glyceryl monooleate
via oral gavage (0, 100, 300, or 1000 mg/kg/day; n=12 rats/sex/dose). Males were dosed for 42
days (starting 14 days prior to mating and continuing through the mating period); females were
dosed up to lactation Day 4. An additional 5 Sprague Dawley rats/sex/dose were maintained for
2 weeks after dosing as a recovery group. No mortality occurred throughout the study period.
There were no treatment-related effects on general condition, clinical observations, sensory
reflex function test, landing leg width, grip strength, locomotor activity, body weight, food
consumption, urinalysis (male only), hematology, organ weight, organ function, clinical
chemistry, necropsy, or histopathology.
A permitted daily exposure (PDE) for glyceryl monooleate is estimated using the NOAEL of
1,000 mg/kg/day in rats and the formula:

Per the CFR, 21 CFR §184.1323, glyceryl monooleate of a purity suitable for its intended use is
an ingredient generally recognized as safe, as a direct human food ingredient. In addition, as
described in a 1986 publication (CIR Expert Panel 1986), federal regulations also allow the use
of glyceryl oleate as a prior-sanctioned food ingredient (21 CFR§181.27) and as both an indirect
(21 CFR §175.300, 21 CFR§75.320) and direct (21 CFR 175.515) food additive.
Thus, based on the totality of the information, glyceryl monooleate is considered adequately
qualified as an excipient in the Applicant’s product.

14. Clinical Pharmacology
14.1. In Vitro Studies
Elinzanetant is also referred to as GSK1144814, BAY 3427080, and NT-814.

14.1.1. Distribution
Plasma Protein Binding (Module 4.2.2.3, PH-42081 for Parent, PH-42138 for Metabolites)
The protein binding of elinzanetant and its metabolites is high in female human plasma. The
mean fu values of elinzanetant, M27, M30/34, M18/21 were 0.332%, 0.0689%, 0.514%, and
0.140%, respectively, in plasma of females.
Blood Plasma Partitioning (Cb/Cp) (Module 4.2.2.3, Report PH-42081)
The measured Cb/Cp was less than 1 and amounted to 0.574 in man and 0.663 in woman. Since
the Cb/Cp was less than 1, more substance distributed into plasma than into the blood cells.
The distribution between blood cells and plasma was investigated in the concentration range of
536 μg/L to 47549 μg/L. No concentration dependent Cb/Cp binding in the tested concentration
range was observed.

14.1.2. Metabolism Studies
Elinzanetant is Primarily Metabolized by CYP3A4 (Module 4.2.2.6, Report R-13657)
The enzymes responsible for the oxidative metabolism of elinzanetant were investigated with
human liver microsomes and recombinant CYP enzymes. [14C] elinzanetant at 5μM was
metabolized in human liver microsomes to oxidized metabolites M18/M21, M24, and
M30&M32/M34 and dehydrogenated metabolite M39 as the major metabolites. M18/M21, M24,
M30&M32/34 and M39 formation, which constituted 7.8%, 9.0%, 29% and 12%, respectively,
of the metabolites generated by human liver microsomes, was inhibited by azamulin, a selective
253
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
CYP3A4 inhibitor. M27, M30&M32/M34 and M39 were also formed in recombinant CYP3A4
incubations as major metabolites. Incubations with recombinant CYP1A2, CYP2B6, CYP2C8,
CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2D6 and CYP2E1 showed little or no metabolism. Data from human
liver microsomes with selective inhibitors and results from recombinant CYP enzyme
incubations suggest that CYP3A4 is the primary CYP enzyme involved in the oxidative
metabolism of elinzanetant in vitro.
Minor Contribution of CYP3A5 and UGT Pathways (Module 4.2.2.6, Report PH-42629)
Oxidation via CYP3A was observed in vitro and in vivo as dominant human biotransformation
route of elinzanetant, while direct glucuronidation of parent drug was a minor pathway. To
estimate the fraction metabolized via UGT and CYP3A from human hepatocytes, reaction
phenotyping experiments were performed applying cobicistat as a potent CYP3A inhibitor and
cyp3cide as a selective CYP3A4 inhibitor. Complete inhibition of all oxidative pathways was
observed in the presence of cobicistat, and the fraction metabolized via CYP3A was calculated to
be in the range of ~88 to 94%, while ~5 to 12% were assigned to the UGT pathway. CYP3A5
contribution to total clearance was in the range of ~6 to 15%. Therefore, a clinically relevant
impact of the CYP3A5 polymorphism on the total clearance of elinzanetant is considered
unlikely.
Elinzanetant is not a Substrate for Aldehyde Oxidase (Module 4.2.2.2, Report 13621)
Metabolic stability of elinzanetant to aldehyde oxidase was evaluated. Following incubation with
human cytosol at a concentration of 0.5μM elinzanetant and in the presence of isovanillin
(known inhibitor of aldehyde oxidase), the rate constants (k) values under both conditions were
less than 0.0055, indicating that elinzanetant is not a substrate for aldehyde oxidase.

14.1.3. In Vitro Metabolism-Mediated Drug Interaction
Studies
CYP and UGT Inhibition
Module 4.2.2.6, PH-42451
The potential of elinzanetant and its metabolites M30/M34, M18/M21 and M27 to act as directacting inhibitors of human cytochrome P450 isoforms (CYP1A1, 1A2, 2A6, 2B6, 2C8, 2C9,
2C19, 2D6, 2E1, 2J2 and 3A4) was evaluated in vitro with pooled human liver microsomes or
recombinant CYP1A1 and 2J2. No direct-acting inhibitory potency up to the highest tested
concentrations (IC50>5μM) for elinzanetant and metabolites M30/M34, M18/M21 and M27 was
observed for CYP1A1, 1A2, 2A6, 2B6, 2C8, 2C9, 2C19, 2D6, 2E1, 2J2 and 3A4 (testosterone
6β-hydroxylation). Applying a rank order approach, elinzanetant (IC50=0.77μM), M30/M34
(IC50=0.98μM), M18/M21 (IC50=1.1μM) and M27 (IC50=1.2μM) showed inhibitory potency on
CYP3A4 (midazolam 1’-hydroxylation).
The potential to act as metabolism-dependent (time-dependent) inhibitors of human cytochrome
P450 isoforms (CYP1A1, 1A2, 2B6, 2C8, 2C9, 2C19, 2D6, and 3A4) was evaluated in vitro with
pooled human liver microsomes or recombinant CYP1A1 after 30 minutes preincubation with
and without NADPH-regenerating system. No clinically relevant metabolism-dependent (time254

dependent) inhibitory potency of elinzanetant on biotransformation reactions catalyzed by
CYP1A1, 1A2, 2B6, 2C8, 2C9, 2C19 and 2D6 was observed. A slight increase in the inhibitory

1’-hydroxylation, elinzanetant: IC50=0.40μM; M30/M34: IC50=0.31μM; M18/M21:

Module 4.2.2.6, B002074
To evaluate elinzanetant (BAY 3427080), M27 (BAY 3462932), M30/34 (BAY 3462933) and

were incubated with marker substrates in the presence or absence of the test compound.
BAY 3427080 directly inhibited UGT1A1 with an IC50 value of 2.6μM. Less than 50% direct

BAY 3427080 (up to concentrations of 5μM) was not a direct inhibitor (<20% maximal
