inhibition by BAY 3462932 (up to concentrations of 5μM) was observed for UGT1A4 and
UGT2B7. BAY 3462932 (up to concentrations of 5μM) was not a direct inhibitor (<20%
maximal inhibition) of UGT1A3, UGT1A6, UGT1A9, UGT2B15 or UGT2B17.
BAY 3462933 directly inhibited UGT1A1 with an IC50 value of 1.8μM. Less than 50% direct
inhibition by BAY 3462933 (up to concentrations of 5μM) was observed for UGT2B7.
BAY 3462933 (up to concentrations of 5μM) was not a direct inhibitor (<20% maximal
inhibition) of UGT1A3, UGT1A4, UGT1A6, UGT1A9, UGT2B15 or UGT2B17.
BAY 3462934 directly inhibited UGT1A1 with an IC50 value of 2.6μM. Less than 50% direct
inhibition by BAY 3462934 (up to concentrations of 5μM) was observed for UGT1A6.
BAY 3462934 (up to concentrations of 5μM) was not a direct inhibitor (<20% maximal
inhibition) of UGT1A3, UGT1A4, UGT1A9, UGT2B7, UGT2B15 or UGT2B17.
CYP Enzyme Induction
Module 4.2.2.6, R-13656
The effects of elinzanetant on mRNA levels of CYP genes (CYP1A2, 2B6 and 3A4) were
evaluated at concentrations from 0.1 to 100μM in cultured human hepatocytes from three donors.
255
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
The mRNA level for each specific CYP was determined using quantitative real-time polymerase
chain reaction technology (TaqMan™). Following exposure of cultured human hepatocytes to
elinzanetant for 48 hours, no notable increases in the mRNA levels of CYP1A2 were observed.
At 10μM elinzanetant, maximal increases in CYP2B6 mRNA levels to a mean ratio of treated
over control of 13 were observed, corresponding to a 66% increase relative to the prototypic
inducer phenytoin.
At 3μM elinzanetant, maximal increases in CYP3A4 mRNA levels to a mean ratio of treated
over control of 8.5 were observed, corresponding to a 45% increase relative to the prototypic
inducer rifampicin.
Module 4.2.2.6, B003095
The objective of this in vitro study in human hepatocytes was to investigate the inductive
potential of elinzanetant and its metabolites M18/21, M27, M30/34 (up to 90000 µg/L) on the
expression of CYP3A4, CYP2B6, CYP2C19, and CYP1A2.
Elinzanetant and its metabolites M18/21, M27 and M30/34 did not induce CYP1A2 mRNA or
activity.
Elinzanetant and its metabolites M18/21, M27 and M30/34 caused concentration-dependent
induction of CYP3A4 mRNA in hepatocytes from all three donors. However, at the enzyme
activity level, elinzanetant and M30/34 did not induce CYP3A4 activity in any of three donors;
for M18/21 and M27, up to 3.5-fold (25% of rifampicin effect) and 3.4-fold (24% of rifampicin
effect) induction was observed, respectively.
In addition, induction of the coregulated CYP isoforms CYP2B6 and CYP2C19 was observed
for elinzanetant and its metabolites M18/21, M27 and M30/34 at both mRNA and enzyme
activity level.
FDA analysis: Based on M12 Drug Interactions Studies guidance, elinzanetant and its
metabolites M18/21, M27, M30/34 have low induction potential on CYP enzymes.
Identification of Transporter Substrate
Passive Membrane Permeability (Module 4.2.2.6, R-13631)
The passive membrane permeability of [14C]-GSK1144814 was determined at pH 7.4 and the
absorptive membrane permeabilities were determined at both pH 5.5 and pH 7.4, using a
biorelevant buffer (FaSSIF, fasted state intestinal fluid), in MDCKII-MDR1 cells, in presence of
the potent P-gp inhibitor, GF120918. [14C]-GSK1144814 was determined to have moderate
passive membrane permeability of 74 nm/s at pH 7.4. The absorptive membrane permeability of
[14C]-GSK1144814 in the presence of FaSSIF was moderate at both pH 7.4 and 5.5 with a
P7.4[abs] value of 28 nm/s and a P5.5[abs] value of 18 nm/s.

P-gp Inhibition (Module 4.2.2.6, B002191)
In transfected LLC-PK1 cells over-expressing human P-gp (L-MDR1 cells), BAY 3427080
showed a concentration dependent inhibition of the efflux of digoxin in the concentration range
from 0.1μM to 10μM with an IC50 of 2.23μM. After correction of the nominal test concentrations
for nonspecific binding (NSB), the IC50 was calculated at 0.22μM.
Additionally, the metabolites BAY 3462932 (M27), BAY 3462933 (M30/34) and BAY 3462934
(M18/M21) inhibited the efflux of P-gp probe substrates digoxin or dipyridamole with IC50
values of 6.28μM, 1.22μM and 10.7μM in the concentration range from 0.1μM to 10μM,
respectively. After correction of the test concentrations for NSB, the IC50s were calculated to be
lower, amounting to 1.51μM, 0.09μM and 2.94μM, respectively.

BCRP Inhibition (Module 4.2.2.6, B002163)
In transfected MDCKII cells over-expressing human BCRP (BCRP-MDCKII cells), elinzanetant
showed a concentration dependent inhibition of the efflux of topotecan in the nominal

concentrations for NSB, the IC50 was calculated at 0.08μM.
Additionally, the metabolites BAY 3462932, BAY 3462933, and BAY 3462934 inhibited the
efflux of BCRP probe substrate topotecan with IC50 values of 2.31μM, 1.99μM and 5.33μM in
the nominal concentration range from 0.1μM to 10μM, respectively. After correction of the test
concentrations for NSB, the IC50s were calculated to be lower, amounting to 0.48μM, 0.17μM,
and 1.38μM, respectively.
In summary, elinzanetant and its metabolites BAY 3462932 (M27), BAY 3462933 (M30/34),
and BAY 3462934 (M18/M21) are inhibitors of BCRP, with IC50 values of 0.08μM, 0.48μM,
0.17μM, and 1.38μM, respectively.

14.2.1. Clinical PK and/or PD Studies in Healthy

14.2.1.1. Healthy Female Subject Multiple Dose
Pharmacokinetics and Single Dose Food Effect, Study
21678
This was a Phase 1, open-label, single-sequence, crossover study in healthy female volunteers,
designed to evaluate the pharmacokinetics of repeated doses of NT-814 (40, 80, 120, and 160 mg
soft gel capsules) across four parallel cohorts. It also assessed the effect of food on NT-814
pharmacokinetics following a single dose at each level. In Part 1, subjects received a single dose
of NT-814 30 minutes after a high-fat breakfast (800 to 1000 kcal, with 500 to 600 kcal from fat
and 250 kcal from carbohydrates) on Study Day 1. In Part 2, subjects received a single dose of
NT-814 in a fasting state on Study Day 11, followed by once-daily dosing from Study Day 12 to
Study Day 17, administered three hours after a regular breakfast (approximately 400 to 500 kcal,
with 150 kcal from fat). The overall study design is provided in Figure 47.

14.2.1.2. Mass Balance Study in Healthy Male Subjects,
Study 21664
This study is a single dose study to assess the mass balance recovery, absorption, metabolism,

cumulative recovery (%) of total radioactivity (TR) in urine and feces are shown in Table 144.

14.2.1.3. Healthy Female Subjects Multiple Dose PK Study for
Elinzanetant and Its Metabolites, Study 21703
This is an open-label study to investigate the pharmacokinetics, safety, and tolerability of
repeated 120 mg doses of NT-814 (elinzanetant) and its metabolites in 12 healthy female
volunteers. On the first and last days of dosing, NT-814 was administered after a minimum of 10
hours of fasting. For the intervening days (Days 2 to 13), the drug was given approximately three
hours after consuming a standard breakfast. Plasma samples for NT-814 and its metabolites were
obtained within 15 minutes before dosing and at 0.25, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5, 4, 5, 6, 8, 12, 24,
36, 48, 72, 96, 120, and 168 hours postdose. Urine PK data were also collected.
Study Results
Study results showed that elinzanetant was rapidly absorbed following single and multiple doses
with a range of median Tmax of 1.2 to 1.5 hours. Primary PK parameters (AUC and Cmax) of
elinzanetant and its metabolites are shown in Table 146. Modest accumulation of elinzanetant
and its metabolites M18/21, M27, and M30/34 was observed at Day 14 compared to Day 1, as
shown in Table 147. Mean apparent terminal elimination half-life (t1/2) was estimated to be 37.4
hours on Day 14. NT-814 accounted for a mean of 41.5% of the total drug-related exposure (sum
of AUC(0-24) of NT-814 and metabolites M27, M30/34, M18/21 and M22) on Study Day 1 and
49.3% on Study Day 14.
The study showed that mean trough elinzanetant plasma concentrations on Study Day 14
(310 ng/mL) were higher than on Days 5 (134 ng/mL) and 11 (164 ng/mL) but were comparable
to on Study Day 15 suggesting that steady state was reached by Study Day 14.

FDA Analysis
This study showed an accumulation ratio of 2.11 for elinzanetant, which is higher than the
accumulation ratio of 1.23 (1.081 to 1.398) observed in Study 21678 (Table 143) following
multiple doses of 120 mg elinzanetant for 7 days. The Applicant did not provide an explanation
for the difference observed across the studies. A possible explanation could be the administration
conditions: in this study, the drug was taken on Day 14 (the last of treatment) under fasting
conditions, whereas in Study 21678, it was administered on Day 17 (the last day of treatment),
three hours after breakfast. Nonetheless, in both cases, the accumulation was modest
(accumulation ratio ~2).
In this study, elinzanetant was the major component in human plasma accounting for an average
of 49.3% of the total exposure. This proportion is notably higher than the total radioactivity
observed for elinzanetant in plasma (39.1%), as observed in mass-balance Study 21664.
In this study, metabolite M30/34 accounted for approximately 24.5% of the total drug-related
material, while metabolites M27 and M18/21 contributed 14.2% and 11.8% of the total drugrelated material, respectively. However, in the mass-balance Study 21664, the total radioactivity
in plasma for metabolites M30/34, M27, and M18/21 were much lower, accounting for 13.7%,
7.6% (including traces of M22), and 4.9% of the total radioactivity, respectively. The reasons for
these discrepancies in exposure remain unexplained.

14.2.1.4. Relative Bioavailability Study (Soft Gel Capsule:
60 mg and 40 mg), Study 21665
This study was a single- and multiple-dose, open-label, randomized, 2 × 2 crossover study
conducted in 18 healthy subjects to evaluate the PK and relative bioavailability of elinzanetant
following a single dose of either 2 × 60 mg soft gel capsules (the to-be-marketed formulation and
the formulation evaluated in Phase 3 studies) or 3 × 40 mg soft gel capsules (an earlier
formulation evaluated in Phase 1 and 2 studies) (Figure 48). The multiple-dose regimen was
included to investigate PK comparison and bioavailability between the two formulations under
clinically relevant conditions. A 120 mg once-daily dose of elinzanetant was selected, as this
dose was tested in Phase 3 studies. Additionally, the multiple doses were administered in the
evening, three hours after a standard meal, aligning with the intended administration scheme
(i.e., at bedtime) for clinical use.
Figure 48. Study Design, Study 21665

Source: Applicant’s submitted Study 21665 report

Results
In the PK analysis, data from 17 subjects were included out of the original 18 subjects. This
exclusion was due to one male subject not completing the study because of an AE related to
COVID-19.
The geometric LS mean ratios for Cmax and AUC of elinzanetant (3 × 40 mg capsules compared
to 2 × 60 mg capsules) were determined to be within the bioequivalence acceptance range of 0.8
to 1.25 following both single dosing under fasted conditions and multiple dosing administered 3
hours after a standardized meal (Table 148).
For Ctrough at Day 13 (Ctrough, D13), the treatment ratio of elinzanetant 3 x 40 mg (A)/ elinzanetant
2 x 60 mg (B) was 1.1698 (1.0361; 1.3208) with the upper 90% CI slightly exceeding the upper
bioequivalence range of 1.25. Ctrough at Day 10, Day 11, Day 12, and Days 10 to 13 (model-based
average) were also investigated, resulting in the treatment ratios A/B of 1.0350 (0.9480; 1.1300),
1.0942 (0.9662; 1.2392), 1.0873 (0.9863; 1.1986), and 1.0955 (1.0136; 1.1841), respectively,
with all values close to 1 and all 90% CIs within the bioequivalence acceptance range.

14.2.2. Clinical PK and/or PD Studies in Intended
Patient Population, SWITCH-1
This study was designed as a dose-finding investigation to evaluate the safety and efficacy of
elinzanetant soft-gel capsules at doses of 40 mg, 80 mg, 120 mg, and 160 mg. The study
employed a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled design with female subjects
experiencing moderate to severe VMS associated with menopause. The study utilized an
adaptive design, allowing for modifications to the total number of subjects recruited and/or the
number of subjects randomized to each treatment group based on emerging safety and efficacy
data.
The study duration for each subject was approximately 19 weeks, comprising a 3-week formal
screening and baseline period. This period included a single-blind (subjects only) placebo run-in
phase for the final 2 weeks, during which subjects received placebo once daily. This was
followed by a 12-week double-blind treatment phase and a final follow-up visit 4 weeks after the
end of the treatment period. During the treatment phase, subjects were randomized in a 1:1:1:1:1
ratio to one of five parallel groups to receive either NT-840 at doses of 40 mg, 80 mg (2 x NT814 40 mg capsules), 120 mg (3 x NT-814 40 mg capsules), or 160 mg (4 x NT-814 40 mg
capsules), or a matching number of placebo capsules for each group, administered QD in the
evening. The study design is depicted in Figure 49.

Results
Efficacy assessment was conducted using two coprimary endpoints: the mean change from
baseline in the mean daily frequency and severity of moderate and severe HFs at Weeks 4 and
12. Efficacy with respect to hot flash frequency and severity was evaluated using diaries
completed daily throughout the study period. A reduction of at least two moderate to severe HFs
per day (equivalent to 14 per week) compared to placebo was deemed clinically meaningful to
establish efficacy in treating VMS. Additionally, a statistically significant decrease in the
frequency and severity of HFs from baseline compared to placebo at Weeks 4 and 12 was also
assessed.
In general, reductions in both frequency and severity from baseline were observed across all
treatment groups, with more substantial reductions noted in the NT-814 treatment groups
compared to the placebo. Overall, the 120 mg and 160 mg doses demonstrated a greater extent of
reduction in both frequency and severity than the 40 mg and 80 mg doses (Figure 50 and Figure
51).

14.2.3.1. Pharmacokinetics and Safety of Elinzanetant in
Subjects With Impaired Renal Function, Study 21669
The study was a Phase 1, multicenter, open-label, nonrandomized, single-dose investigation
designed to evaluate the pharmacokinetics of elinzanetant following a single 120 mg
administration. This dose was administered as two 60 mg soft gel capsules to both male and
female subjects. The study comprised four parallel groups: subjects with renal impairment
classified as mild, moderate, and severe, as well as normal healthy subjects.
In the original submission of this application, the Applicant classified subjects with renal
impairment based on eGFR values expressed in mL/min/1.73 m². To align with the Agency’s
current guidance for industry Pharmacokinetics in Patients with Impaired Renal Function—
Study Design, Data Analysis, and Impact on Dosing (March 2024) which recommends
considering eGFR values expressed in mL/min, the Applicant conducted a reanalysis of the study
results as a response to the clinical pharmacology review team’s information request. This
section of this review discusses the study results based on the Applicant’s reanalysis.
In this study, a cohort of 31 subjects were initially enrolled. However, one subject was excluded
from the PK analysis due to the use of a forbidden concomitant medication, leaving 30 subjects
eligible for inclusion in the PK calculations. The reanalysis of the study results incorporated data
from these 30 subjects, who were subsequently categorized into four distinct groups based on the
Agency’s current renal impairment guidance. These groups consisted of 5 individuals with mild
renal impairment (eGFR 60 to 90 mL/min), 6 with moderate renal impairment (eGFR 30 to
60 mL/min), 8 with severe renal impairment (eGFR <30 mL/min), of whom at least four were
undergoing hemodialysis, and 11 subjects with normal renal function (eGFR >90 mL/min).
Results
Plasma concentration of elinzanetant and its metabolite M18/21, M27, and M30/34 were
measured up to 120 hours following single dose administration. Cmax and AUC of elinzanetant
and its metabolites are shown in Table 151.

14.2.3.2. Pharmacokinetics and Safety of Elinzanetant in
Subjects With Impaired Liver Function, Study 21668
This open-label study aimed to evaluate the pharmacokinetics, safety, and tolerability of
elinzanetant in subjects with impaired hepatic function, classified as Child-Pugh A (mild) or B
(moderate), compared to matched controls with normal hepatic function. Both unbound and total
concentrations of elinzanetant were measured following single and multiple doses of elinzanetant
in the study to evaluate the effects of liver impairment on the pharmacokinetics of elinzanetant.
A total of 33 subjects were divided into four groups: Group A, comprising 8 subjects with mild
hepatic impairment, and their matched Control A group with 8 individuals with normal hepatic
function; and Group B, consisting of 9 subjects with moderate hepatic impairment, and their
matched Control B with 8 individuals with normal hepatic function. Each subject received
120 mg of elinzanetant (two 60 mg soft gel capsules) orally once daily on Day 1 and
subsequently from Days 3 to 8. The multiple dose design was selected to accommodate potential
drug exposure increase due to accumulation and a potential time-dependent pharmacokinetic
profile following multiple dosing.
Results
The total elinzanetant Cmax and AUC(0-tlast) after a single dose, as well as Cmax at steady state
(Cmax, md) and AUC over 24 hours at steady state (AUC0-24, md) after multiple doses across all
treatment groups are presented in Table 152.

14.2.4. Clinical DDI Studies
14.2.4.1. DDI Between Elinzanetant and Itraconazole, Study
21679 (R-13587)
Title
An open-label single-sequence crossover study in healthy female subjects to investigate the
effect of an inhibitor of cytochrome P450 3A and p-glycoprotein (itraconazole) on exposure to
elinzanetant (NT-814)
Study Design
All subjects received a single oral dose of NT-814 40 mg alone (Reference) in Part 1 and then a
second single oral dose of NT-814 40 mg in the presence of itraconazole (Test) in Part 2.
In Part 1, NT-814 was administered 90 minutes after the start of a standard breakfast on Study
Day 1. Blood samples were collected at intervals up to 168 hours after dosing for assay of
plasma concentration of NT-814. After a washout period, subjects entered Part 2 of the study.
Subjects received itraconazole 200 mg (2x100 mg capsules) once daily in the morning from
Study Days 12 to 21. All doses of itraconazole were taken following an overnight fast of at least
10 hours and 30 minutes after the start of a standard breakfast. On Study Day 15, NT-814 was
administered 90 minutes after the start of the standard breakfast, i.e., 60 minutes after the
administration of itraconazole. Blood samples were collected at the same intervals relative to the
NT-814 as in Part 1 for assay of plasma concentration of NT-814.
Sentinel dosing applied to Part 2, with two subjects receiving the combination treatment
(itraconazole and NT-814) at least 24 hours before the main group of subjects. Dosing of the
remaining subjects only proceeded after satisfactory review of safety data from the sentinel
subjects collected up to 24 hours after dosing.

14.2.4.2. DDI Between Elinzanetant and Carbamazepine,
Study 21667 (PH-42357)
Title
Open-label, fixed sequence crossover study to investigate the effects of carbamazepine on the
pharmacokinetics of elinzanetant (BAY 3427080) in healthy subjects
Study Design
The study evaluated the drug-drug-interaction potential of carbamazepine (precipitant, inducer of
cytochrome CYP3A4) on the pharmacokinetics of elinzanetant (object).
Midazolam was used as probe substrate (object) for CYP3A4 to confirm CYP3A4 induction by
carbamazepine and to investigate the inhibitory potential of elinzanetant (precipitant) on
CYP3A4.
Study Schema is shown in Figure 54.
Figure 54. Study Schema, Study 21667

Source: Figure 7-1 of CSR

In Period 1, midazolam was administered alone, and the pharmacokinetics of midazolam was
assessed on Day -1, while on Day 1, midazolam and elinzanetant were coadministered and the
pharmacokinetics for both drugs were assessed. In Period 2, carbamazepine was given from Day
-15 until Day 6. Midazolam was administered on Day -1. Elinzanetant was administered on
Day 1, and the pharmacokinetics for elinzanetant was assessed.

Pharmacokinetics of Midazolam With and Without Carbamazepine
After a single dose of 1 mg midazolam alone on Day -1 of Period 1, geometric mean AUC was
11.7 μg·h/L and geometric mean Cmax 4.20 μg/L. When midazolam was administered on top of
multiple doses of carbamazepine on Day -1 of Period 2, AUC and Cmax were significantly
decreased, with values of 3.29 μg·h/L and 1.85 μg/L, respectively. Interindividual variability was
moderate with geometric mean CVs for AUC and Cmax ranging from 35.5% to 48.5%.
Concomitant use of 600 mg carbamazepine daily reduced midazolam exposure by 56% (Cmax)
and 72% (AUC), indicating carbamazepine is a moderate CYP3A inducer at the dose tested.

FDA Analysis


Following coadministration of a single dose of 120 mg elinzanetant, total systemic exposure
(AUC) and peak exposure (Cmax) of 1 mg midazolam increased by 50% and 15%,
respectively, compared to midazolam alone.



Following multiple doses of 120 mg elinzanetant, AUC and Cmax of 1 mg midazolam
increase by 80% and 49%, respectively, compared to midazolam alone.



AUC0-24 and Cmax of elinzanetant increased by ~50% and ~32%, respectively, after multiple
oral doses than after a single dose.



Exposure of all three metabolites was increased with the approximately same magnitude as
the parent drug after multiple dosing.

14.2.4.5. DDI Between Elinzanetant and Rosuvastatin, Study
21666 (PH-42048)
Title
Open-label, one-sequence crossover study to determine the effects of multiple doses of
elinzanetant on the pharmacokinetics of rosuvastatin in healthy subjects
Rationale
Based on in vitro data, elinzanetant showed a moderate inhibition of human OATP1B1 and
BCRP. Therefore, the in vivo interaction potential of elinzanetant as perpetrator on OATP1B1
and BCRP was investigated in the study using rosuvastatin, a sensitive probe substrate for
BCRP, OATP1B1/OATP1B3. The potential inhibition of these transporters by elinzanetant
120 mg/day at steady state was evaluated in two different ways:


To investigate the overall interaction potential including maximum inhibition at the
gastrointestinal tract plus systemic inhibition, elinzanetant and rosuvastatin were
administered concomitantly at the same time point.



To investigate overall interaction potential including maximum systemic inhibition and
inhibition at the gastrointestinal tract, rosuvastatin was administered staggered, with a time
delay of 3 hours after the elinzanetant administration in order to separately assess the
potential BCRP-mediated interaction at the gut wall from the potential systemic (hepatic)
interactions on OATP1B1 and OATP1B3.

Study Design
This was a single-center, open-label, one-sequence crossover study. Study schema and blood
sampling for pharmacokinetics are shown in Figure 56 and Figure 57.

14.2.4.6. DDI Between Elinzanetant and Tamoxifen, Study
22004 (PH-42712)
Title
A Phase 1 study with a fixed-sequence, crossover, open-label design to investigate the effects of
elinzanetant (BAY 3427080) soft gel capsules on the pharmacokinetics of tamoxifen immediate
release tablets in healthy female and male subjects
Study Design
This study was conducted in a single-center with nonrandomized, open-label, fixed-sequence
design. The study had two periods separated by a washout period of 7 days. Subjects were
administered with a single dose of 20 mg tamoxifen (immediate release tablet), a recommended
clinical standard dose, on Day 1 of Period 1. In Period 2, subjects received 28 QD doses of
120 mg elinzanetant (administered as 2 x 60 mg soft capsules) (Day -7 to Day 22) and a single
dose of 20 mg tamoxifen (Day 1).
A schema of the overall study design is presented in Figure 58.
Figure 58. Study Design, Study 22004

Source: Applicant’s submitted Study 22004 CSR
Additional PK samples for tamoxifen and its main metabolites were collected from D -6 to D -1 of Period 2 to determine the potential
carry-over.
Abbreviations: D, study day; EZN, elinzanetant; Metab, metabolites; PK, pharmacokinetics; TMX, tamoxifen

Scientific Rationale for the Study
A fixed treatment sequence was applied, starting with tamoxifen in Period 1 followed by a PK
monitoring phase of 21 days (baseline PK profiles). In Period 2, elinzanetant was administered
over 6 days (Days -6 to -1) prior to the combined administration with a single dose of tamoxifen
on Day 1, to achieve steady-state concentrations and thus maximum inhibition of metabolic
enzymes and/or drug transporters. Treatment with elinzanetant alone continued until 21 days
after combined administration of elinzanetant with tamoxifen to maintain maximum CYP3A4
and/or drug transporter inhibition during disposition of elinzanetant.

299
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
PK samples for tamoxifen and its principal metabolites 4-hydroxytamoxifen, Ndesmethyltamoxifen, and endoxifen were collected until 21 days (504 hours) after tamoxifen
administration in both periods and from Day -6 to Day -1 of Period 2, due to the long half-lives
of tamoxifen (~7 days) and endoxifen (approximately 207 hours). Corrected PK parameters were
calculated for analytes that had concentrations in Period 2 prior to second tamoxifen dosing
greater than 5% of Cmax in Period 1.
PK samples for elinzanetant and its principal metabolites M18/M21, M27, and M30/M34 were
collected until 24 hours after tamoxifen administration in Period 2.
Healthy male subjects aged 18 to 65 years and female subjects aged 30 to 65 years were included
in the study. PK properties of tamoxifen and elinzanetant show no relevant gender-related
differences. Results obtained in this population were therefore deemed as translatable to breast
cancer patients who are receiving tamoxifen for therapeutic reasons.
Study Population
A total of 20 subjects were assigned to treatment sequence (tamoxifen – tamoxifen
+Elinzanetant). PKS1 dataset included 17 subjects (2 subjects dropped out and 1 subject was
excluded as she was identified as a CYP2D6 poor metabolizer. PKS2 dataset included 18
subjects (all but 2 dropouts).

equals AUC(0-504 h) (504 hours=21 days).

14.2.4.7. DDI Between Elinzanetant and Esomeprazole,
Study 21772 (PH-42383)
Title
An open-label, nonrandomized, fixed-sequence crossover study to investigate the effects of the
proton pump inhibitor esomeprazole on the pharmacokinetics of elinzanetant (BAY 3427080) as
well as assessment of the absolute bioavailability of elinzanetant using a single intravenous
microtracer dose of [13C5] BAY 3427080 in male and female healthy subjects
Study Design
A schema of the study design is presented in Figure 60.
Figure 60. Study Design, Study 21772

Source: Figure 7-1 of the CSR
Abbreviations: CSR, clinical study report; D, day; FU, follow-up; i.v., intravenous; PK, pharmacokinetics; SD, single dose; SIL, stable
isotope labeled

Justification for Dose


120 mg elinzanetant was selected because it is the proposed therapeutic dose.



100 μg [13C5] BAY 3427080 is the highest appropriate dose in the microdosing approach per
ICH guidance for industry M3(R2) Nonclinical Safety Studies for the Conduct of Human
Clinical Trials and Marketing Authorization for Pharmaceuticals (January 2010). This dose
is predicted to allow proper quantification of the tracer over the course of 168 hours.



Administration of 40 mg esomeprazole once daily is the highest recommended dosage for its
approved indications (e.g., for the treatment of gastric ulcers). Administration for 5 days
ensured a maximum increase of gastric pH for investigation of the interaction with
elinzanetant (as recommended by the FDA guidance for industry Evaluation of Gastric pHDependent Drug Interactions With Acid-Reducing Agents: Study Design, Data Analysis, and
Clinical Implications (March 2023).

Study Population
A total of 14 male and female healthy subjects were assigned to treatment sequence (elinzanetant
+ [13C5] BAY 3427080  elinzanetant + esomeprazole). All 14 subjects received assigned
treatments. One subject did not complete the study (subject decision) and dropped out during the
second treatment phase (Period 2).
Treatment Administered
Each subject was administrated one single dose of elinzanetant together with 240 mL
noncarbonated water at room temperature on Day 1 of each period. Following study drug
administration, subjects remained in an upright sitting position for 1 hour.

14.2.4.8. DDI Between Elinzanetant and Midazolam, Study
21674
This study was divided into two distinct parts. Part A employed a parallel group, randomized,
placebo-controlled design to assess the safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics of multiple
ascending doses of GSK1144814 (elinzanetant). This segment consisted of three cohorts.
Cohorts 1 and 2 focused on the pharmacokinetics of elinzanetant following single and repeated
oral doses of 30 mg, 90 mg, and 200 mg. Cohort 3 examined the safety, tolerability, and
pharmacokinetics of a 200 mg once-daily dose of GSK1144814 administered for 28 days, and its
308
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469

impact on the pharmacokinetics of a single oral 2.5 mg dose of midazolam, a CYP3A4-sensitive
substrate.
Part B involved four healthy male subjects and aimed to evaluate NK1 receptor occupancy of
elinzanetant after repeated oral dosing. This was accomplished through PET scanning using the
NK1 radiotracer ligand [11C]GR205171.
This review will focus on the effect of elinzanetant on the pharmacokinetics of midazolam,
specifically addressing Cohort 3 of Part A. The study design for cohort 3 of part A is given in

FDA Analysis
A mean increase of 90% and 71% increase in the AUC and Cmax of midazolam was observed,
respectively, when midazolam was administered after treatment with elinzanetant 200 mg once
daily compared to when midazolam was administered alone. These results indicate that
elinzanetant is a weak inhibitor of CYP3A4 at the dose of 200 mg administered once daily.

analytical methods utilized protein precipitation followed by LC-MS/MS. Quantification was

no significant discordance identified.

14.5.1.2. Introduction
The primary objectives of the Applicant’s analysis were:
(1) To develop a population pharmacokinetic model for elinzanetant, based on the existing
model, to robustly describe the observed pharmacokinetics in OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and
OASIS 3 studies.
(2) To assess the variability in pharmacokinetics of elinzanetant in healthy subjects and patients
with vasomotor symptoms.
(3) To evaluate the contributions of intrinsic and extrinsic covariates to the variability of
elinzanetant pharmacokinetics in healthy subjects and patients with VMS.
(4) To derive individual pharmacokinetic exposure variables for each patient of OASIS 1,
OASIS 2, and OASIS 3 studies to be used in future E-R analyses.
(5) To implement an exploratory PK/PD assessment which will simulate occupancy at the NK1
and NK3 receptors for patients in the OASIS 1, OASIS 2 and OASIS 3 studies.

14.5.1.3. Model Development
14.5.1.3.1. Data
The PK analyses for elinzanetant were based on PK data from 11 Phase 1 studies in female
healthy subjects, 1 Phase 2 study in women with VMS, and 3 Phase 3 studies in women with
VMS. Brief descriptions of the studies included are presented in Table 203.
The overall percent of BLQ samples for elinzanetant, M30/34, M27, and M18/21 was 4.60%,
6.86%, 7.79%, and 8.93%, respectively. These observations were excluded from PK model
development but included in model qualification. It seems to be reasonable to exclude BLQ
samples. The final NONMEM data file for elinzanetant model development contained 8,703
elinzanetant observations from 1,318 subjects and 5,932 M30/34, 5,873 M27, and 5,800 M18/21
observations from 1,079 subjects. Table 204 provides summary statistics of the baseline
demographic covariates in the PK analysis dataset.

14.5.1.3.2. Base Model
The population PK model was developed using a nonlinear mixed-effects modeling approach
with the first-order conditional estimation with interaction method in NONMEM (Version 7.4.3).
A population PK model for elinzanetant and its three metabolites was previously developed
using data from 10 Phase 1 and 2 studies. A circadian influence on the clearance of elinzanetant
and the clearance and Vmax parameters of the three metabolites was included in the previous
model. The structure of base popPK model was developed by re-estimating and reassessing the
previous base popPK model and based on final analysis datafile.
Interindividual variability was modelled assuming a log-normal distribution for patient level
random effects. Residual variability was described using additive error model on log-transformed
data. The quality of the model fit was assessed by diagnostic plots.
14.5.1.3.3. Covariate Analysis
The preliminary popPK covariate model was reinferred using the final analysis datafile, a new
set of post hoc individual random effects (ETA) estimates was derived, and the univariate
covariate exploration was repeated using the new ETA estimates. A stepwise forward inclusion
(p<0.01) and backward deletion (p<0.001) covariate search procedure was implemented. In this
process, if any new covariates were found to have p<0.01 in the updated univariate covariate
exploration, they would enter a second forward inclusion (p<0.01) and backward deletion
(p<0.001) covariate search with the reinferred preliminary popPK covariate model as the starting
point.
In the covariate searches, the influence of body weight and lean body weight on clearance and
volume parameters was tested using an allometric relationship. Other continuous covariates were
evaluated using an exponential function and categorical covariates were parameterized as a
fractional change.

336
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)

Primary covariates evaluated in the development of PK model was included in Table 204.
14.5.1.4. Final Model
A 2-compartment model with first-order absorption and elimination for elinzanetant coupled
with a 2-compartment model with linear plus nonlinear elimination for M30/34 adequately
described the PK data of elinzanetant and M30/34 (Figure 63, Figure 64, and Figure 66).
Statistically significant covariate effects on PK model parameters were the following: study
population and BMI on clearance of elinzanetant, and age and BMI on clearance of M30/34.
Race, mild hepatic impairment and mild/moderate renal impairment are not significant
covariates. The parameter estimates for the final covariate model are listed in Table 205. The
RSE for all parameters was <30%. Moderate eta-shrinkage (<30%) was observed for all
parameters.
In addition, given the strong correlations between the concentrations of metabolites in the
observed data (Figure 62), the concentrations of metabolite M27 and M18/21 for subjects in
Phase 3 studies was adequately described by a separate direct linear mixed effects models and
based on the concentrations of M30/34 in these subjects (Figure 65, Figure 67). The parameter
estimates for the metabolite correlation model are listed in Table 206.
The effects of race, age, body weight, height, BMI, and bilirubin on the AUC(0-24),ss of
elinzanetant and M30/34 are explored in Figure 68. The effects of evaluated intrinsic factors
(race, age, body weight, height, BMI, and bilirubin) are generally small, and unlikely to be
clinically meaningful. Subjects who had lower body weights had lower AUC(0-24),ss, and vice
versa, due to the negative association between BMI and elinzanetant CL identified in the
covariate analysis (Table 205). According to the Applicant, potential explanation for the negative
association between BMI and elinzanetant CL included reduction in free fraction of elinzanetant
in subjects with higher BMI due to higher fatty acid concentrations in these subjects and
decreased levels of hepatic CYP3A4 expression in subjects with higher BMI. Of note, fatty acid
concentrations in the plasma of study subjects were not available and there was no evidence to
support the first explanation. There was similar AUC(0-24),ss of elinzanetant in subjects with mild
hepatic impairment compared to subjects with normal hepatic function (Figure 70). This result is
consistent with that from the dedicated hepatic impairment study for the effect of mild hepatic
impairment. The effect of moderate hepatic impairment on PK parameters was not evaluated in
the popPK analysis due to the limited number of subjects with moderate hepatic impairment
(n=1) in the popPK dataset. There were similar exposure of elinzanetant in subjects with mild
(n=23) and moderate (n=402) renal impairment compared to subjects with normal renal function
(n=586) (Figure 70). In the final PK model, healthy subjects were estimated to have 59.6%
higher clearance compared to subjects with VMS in the final model.
The geometric mean terminal half-lives of elinzanetant based on individual post hoc PK
estimates for subjects in the three Phase 3 studies from the final model was 45.3 hours (Table
207). The model-predicted geometric mean AUCtau,ss, Cmax,ss, and Cmin,ss of elinzanetant are
8572.0 μg*h/L, 1422.7 μg/L, and 142.8 μg/L, respectively, in subjects treated with 120 mg daily
dose of elinzanetant (Table 207).

The influence of weak CYP3A4 inhibitor on the exposure of elinzanetant and its metabolite
M30/34 was explored. The geometric mean ratios of AUC(0-24),ss for both elinzanetant and
M30/34 (1.125 for elinzanetant and 1.130 for M30/34) increased by about 13% upon
coadministration of weak CYP3A4 inhibitors (Figure 69). The increase in the geometric mean
Cmax,ss for both elinzanetant and M30/34 (1.092 for elinzanetant and 1.064 for M30/34) was
<10% upon coadministration of weak CYP3A4 inhibitors (Figure 69).

14.5.1.5. Exploratory PK/PD Assessment
After the popPK model was developed, the plasma concentrations of elinzanetant across a 24hour dosing interval (once-daily dosing at 120 mg) at steady-state in subjects from the three
Phase 3 studies (OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and OASIS 3) were simulated using the final popPK model
and individual EBE parameter estimates. Based on the simulated plasma concentrations of
elinzanetant in these subjects, the NK1 and NK3 receptor occupancy in the human brain were
simulated using a standard occupancy model. In this model, Occupancy (%) =100*Celin/(Celin
+ EC50), where Celin is the simulated plasma concentration of elinzanetant at steady state and
EC50 is a parameter describing the plasma concentration of elinzanetant at which the NK1 or
NK3 receptor is 50% occupied. The in vivo EC50 for NK1 in the brain of healthy adult males
(N=4) was previously estimated to be 0.97 µg/L. The EC50 for NK3 receptor was approximated
to be 9.7 µg/L based on the EC50 for NK1 and the 10-fold difference in in vitro affinity between
NK1 and NK3.

The simulation results suggested that >95% of subjects are expected to have >95% occupancy of
the NK1 receptor across the dosing interval (Figure 71). For NK3 receptor, due to approximately
10-fold lower affinity of elinzanetant, >95% of subjects are expected to have >80% occupancy
across the dosing interval (Figure 71). Of note, the EC50 for NK1 was estimated using data from
limited number of subjects, and EC50 for NK3 was approximated based on EC50 for NK1 and
difference in in vitro affinity between NK1 and NK3. Given the uncertainty in the estimate of
EC50 for NK1 and NK3, the results of the PK/PD simulations should be interpreted with caution.

14.5.1.6. Simulation of Missed Dose Scenarios
The elinzanetant exposure metrics (AUC(0-24), Cmin, Ctrough and Cmax) and time-averaged average
receptor occupancies (NK1 and NK3) over consecutive 24-hour periods under different dose
scenarios for missing up to two doses (Table 208) were simulated for all subjects (who
contributed PK data) in FAS from the OASIS 1, OASIS 2 and OASIS 3 studies using the
selected popPK covariate model (with use of individual parameter estimates and subject
covariates).
In the 24-hour period following a single missed dose (miss a single dose, resume dose intake the
following evening), the median AUC(0-24) reduces to approximately 40% of its value at steadystate, however the median of time-averaged receptor occupancies for NK1 and NK3 reduce by
less than 0.3% and 3% of steady-state levels, respectively (Table 209, Figure 72). A further
reduction is observed in the 24-hour period following two consecutive missed doses (miss two
consecutive doses, resume dose intake the following evening); the median AUC(0-24) reduces to
approximately 28% of its value at steady-state, and the median of time-averaged receptor
occupancies for NK1 and NK3 reduce by less than 1% and 5.5% of steady-state levels,
respectively (Table 210, Figure 73).

14.5.2. Exposure-Response Analysis
14.5.2.1. Review Summary
There was a positive relationship between elinzanetant Ctrough at steady state and reduction in hot
flash frequency and severity. This relationship was adequately described by the E-R model. The
exploratory E-R analysis for safety did not identify a significant relationship between
elinzanetant exposure and elevated AST/ALT and AE of special interest. The Applicant’s
analyses were verified by the reviewer.
14.5.2.2. Introductions
The primary objectives of Applicant’s E-R analysis were to:
(1) Evaluate E-R relationship of HF frequency and HF severity.
(2) Evaluate E-R relationship of responder who had at least 50% reduction in HF frequency.
(3) Explore the occurrence of (i) abnormal elevations in AST or ALT, and (ii) fatigue,
somnolence or dizziness reported as AE and the relationship to treatment with elinzanetant
and exposure and other intrinsic or extrinsic factors.
PK exposure metrices at steady-state (AUC(0-24),ss, Cavg,ss, Ctrough,ss, Cmax,ss, Cmin,ss) were predicted
based on post hoc parameter estimates from the final population PK model. Due to the high
correlation between exposure metrics, only Ctrough,ss, Cmax,ss were selected as exposure candidates
to be evaluated in the E-R analyses.
14.5.2.3. E-R Analysis for Efficacy
The efficacy E-R analysis was based on data from Phase 3 studies OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and
OASIS 3. The primary efficacy endpoints were HF frequency and severity, and HF responder.
HF responders were defined as subjects which reported at least 50% reduction in HF frequency
at Week 12 compared to baseline.
NONMEM (Version 7.3.0) and R software (Version 4.2.1) were used for the E-R analysis.
The analysis data included 16,539 HF frequency records and 16.539 severity records from 1,418
subjects, of which 1,108 subjects could be classified as HF responder or nonresponder.
Longitudinal HF frequency and severity was analyzed by means of (non)linear mixed effects
modeling. The E-R relationship for HF frequency was described using the following structural
model.

relationship for HF severity could be adequately described using the same (fixed) EC50 estimate

data from the Phase 2b dose ranging study (SWITCH-1), which was an adaptive design study on
elinzanetant doses of 40 mg, 80 mg, 120 mg and 160 mg, and placebo for 12 weeks (Figure 76).
None of the covariates (age, race, body mass index, body weight, time since last amenorrhea,
oophorectomy status, Menopause-specific Quality of Life Questionnaire) were likely to have
clinically meaningful impact on the effectiveness of elinzanetant in reducing HF frequency or
severity. The simulation based on E-R model and projected Ctrough,ss at different dose levels
showed the reduction of HF frequency approaching a plateau at the studied dose of 120 mg
(Figure 77).

14.5.2.4. E-R Analysis for Safety
The safety E-R analysis was based on data from Phase 3 studies OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and
OASIS 3. The safety endpoints included AST, ALT, and AEs of special interest (fatigue,
somnolence, or dizziness).
The analysis data included a total of 11,527 ALT records and 11,684 AST records from N=1,420
subjects, and records for AESI from 1,059 subjects who received elinzanetant.
A regression analysis testing the influence of exposure on the maximum AST and ALT value per
subject and on the occurrence of elevations >1xULN was performed. For both AST and ALT, a
visual exploration of the time-trajectories revealed no differences between the study arms across
the three studies. An exploratory regression analysis of the maximum observed value per subject
under treatment with elinzanetant revealed no association with elinzanetant exposure for both
liver markers.
The E-R for AESI was explored visually by comparing the incidence rates across exposure
quartiles followed by a logistic regression analysis of occurrence of ≥1 event of interest versus
no event of interest under elinzanetant treatment. No association between the risk for an AE of
special interest and individual elinzanetant steady-state exposure could be identified within the
subjects treated with 120 mg elinzanetant (Figure 78).

14.5.3. PBPK Analysis
Excusive Summary
The objective of this review is to evaluate the adequacy of the Applicant’s PBPK analyses to
evaluate the DDI potentials of elinzanetant with CYP3A4 inhibitors.
The Division of Pharmacometrics has reviewed the PBPK report CPMX50214, Responses to
FDA’s request for information dated October 30 and December 17, 2024, and supporting
modeling files, to conclude the following:


PBPK analysis predicts that a moderate CYP3A4 inhibitor such as erythromycin could
increase AUC and Cmax of elinzanetant by 3.0 and 2.0-fold, respectively.



PBPK analysis predicts that the exposure to 60 mg elinzanetant following administration of a
moderate CYP3A4 inhibitor, such as erythromycin, is comparable to the exposure of 120 mg
elinzanetant, with an increase in AUC and Ctrough by 1.39-fold and 1.91-fold, respectively.



PBPK analysis predicts no clinically significant effect on elinzanetant exposure when
coadministered with a weak CYP3A inhibitor such as cimetidine.

LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
Background
Elinzanetant (LYNKUET, BAY3427080, NT-814) is developed for the treatment of vasomotor
symptoms associated with menopause. The proposed dosing of elinzanetant is 120 mg orally
(two 60 mg capsules) once daily at bedtime with or without food.
Dose-exposure relationships were slightly greater than dose proportional in the dose range of 40
to 120 mg and dose proportional increase at doses >120 mg (Applicant’s Summary of Clinical
Pharmacology Studies). Human mass balance study (Study 21664) reported approximately 15%
of administered [14C] NT-814 was excreted in feces (ranges 0 to 40% of administered dose) in
the first 48 hours and >90% by Day 15, while <1% drug was detected in urine by Day 15. The
Applicant considered the drug eliminated in feces within the first 48 hours as unabsorbed, given
the low solubility of NT-814 in aqueous solution. The parent compound was the major
circulating component in plasma, accounting for 31% of the total drug-related exposure. M30/34,
an active metabolite, was the only major metabolite, contributing approximately 10% of the total
drug-related material in plasma.
The Applicant reported that the mean apparent oral clearance in subjects ranged from 15.5 to
23.2 L/h (as observed in Study 21756 and Study 21669, Clinical Pharmacology Studies)
following a single 120 mg dose of elinzanetant. Similar terminal half-lives of elinzanetant were
observed after both single and multiple dose administrations. Elinzanetant is highly bound to
human plasma proteins (99.7%). The plasma fraction unbound was reported to be higher (within
a two-fold increase) under fed conditions and in subjects with renal impairment (Study 21669).
However, the plasma fraction unbound was reduced in subjects with hepatic impairment
(Study 21668).
In vitro DDI data suggested that elinzanetant is mainly metabolized by CYP3A and minorly by
UGT and is a substrate of P-gp. Elinzanetant is an inducer and competitive and mechanisticbased inhibitor for CYP3A and an inhibitor for P-gp and BCRP/OATP in vitro. Several clinical
DDI studies were conducted to evaluate the DDI potential of elinzanetant as a CYP3A substrate
or as a perpetrator for CYP3A, P-gp and BCRP/OATP. Results of clinical DDI studies indicated
that elinzanetant (120 mg QD) does not impact the exposure of dabigatran etexilate (P-gp
substrate), and rosuvastatin (BCRP/OATP substrate). Additionally, the Applicant measured
endogenous biomarker data for 4β-hydroxycholesterol and coproporphyrin-I. Changes in 4βhydroxycholesterol and coproporphyrin-I levels following elinzanetant administration were less
than 20%. Therefore, the in vivo DDI potential of elinzanetant as a CYP3A inducer and
OATP1B inhibitor is likely low. Table 212 summarizes the results of clinical DDI studies
evaluating elinzanetant as a CYP3A substrate and as a CYP3A inhibitor.

The Applicant developed the PBPK modeling analysis (Study CPMX50214) to predict the
changes in exposure of elinzanetant and M30/34 with erythromycin (a CYP3A moderate
inhibitor) and cimetidine (a weak CYP3A inhibitor). The PBPK simulated results are used to
inform the DDI dosing in the USPI. Additionally, the Applicant conducted a PBPK analysis
(Study CPMX50217) to evaluate the effects of elinzanetant on the pharmacokinetics of
tamoxifen and its metabolites. Given the absence of a DDI dosing recommendation for
tamoxifen when coadministered with a moderate CYP3A inhibitor, the PBPK study report
CPMX50217 was not reviewed.
Methods
Model Development
The PBPK analyses were performed using PKsim and MoBi softwares
(Open Systems Pharmacology 2025b).
A based model was first built where drug specific physicochemical properties, solubility,
baseline fu, pathway-specific intrinsic clearances of elinzanetant and metabolite M30/34, and
CYP3A inhibition parameters were obtained from relevant in vitro experiments. The Applicant
noted that circadian fluctuations of fu informed by clinical data was also included in the model.
During the model development, the parameter identification tool in MoBi was used to estimate
selected model parameters. PBPK parameters such as dissolution parameters, scaling factor for
the elinzanetant metabolism (vmax_factor) and M30/34 catalytic constant (kcat), UGT clearance,
permeability, and the extent of gut wall metabolism were optimized using clinical dataset. Figure
79 presents a diagram of the overall modelling strategy for elinzanetant. Table 213 presents the
list of PBPK input parameters.

FDA Analysis
Although in vitro data suggested that elinzanetant is a P-gp substrate, the Applicant did not
include P-gp mediated clearance in elinzanetant PBPK model. The Applicant’s rational is that (1)
elinzanetant has a good in vitro permeability and (2) the efflux ratio is less than one in Caco 2
assay. The reviewer noted that the recovery rate of elinzanetant is very low in the Caco 2 in vitro
study (KINE 240041-ELB) and it could impact the interpretation of the efflux ratio data. In
369
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
addition, the absolute bioavailability of 52%, and approximately parallel concentration-time
profiles with or without coadministered itraconazole (Study 21679 figures in Section 14.2) could
suggest a significant P-gp elimination. However, given a mean of 16% of total radiolabel
elinzanetant was found in feces in the first 48 hours after elinzanetant oral administration
(Study 21664), P-gp mediated pathway of elinzanetant could be much less than CYP3Amediated clearance.
Another concern is that the elimination pathway of M30/M34 was not well characterized. The
reviewer issued an information request to the Applicant to assess and discuss the impact of
concomitant use of CYP3A4 inhibitors and inducers on the total pharmacological activity of
elinzanetant, including the parent drug and its metabolites.
The Applicant stated that they assume M30/M34 being cleared primarily via the CYP3A
pathway based on: (1) in vitro study suggesting that M30/M34 undergoes oxidative
biotransformation and (2) the relative decrease in M30/M34 exposure similar to that observed
with elinzanetant when coadministered with carbamazepine, indicating that the production and
elimination pathway of M30/M34 is likely mediated mainly by CYP3A. Figure 80 presents the
metabolism pathways of elinzanetant in the PBPK model.
The reviewer found the Applicant’s assumption that CYP3A is the main pathway for M30/M34
elimination to be uncertain due to the following reasons: (1) No metabolite data were collected in
the itraconazole DDI study and (2) Carbamazepine is known to induce multiple enzymes and
transporters, complicating pathway characterization.
Despite these uncertainties, given that the production of M30/M34 is expected to be reduced
when coadministered with a CYP3A inhibitor, the DDI effects on elinzanetant exposure serve as
a reasonable surrogate for its total pharmacological activity. The uncertainty in the clearance
pathway of M30/M34 may be more relevant when PBPK modeling is used to assess the effect of
CYP inducers (such as efavirenz) on the exposure of elinzanetant and M30/M34. The reviewer
noted that no simulations were conducted for the coadministration of elinzanetant with a
moderate inducer.

The Applicant noted that only clinical studies involving IV or soft gel capsule administration

Sensitivity Analysis
The Applicant conducted a sensitivity analysis for parameters governing: (1) the fraction
metabolized by UGT (fmUGT), which subsequently impacts the fmCYP3A4 values, and (2) the
gut wall metabolism factor, which describes the ratio between metabolism by CYP3A4 in the
liver and the gut wall (kcat_GI_factor).
fmUGT: Under the assumption that UGT is only expressed in the liver, the fmUGT was set to be
6.3% after oral administration in elinzanetant PBPK model. The values of the fraction
metabolized of UGT for testing were determined as 0% and 11.9% total UGT contribution.
kcat_GI_factor: The initial model simulations showed that the extent of gut wall metabolization
(kcat_GI_factor) was too low in the PBPK model. Thus, kcat_GI_factor was optimized to fit
clinical PK and carbamazepine DDI data. The value of kcat_GI_factor is 25 in elinzanetant
PBPK model. The values of kcat_GI_factor for testing were ranging 0.01 to 10-fold of the
reference value of 25.
Figure 81 and Figure 82 present the sensitivity of the AUC ratio (AUCR) and Cmax ratio (CmaxR)
of elinzanetant and M30/34 to changes in the values of fmUGT and kcat_GI_factor when
coadministered with various CYP3A percipients. Figure 81 shows the effect of different fmUGT

FDA Analysis
As shown in Figure 81, changing the values of fmUGT and fmCYP3A has modest effect on
predicted DDI with CYP inhibitors and inducer. For example, the predicted DDI effect with a
moderate CYP3A inhibitor, erythromycin, is about 30% higher (AUCR 3.82 versus 3.01) when
assuming the highest contribution of CYP3A-mediated clearance (i.e., fmUGT =0). Similar
sensitivity was predicted for M30/34 (results not shown).
373
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
As shown in Figure 82, a lower DDI effects were simulated for elinzanetant and M30/34 when a
lower contribution of gut metabolism was assumed. However, the predicted DDI of elinzanetant
with erythromycin could be 2-fold higher than the reference PBPK model (AUCR 3.01 versus
6.23) when assuming a higher contribution of gut metabolism (kcat_GI_factor =250). This
setting (10-fold of reference kcat_GI_factor value) is considered less possible as the model
would significantly underestimate the observed Cmax in clinical PK studies and is inconsistent
with observed IV PK data.
As previously discussed, there is uncertainty regarding the extent of P-gp-mediated clearance for
elinzanetant. The need to assign a higher contribution of gut metabolism in the final elinzanetant
PBPK model (kcat_GI_factor of 25) may be due to P-gp involvement. Consequently, the model
might overestimate rather than underestimate the contribution of gut metabolism. When the
kcat_GI_factor value is reduced by 100-fold from the reference value, as shown in Figure 82, the
predicted DDI effect with the moderate CYP3A inhibitor erythromycin is approximately 30%
lower (AUCR 1.78 versus 3.01).
For this application, the PBPK analysis is used to inform elinzanetant DDI dosing
recommendation when coadministered with a moderate CYP3A inhibitor. The reviewer
concluded that the changes in fmUGT (0–11%) or a lower kcat_GI_factor (0.25–25) affect the
predicted DDI effects of elinzanetant and M30/34 by about 30%. This impact is not expected to
affect the applicability of using this PBPK model to support DDI dosing recommendations for
moderate CYP3A inhibitors.
Supportive Compound Files

(Open Systems Pharmacology 2025a)
FDA Analysis
The reviewer notes that although a detailed evaluation of reports for all PBPK models supporting
the development of a new drug is preferred, the extent of this evaluation can be guided by model
risk, as recommended in the ICH guidance for industry M15 General Principles for ModelInformed Drug Development (December 2024). In the case of elinzanetant, given the extensive
clinical PK and DDI studies available, and considering that the magnitude of DDI for
elinzanetant with a moderate CYP3A inhibitor can be interpolated from the clinical DDI data
with a strong CYP3A inhibitor and inducer, only a high-level review was conducted for key
supportive PBPK models, including those for itraconazole, erythromycin, cimetidine,
carbamazepine, and midazolam. The reviewer also notes prior evaluation of model reports and
regulatory experience with PK-Sim PBPK modeling for predicting CYP3A DDI has been
reported (e.g., NDA 215341 and NDA 214133).

An information request was sent on December 17, 2024, requesting the simulated Ctrough,ss and
AUCss of elinzanetant following elinzanetant 60 mg QD at steady state with concomitant use of
the moderate CYP3A inhibitor erythromycin. In the presence of erythromycin, the geometric
mean AUCss and Ctrough,ss ratios of elinzanetant were 1.39 and 1.91, respectively. The Applicant
379
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
stated that the efficacy would be maintained at the simulated Ctrough,ss level based on the E-R
analysis (Study CPMX50130). Dosing reduction to 60 mg QD is then recommended with
coadministration of a moderate CYP3A inhibitor. No dosing modification of elinzanetant was
considered necessary with coadministration of a weak CYP3A inhibitor, based on the predicted
DDI effect with cimetidine.
Similarly, simulations assessed the AUCss and Ctrough,ss of elinzanetant following elinzanetant of
120 mg QD at steady state with concomitant use of the strong CYP3A inducer carbamazepine
(300 mg BID). In the presence of carbamazepine, the geometric mean AUCss and Ctrough,ss of
elinzanetant reduced by 68% and 81%. Exposure reduction with carbamazepine was considered
clinically relevant. Refer to clinical pharmacology review for further discussion.
Conclusions
The PBPK modeling analysis can predict the effect of weak and moderate CYP3A inhibitors on
the pharmacokinetics of elinzanetant and serve as the regulatory basis for DDI risk management
recommendations in the prescribing information.

16. Efficacy
16.1. Handling of Missing Data in Primary
Analyses of Coprimary Endpoints, OASIS 1,
OASIS 2, and OASIS 3
In the prespecified primary analysis of the coprimary endpoints in OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and
OASIS 3, the nonmonotone (intermittent) missing data and (2) the monotone missing data after
the discontinuation of randomized treatment were imputed using the following two steps.
Step (1): Imputation of Nonmonotone (Intermittent) Missing Data
Monte Carlo Markov Chain MI method was used to impute intermittent missing baseline and
postbaseline missing values (missing baseline values were imputed together with intermittent
missing values). For the baseline value to be imputed, at least two out of the four postbaseline
values (i.e., Weeks 1, 4, 8, and 12) need to be available. If not, the subject with missing baseline
value was removed from the study. In OASIS 1, all subjects in the FAS had baseline values. In
OASIS 2, one subject in the FAS with missing baseline value was removed from the analysis
because she had only one (Week 8) out of the four postbaseline values. In OASIS 3, one subject
380
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
had missing baseline value; however, she was kept in the analysis because she had three
(Weeks 1, 4, and 8) out of the four postbaseline values.
Step (2): Imputation of Monotone Missing Data After the Discontinuation of Randomized
Treatment
MI method was used to impute the monotone missing data after the discontinuation of
randomized treatment. The MI imputation model included auxiliary variables indicating (yes/or)
whether the subject has permanently discontinued from the randomized treatment at each visit of
Week 1, 4, 8, and 12. In addition, baseline measurement of frequency/severity of VMS, region
and treatment as well as previous postbaseline endpoint values were also included in the
imputation model. Per the statistical analysis plan, when there were less than 10 subjects (who
permanently discontinued the randomized treatment) across both treatment groups with available
postdiscontinuation data at any intermediate time point, the indicator variable was not included
in the imputation model for that time point.
Note, in both steps (1) and (2), the imputed negative values were set to zero since VMS
frequency and severity values cannot be negative.
After the completion of imputation steps, each imputed dataset was analyzed using the MMRM
model specified for the primary analysis of four coprimary endpoints. The results were combined
using the Rubin’s rule (Rubin 1987) to obtain an overall estimated treatment effect. A total of
500 multiple imputed datasets was generated. Seed numbers 21651, 21652, and 21653 were used
for multiple imputations for OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and OASIS 3, respectively.

17. Clinical Safety
This section includes supportive information regarding safety assessment.

17.1. Additional Safety Analyses
Alcohol Considerations
In Study 21676, psychomotor and cognitive effects of alcohol plus elinzanetant were
investigated in healthy subjects. The study was a single-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled,
2-period crossover, single dose study in 20 healthy subjects. Subjects participated in two
treatment periods and were administered a single oral dose of elinzanetant 200 mg or matching
placebo, while alcohol was administered intravenously.
(b) (4)

390
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)
In comparison to alcohol plus placebo, administration of alcohol plus elinzanetant was associated
with a decrease of peak velocity and increase in reaction times of saccadic eye movements, a
reduction in adaptive tracking performance, an increase of the sleepiness (Epworth scale) and a
decrease of alertness (Bond Lader scale), and a worsening of recognition score and recognition
times in the Visual Verbal Learning Test. Changes in the PD endpoints correlated with the
pharmacokinetics of elinzanetant. For sleepiness, on average, considering all time points, there
was a 2-point increase, relative to a maximum score of 24 points on this scale. The largest
differences were observed in the first 3 hours postdosing.
In terms of safety parameters, no vital sign abnormalities were reported as an adverse event by
the investigator. Somnolence and fatigue were the most common AEs reported in the study.
Fatigue was more common in placebo-treated subjects (35%) compared to elinzanetant-treated
subjects (15%). In contrast, somnolence was more common in elinzanetant-treated subjects
(40%) compared to placebo-treated subjects (15%). Given the small sample size and single dose
nature of the study, limited conclusions are possible, however there were no new safety
considerations identified in this study.
Safety Update
The 120-day safety update was submitted November 24, 2024, and is summarized as follows:
There were no deaths.
In the ongoing Phase 1 study (Study 22382: “A combined single- and multiple-dose, open-label,
fixed sequence, 2 x 3 crossover study to investigate the relative bioavailability, safety and
tolerability of elinzanetant in healthy female and male participants”), there was no new relevant
safety information. The clinical portion of this study has been completed.
In both ongoing clinical studies (NIRVANA, a Phase 2 study in postmenopausal women and
OASIS 4, a Phase 3 study in women with or at high risk of developing hormone-receptor
positive breast cancer), data remain blinded. In NIRVANA, there were two SAEs: diverticulitis
and basal cell carcinoma that were deemed “unrelated to study drug”. No SAEs pertaining to
AESIs of somnolence/fatigue, phototoxicity, and postmenopausal uterine bleeding were
identified during the period covered by this report. In OASIS 4, there were nine SAEs in eight
subjects including correction of breast asymmetry, pain in trigeminal nerve distribution,
pulmonary embolism, deep vein thrombosis, endometrectomy, ischemic CVA, progression of
breast cancer, anterior wall adhesions, and pelvic adhesions. Since both studies remain blinded
causality cannot be fully assessed. OASIS 4 is further confounded by high-risk status or
concurrent malignancy.
The Applicant provided a report of liver safety, another listed AESI.
The respective liver injury data (referred to as CLO by the Applicant) from the two ongoing
studies, NIRVANA (Phase 2) and OASIS 4 (Phase 3) are reviewed below.

391
Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23)
Reference ID: 5682958

NDA 219469
LYNKUET (elinzanetant)


There were two cases of liver injury in the NIRVANA study.
- Case #1: 58-year-old woman, nonsmoker, obesity, and medical history of elevated liver
enzymes (1.6 to 2.6xULN at baseline) and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease. At Week 12,
liver markers were 1.2 to 5.7xULN and returned to baseline levels within 16 days after
stopping (blinded) treatment. The adverse event (“worsening of elevated liver enzymes”)
was nonserious and of mild intensity as assessed by investigator. The external liver expert
assessed the case in a blinded fashion as a case of “mild acute mixed pattern liver injury
(Ratio ALT/ALP =4.5) over chronic steatosis.” Causality was assessed as probable.
- Case #2: 55-year-old woman, nonsmoker, nonalcohol drinker with type II diabetes, with
mild elevation in liver markers at baseline. Following 4 weeks of blinded treatment her
liver markers increased by 4 to 6xULN. She was asymptomatic. Her fibroscan findings
were compatible with mild-moderate fibrosis. The evaluation is still ongoing including
liver expert assessment.

For OASIS 4, four of the overall five CLO cases in this study have been assessed by the LSMB.
Of these, two were assessed as unlikely and two as possibly related to elinzanetant use (cannot
definitively exclude the possibility). For all four cases an alternative etiology was proposed by
the LSMB. Assessment of the one case reported during the reporting period is still pending. Of
note, all women in OASIS 4 study were receiving adjuvant endocrine therapy (e.g., tamoxifen or
aromatase inhibitor) for underlying disease of breast cancer.
Two of the five CLO cases were already reported in expedited manner to FDA (2023A147501
and 2023A157847) in 2023. Both cases were assessed as possibly related to the study drug use
by the LSMB. The LSMB identified for both cases an alternative etiology, namely possible
biliary obstruction at level of the ampulla and acetaminophen use, respectively.
During the reporting period of this 120-day safety update report, one subject meeting the criteria

safety monitoring board (DSMB) members, last DSMB meeting took place on June 21, 2024,
next was planned for December 2024 (after the date of the 120-day safety update submission).
The liver cases were confounded by underlying liver disease. The majority of the SAEs were
confounded by an underlying medical diagnosis. As the data remains blinded, we agree with the
DSMB, that no conclusions on causality for elinzanetant can be drawn at this stage based on the
available information. No new signals were identified.

22. Data Integrity–Related Consults (Office of
Scientific Investigations, Other Inspections)
In support of this NDA, the Applicant submitted clinical data from three Phase 3 studies:
OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and OASIS 3. OASIS 1 and OASIS 2 were pivotal efficacy studies and
OASIS 3 was primarily a long-term safety study but also provided additional supportive efficacy
data. The Applicant attested that all three clinical studies were conducted in accordance with the
Code of Federal Regulations governing the protection of human subjects (21 CFR part 50),
institutional review boards (21 CFR part 56), and the obligations of clinical investigators (21
CFR 312.50 to 312.70) in accordance with GCP.

oversight of OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and OASIS 3 as the Applicant of these clinical studies. The
inspection found no compliance deficiencies in Bayer’s conduct and oversight of the OASIS
studies. The numbers of subjects randomized in the study and participating investigator sites
were consistent with those reported in the NDA. Data management, including data capture and
analyses, was found to be adequate, with no issues noted.

concerns regarding the conduct and the oversight of the clinical studies or GCP or regulatory
compliance. Based on the results of these inspections, OSI concluded that the data generated by
the inspected investigators and submitted by the Applicant are acceptable in support of the
proposed indication.

Introduction
LYNKUET or Elinzanetant [synonyms BAY 3427080, NT-814, GSK1144814] is a
neurokinin 1 (NK1) and neurokinin 3 (NK3) receptor antagonist indicated for the
treatment of moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms (VMS) associated with
menopause.
The Applicant has submitted this NDA under the 505(b)(1) pathway as a New Molecular
Entity (NME), and as such a full battery of nonclinical pharmacology, pharmacokinetic,
and toxicology studies had been completed to support the nonclinical safety of this drug
component has been submitted.

Executive Summary
1.1

Introduction

NDA 219469 is a 505(b)(1) application submitted by Bayer Healthcare Pharmaceuticals,
Inc. for elinzanetant (BAY 3427080); as 60-mg soft gelatin capsule for the treatment of
moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms (VMS) associated with menopause.
Elinzanetant is a new molecular entity that acts as a noncompetitive antagonist of both
the human neurokinin (NK)1 and NK3 receptors (NK1R and NK3R, respectively).
Elinzanetant has ~10-fold higher affinity to human NK1R compared to human NK3R,
with mean pKi values of 9.43 and 8.42 for NK1R and NK3R, respectively. Elinzanetant
has three principal metabolites M27, M30/34, and M18/21, which also act as
noncompetitive antagonists at NK1R and NK3R.
NK1R and NK3R antagonists are thought to act by inhibiting the activity of KNDy (i.e.,
kisspeptin/neurokinin B [NKB]/dynorphin) neurons, which project to the vasomotor
center in the median pre-optic nucleus to modulate neuronal activity involved in
thermoregulation. This inhibition of KNDy neurons, which are thought to be in a
hyperactivated state because of estrogen decline in menopause, is proposed to result in
improvement of menopause-associated VMS [also called hot flushes (HFs)].
Fezolinetant [VEOZAH, approved in 2023], was the first-in-class NK3R antagonist
indicated for the treatment of VMS in postmenopausal women. Antagonists of the NK1R
(Aprepitant [EMED, approved in 2003], Rolapitant [VARUBI, approved in 2015], and
Fosaprepitant [FOCINVEZ®; approved in 2008]) have also been approved for the
indication of nausea and vomiting associated with emetogenic cancer chemotherapy.
The clinical program for elinzanetant includes 29 completed studies: There are 24
Phase 1 studies, 2 Phase 2 studies, and 3 Phase 3 studies. Safety and efficacy of
elinzanetant were evaluated in 3 phase 3 studies: OASIS 1, OASIS 2, and OASIS 3.
The nonclinical program for elinzanetant includes studies of pharmacodynamics (PD),
pharmacokinetics (PK), repeat dose toxicity (up to 26 weeks in rats and 39 weeks in
monkeys), reproductive and developmental toxicity (in rats and rabbits), genotoxicity
and carcinogenicity (in transgenic mice and rats), and phototoxicity. Since elinzanetant
was established to have disproportionate human metabolite (M27) early in nonclinical
development, additional nonclinical studies were also conducted with this metabolite.
The main metabolites M18/21 and M30/34 were also further assessed in nonclinical
studies (for example, genotoxicity studies).
In January 2024, the Applicant met with the Agency for a pre-NDA meeting under IND
129492, and it was established that the nonclinical package and nonclinical data
supporting the mechanism of action of elinzanetant appeared to be adequate to support
an NDA submission (see more details in Meeting Minutes in DARRTS dated
02/06/2024).

8

Reference ID: 5623053

NDA #219469

Edna Albuquerque, Ph.D.
Pratistha Tamrakar, Ph.D.
Sarah Lee, Ph.D.

The Applicant submitted the NDA in July 2024, along with additional nonclinical studies
including the rat pre-/post-natal development (PPND) study, carcinogenicity studies in
rat and transgenic mice, and abuse potential studies.
1.2

Brief Discussion of Nonclinical Findings

Pharmacology
Elinzanetant is a new molecular entity that acts as a noncompetitive antagonist of both
the human neurokinin (NK)1 and NK3 receptors (NK1R and NK3R, respectively). In
binding assays, elinzanetant displayed high affinity for human NK1R [pKi values of 8.71
– 10.15 (mean pKi of 9.43)] and NK3R [pKi values of 8.03 – 8.8 (mean pKi of 8.42)].
Elinzanetant has ~10-fold lower affinity towards human NK3R compared to human
NK1R. Additionally, elinzanetant has higher affinity for human NK1R and NK3R
receptors than for human NK2 receptors (pKi values of approximately 6.0). In functional
in-vitro assays, elinzanetant inhibited the activity of human NK1R and NK3R, with
calculated pKB values of 9.02 - 9.1 for human NK1R and 8.17 - 8.5 for human NK3R.
Ex-vivo receptor occupancy studies in human putamen showed that elinzanetant
occupied NK1Rs in the human putamen in a concentration-dependent manner with a
pKi of 9.44.
Each of the principal metabolites of interest – M27, M30/34 and M18/21, which
accounted for 6%, 11% and 5.5%, respectively, of total radioactivity in the human
biotransformation clinical study # CPMX 50130/B002427 – showed high affinity and
noncompetitive antagonistic activity at the human NK1R and NK3R. The affinities and
potencies of the metabolites at human NK1R and NK3R are similar to those of
elinzanetant.
In-vivo pharmacodynamic activity of elinzanetant was investigated in a gerbil foot
tapping model of NK1 activity and in the guinea pig wet-dog shake model of NK3
activity. After oral dosing with elinzanetant, foot tapping induced by the NK1R agonist
GR73632 in male gerbils was blocked [ID50 (dose resulting a 50% reduction in time
spent foot tapping) = 1.36 mg/kg]. Similarly, elinzanetant doses of 8.5 and 25.5 mg/kg
significantly inhibited wet-dog shake behavior induced by the NK3R agonist senktide in
the guinea pigs, indicating central NK3R antagonist activity. While the Applicant did not
conduct studies in animal models to demonstrate the effects of elinzanetant in reducing
HF-like symptoms, overall, the pharmacology data support the Applicant’s therapeutic
rationale for the use of elinzanetant to modulate neuronal activity in the vasomotor
center.
(b) (4) were performed to evaluate the potential for off-target
Selectivity screens
binding for elinzanetant and the 3 principal human metabolites of elinzanetant (M27,
M30/34, and M18/21). Elinzanetant was >100-fold more selective for the human NK3R
and >300-fold more selective for the human NK1R versus 88 other non-tachykinin
human receptors, enzymes, and transporters.
