The pharmacologic class term for elinzanetant is neurokinin 1 (NK1) and neurokinin 3
(NK3) receptor antagonist.
Mechanism of Action
NK1R and NK3R antagonists are thought to act by inhibiting the activity of KNDy (i.e.,
kisspeptin/neurokinin B [NKB]/dynorphin) neurons, which project to the vasomotor
center in the median pre-optic nucleus to modulate neuronal activity involved in
thermoregulation. This inhibition of KNDy neurons, which are thought to be in a
hyperactivated state because of estrogen decline in menopause, is proposed to result in
improvement of menopause-associated VMS (also called HFs).

Abbreviations: Dyn, dynorphin; GnRH, gonadotropin releasing hormone; KNDY, kisspeptin, neurokinin B, and
dynorphin; KOR, kappa opioid receptor; LH, luteinizing hormone; NKB, neurokinin B; NK3R, NKB receptor; SP,
substance P; WS, wide spiking

Figure 1: NK1/NK3R and schematic of the links between KNDy neurons, the regulation of GnRH
secretion, and the vasomotor area in the hypothalamus.1

Pharmacokinetic
PK studies in rats, monkeys, and dogs demonstrated that elinzanetant is absorbed
following oral administration, with its oral bioavailability being moderate in male and
female rats (77% and 47%, respectively) and low in monkeys and dogs (19%).
Autoradiographic studies revealed that, following the oral administration of radiolabeled
elinzanetant to different species, radioactivity distributed to major organs, including the
liver and pigmented tissues (e.g., the uveal tract and the retina). In typical PK studies,
elinzanetant was found to cross the blood brain barrier. In pregnant rats, the organ
distribution of elinzanetant was similar to that in non-pregnant rats. In addition,
elinzanetant crossed the placenta, and elinzanetant and its metabolites were detected
in different fetal organs, including the brain. Collectively, these findings suggest that the
1 Sassarini, J., & Anderson, R. A. (2024). Elinzanetant: a phase III therapy for postmenopausal patients with vasomotor

symptoms. Expert Opinion on Investigational Drugs, 33(1), 19–26.

10

Reference ID: 5623053

NDA #219469

Edna Albuquerque, Ph.D.
Pratistha Tamrakar, Ph.D.
Sarah Lee, Ph.D.

brain, the liver, pigmented tissues, and the developing fetus can be important targets for
elinzanetant-related effects. Following administration of radiolabeled elinzanetant to
lactating rats, approximately 6% of the elinzanetant dose was excreted in milk within 48
hours (h) post administration.
Plasma protein binding was high across all preclinical species tested (99.5 to 99.9%)
and higher in humans (>99.9%) for elinzanetant and its principal metabolites (M27,
M30/34 and M18/21). As such, whenever appropriate for the nonclinical safety
assessments, the extent of protein binding is included in the calculations of safety and
exposure margins. The nonclinical safety assessment further considers the finding that
in animals, as in humans, elinzanetant is metabolized primarily by oxidation at the
methyl-phenyl moiety and the morpholine ring mainly to metabolites M27, M30/34 (a
major human metabolite), and M18/21.
Pivotal Chronic Repeat-dose Toxicity
o In the 26-week rat study (Study No R-13894), elinzanetant was administered
orally, twice a day (BID) 6 h apart, by gavage to sexually mature rats at a dose of
0, 25, 60, or 90 mg/kg BID for a total daily dose of 0, 50, 120, or 180 mg/kg/day
in males and 0, 10, 25, or 40 mg/kg BID for a total daily dose of 0, 20, 50, or 80
mg/kg/day in females. Clinical pathology changes suggesting mild impairment of
hepatic function were reported in high-dose males without correlating
microscopic findings of liver damage. Dose-related incidence of macrophage
infiltrations in the alveoli was noted in both sexes, without increase in severity.
Minimal infiltrates were noted starting in males and females at 50 and 20
mg/kg/day, respectively. Tubular basophilia, hyaline casts and cortical scars
were observed in males and correlated with increased kidney weights. Systemic
exposure (Cmax and AUC) in females was >2-fold that in males at the 50
mg/kg/day level (only comparable dose level) at both Day 1 and Week 26. At
Week 26, females had evidence of drug accumulation at all doses with repeat
administration (e.g., 2 to 3-fold accumulation for Cmax and AUC from Day 1 to
Week 26).
The no-observed-adverse-effect-level (NOAEL) was the high-dose of 80
mg/kg/day (females) and mid-dose of 120 mg/kg/day (males), with male AUC(0-24)
= 76100 µg.h/L (8.8 X the maximal recommended human dose [MRHD] of 120
mg/day) and female AUC(0-24) = 311000 µg.h/L (36 X MRHD of 120 mg/day).
Safety margins are based on the human AUC(0-24) of 8572 µg.h/L obtained from
the MRHD in the clinical study B002427.
o In the 39-week monkey study (Study No R-13895), elinzanetant was
administered orally, BID, 6 h apart, by gavage to sexually mature male and
female monkeys at a dose of 0, 15, 30, or 40 mg/kg BID leading to a total daily
dose of 0, 30, 60, or 80 mg/kg/day for 39 weeks. At the high-dose, adverse drugrelated weight loss and gastrointestinal clinical signs were observed in females
and were generally accompanied by inflammatory cell infiltrate and in one female

mild hyperplasia of the mucosa of the cecum and colon. Gastrointestinal signs of
disturbances (loose and/or liquid feces) were also seen in males starting at 30
mg/kg/day. A lack of estrus cycle activity was observed in females at 60 and 80

Increased liver weight and sinusoidal compression, presenting as narrowing of

o A 26-week rat study for the M27 metabolite (Study R-13953) was conducted to
qualify the safety of this metabolite in rat [systemic exposure of M27 and M18/21
were very low in rats after administration of elinzanetant, and M27 was

increase was noted in females but there were no correlating findings of

was considered to be related to the sublingual blood sampling, rather than the
test item, based on the location and characteristics of this finding (Heimann et al,
2009). The NOAEL for both males and females was considered to be 20
mg/kg/day, with AUC(0-24) = 13700 µg.h/L (5.4 X MRHD) in male and AUC(0-24)=
38300 µg.h/L (15 X MRHD in female rat). Safety margins are based on the
AUC(0-24) of 2496.3 µg.h/L for M27 obtained from the MRHD of elinzanetant in
clinical study B002427
Genotoxicity
In-vitro and in-vivo genotoxicity studies with elinzanetant and in-vitro genotoxicity
studies with its three principal metabolites (M27, M30/34, and M18/21) did not reveal
any evidence of a genotoxic potential.

Safety and exposure margins:
No Observed Adverse Effect Level (NOAEL): The oral dose of 20 mg/kg/day with
AUC(0-24) = 64000 µg.h/L was the highest test dose not associated with
carcinogenic signals in female rats. Based on the elinzanetant AUC(0-24) of 8572
µg.h/L obtained from the MRHD in the clinical study B002427, the clinical safety
margin provided by the highest noncarcinogenic dose to the MRHD is ~7.5 X.
Based on the AUC(0-24) for the metabolites, safety margins are ~0.2 X, 3.7 X, and
0.05 X for the metabolite M27, M30/34, and M18/21, respectively.
The oral dose of 60 mg/kg/day (elinzanetant AUC(0-24) = 252000) was the lowest
tested dose associated with carcinogenic signals in female rats. Based on AUCs,
the clinical exposure margins provided by this dose to the MRHD are ~29.4 X for
elinzanetant and ~0.8 X, 7.0 X, and 0.1 X for the metabolites M27, M30/34, and
M18/21, respectively.
Of note, CNS-related signs were observed in rats during the study and are
described further under the subheading ‘CNS-related findings’ below.
CNS-related findings
Clinically relevant CNS-related safety signals were reported in two studies – a 2-year
carcinogenicity study conducted in female Sprague-Dawley (SD) rats (Envigo – formerly
Harlan – USA) and a 13-week repeat-dose toxicity study conducted in male and female
SD rats (Envigo, Netherlands). The substrain of SD rats from Envigo is referred to as
SD:Hsd.
In the 2-year carcinogenicity study (study B003186), female SD:Hsd rats were treated
with the dose of 0, 3.5, 10, 30, or 40 mg/kg, BID, by oral gavage for 104 weeks (n = 50
rats/group). Increased incidence of convulsions was noted in rats treated with doses
≥60 mg/kg/day. At doses ≥60 mg/kg/day, prodromal signs of convulsions (e.g.,
increased sensitivity to touch and decreased activity) generally preceded detection of
13

Pratistha Tamrakar, Ph.D.
Sarah Lee, Ph.D.

convulsions, which were first noted around day 162 and 106 after start of treatment with
the doses of 60 mg/kg/day and 80 mg/kg/day, respectively.
In the 13-week repeat-dose toxicity study (study R-13628), male SD:Hsd rats were
treated with the dose of 0, 25, 60, or 150 mg/kg (highest dose decreased to 87.5 after
day 9), BID, and female SD:Hsd rats were treated with the dose of 0, 10, 25, or 50
mg/kg, BID. Treatments were delivered by oral gavage for 13 weeks. Muscle spasms
(lasting up to 3 min) and tremors were noted in some female rats around day 24 after
start of treatments and were followed by convulsions (starting around treatment day 34)
in 2 out of 16 females at 20 mg/kg, 3 out of 16 females at 50 mg/kg, and 3 out of 21
females at 100 mg/kg. Likewise, 1 out of 16 males in the groups that received the low
and mid doses (50 and 120 mg/kg/day, respectively) had tremors, whole-body rigidity,
spams (lasting up to 1-3 min), stiff tail, and involuntary muscle contractions
(convulsions). Male rats treated with the highest tested dose (300/175 mg/kg/day) died
prematurely after presenting with reduced activity, hunched posture, abnormal gait,
piloerection, and prostration. There were no histopathological findings in the brain.
Reproductive and developmental toxicity
In the fertility and early embryonic developmental (FEED) study conducted in rat [study
R-13611], female rats were treated with 0, 5, 25, or 100 mg/kg/day of elinzanetant via
oral gavage for 22 days before cohabitation with untreated males, days 1 to 14 during
cohabitation with untreated males, and on postcoital days 0 to 6. Increased percentage
of pre-implantation and post-implantation embryo loss, resulting in reduced litter size,
and lower fetal body weights were seen at the dose of 100 mg/kg/day (14-fold the
AUC(0-24) at the human therapeutic dose). These effects were not observed following
dosing at 25 mg/kg/day (3-fold the AUC(0-24) at the human therapeutic dose). Since no
PK/TK parameters were collected in the FEED study, calculations of margins of
exposure were done based on the 13-week exposures from the 13-week toxicity study
R-13596 in rats [13-week AUCs were 32200 μg.h/mL at 25 mg/kg/day and 135000
μg.h/mL at 100 mg/kg/day in female rats].
In the embryofetal developmental (EFD) study in rat [R-13610], female rats were treated
with 0, 5, 25 or 100 mg/kg/day of elinzanetant via oral gavage once daily from gestation
day (GD) 6 to 17. No evidence of embryofetal lethality or teratogenicity occurred at
doses ≤100 mg/kg/day, with AUC(0-24) = 197000 µg.h/L (23-fold the AUC(0-24) at the
human therapeutic dose), and no maternal toxicity occurred at doses ≤25 mg/kg/day,
with AUC(0-24) = 57200 µg.h/L (7-fold the AUC(0-24) at the human therapeutic dose).
In the embryofetal developmental (EFD) study in rabbit [R-13597], female rabbits were
treated with 0, 30, 45, or 70 mg/kg twice daily (BID) or a total daily dose of 0, 60, 90, or
140 mg/kg/day elinzanetant administered via oral gavage from GD 7 to 19. Maternal
toxicity in the form of marked body weight loss and decreased food consumption
leading to early sacrifice in 4 out of 27 females was observed at the highest tested dose
of 140 mg/kg/day, with AUC(0-24) = 10600 µg.h/L (~equivalent to the AUC(0-24) at the

In the pre- and postnatal development (PPND) study in rat [study B003187], female rats

Phototoxicity study
Elinzanetant has several characteristics that, per the Guidance for Industry: S10
Photosafety Evaluation of Pharmaceuticals (January 2015), available at
https://www.fda.gov/media/85076/download, make it a potential phototoxicant.
Elinzanetant absorbs photons in the ultraviolet (UV) spectrum (290-700 nm). In the invitro Balb/c 3T3 neutral red uptake phototoxicity assay (Study Report R-13578), one
peak was detected at 321.4 nm with a calculated molar extinction coefficient (MEC) of
3762.3 L•mol-1, which exceeds the threshold of 1000 L•mol-1 for phototoxicity. In the
same study, elinzanetant was found to be cytotoxic with an IC50 of 0.845 µg/mL in
presence of UV-A. Elinzanetant distributes to and accumulates in melanin-rich tissues in
the rat, with radioactivity that was still present in the pigmented eye uvea at day 35 (840
h) post-dose, a finding that suggests long-term retention or irreversible tissue binding of
elinzanetant in pigmented tissues (Study Report R-13624; Study Report R-14368).
Potential Safety Concerns of Clinical Relevance based on Nonclinical Findings
The main clinically relevant nonclinical safety signals were identified as: (i) central
nervous system (CNS)-related signals, including tremors and convulsions in rats, (ii)
skeletal muscle degeneration in rats, (iii) malignant adenocarcinoma of the uterus, the
combination of malignant and benign endometrial tumors and squamous cell carcinoma
of the uterus, and lymphomas of the hematolymphoid system in the 2-year rat
carcinogenicity study, (iv) in-vitro phototoxic signals, (v) gastrointestinal (GI)-related
signals in rats and monkeys, and (vi) reproductive and developmental toxicity signals in
rat and rabbit. Some topics have been briefly described above. Refer to Section 11

Glyceryl monooleate
Api et al. (2021)2 reported that the oral NOAEL for glyceryl monooleate in a repeat-dose
toxicity study in rats was 1,000 mg/kg/day (the highest test dose). In this GLPcompliant, combined repeat-dose and reproductive study, Sprague Dawley rats were
administered glyceryl monooleate via oral gavage (0, 100, 300, or 1000 mg/kg/day; n =
12 rats/sex/dose). Males were dosed for 42 days (starting 14 days prior to mating and
continuing through the mating period); females were dosed up to lactation day 4.
Additional groups of 5 Sprague Dawley rats/sex/dose were maintained for 2 weeks after
dosing as a recovery group. No mortality occurred throughout the study period. There
were no treatment-related effects on general condition, clinical observations, sensory
reflex function test, landing leg width, grip strength, locomotor activity, body weight, food
consumption, urinalysis (male only), hematology, organ weight, organ function, clinical
chemistry, necropsy, or histopathology.

Glyceryl monocaprylocaprate
The MDE for glyceryl monocaprylocaprate in previously approved oral products is only
501.9 mg (~ (b) (4) % the maximal daily dose of this excipient in the MRHD of
elinzanetant). However, a glyceryl mono- and dicaprylocaprate mix is an excipient in a
previously approved oral drug product at an MDE of 13,770 mg per the FDA IIR.
According to the US Pharmacopeia, no less than 75% of the glyceryl mono- and
dicaprylocaprate mix (a product also referred to as glyceryl monoprylocaprate Type I3) is
the monoester.4 With this consideration, the MDE to glyceryl monocaprylocaprate in the
previously approved oral drug product is no less than ~10,328 mg. Therefore, glyceryl
monocaprylocaprate at the amount in the Applicant’s product is considered adequately
qualified.

2.6

Proposed Clinical Population and Dosing Regimen

The recommended dose of elinzanetant is 120 mg per day (two 60 mg soft gel
capsules) taken once daily at bedtime in the general population of individuals with
moderate to severe VMS associated with menopause.

Regulatory Background

The molecule was initially discovered by GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) under the code name
GSK1144814. The drug product was subsequently acquired by NeRRE Therapeutics
and KaNDy Therapeutics Ltd and repurposed for the current indication (moderate to
severe VMS associated with menopause) under the code name NT-814 and submitted
under IND 129492. On September 8, 2020, Bayer HealthCare Pharmaceuticals Inc.
(Bayer) took over the sponsorship of IND 129492. Bayer has renamed the compound as
BAY 3427080 or elinzanetant.

Three forms of elinzanetant [free base (BAY 3427080), hydrochloride (HCl) salt (BAY
3453656), and tosylate salt (BAY 3453651)] have been used in nonclinical studies.
The following associated synonyms are noted in some tables below and provided here
for ease of reference.
▪
▪
▪

GSK1144814 or GSK1144814A: elinzanetant free base
GSK1144814B: elinzanetant HCl
GSK1144814C: tosylate salt

However, all doses and concentrations in the tables are expressed in terms of free
base.

Figure 6: Effect of elinzanetant on NKB-induced neuronal firing in

Source: Figure extracted from study report R-13877
Reviewer’s comments:
1. The habenula is synaptically connected to brain regions
such as the amygdala, which plays a central role in
seizures, and the hippocampus, which is essential for
cognitive processing (Norden et al. 2002).5
2. The finding that elinzanetant inhibits neuronal
excitability suggests that the seizures noted in some
repeat-dose toxicity studies of elinzanetant-treated rats
are unrelated to elinzanetant-induced NK3R inhibition.
3. Elinzanetant-induced inhibition of NK3Rs in the habenula
(and other brain regions involved in cognitive
processing) could contribute to cognitive deficits noted
in elinzanetant-treated human subjects.

5

Norden AD, Blumenfeld H. The role of subcortical structures in human epilepsy. Epilepsy Behav. 2002 Jun;3(3):219-231.

Findings
Treatment of guinea pigs with haloperidol (Hal) had no

dose of elinzanetant correlated with higher exposure of
the Hal-treated animals to elinzanetant.
• The data suggest that NK1R/NK3R occupancy by
elinzanetant was not affected by the dopamine D2
receptor antagonist Hal.

Reviewer’s comment: The Applicant notes that radioactivity in the
uveal tract/retina at post-dosing day 35 indicate long-term
association of drug-related material with melanin. In an in-vitro
study, elinzanetant produced a positive phototoxicity signal (see
Section 10
Special Toxicology Studies). Considering the
highest level of elinzanetant accumulation in the eyes and
pigmented skin of rats and the IC50 for elinzanetant to induce invitro phototoxicity, a safety margin of ~11 was estimated. Caution
is warranted when interpreting this margin, because the degree of
elinzanetant accumulation in melanin-rich human tissue is
unknown. The potential for elinzanetant to cause photosensitivity
in humans cannot be ruled out and is further discussed in Section
11 Integrated Summary and Safety Evaluation and the full review
of the phototoxicity study in the Appendix section at the end of
this review. In addition, photosensitivity adverse events were

Main objective of the study was to investigate the tissue distribution, and
penetration of radioactivity across the placental barrier.
Radioactivity widely distributed from blood to most peripheral organs,
tissues, and less in the tissues of fetuses.
As in the non-pregnant rats (i.e., male lister hooded rats), the maternal
tissues with the highest concentrations were brown adipose, adrenal
gland (average of adrenal cortex and medulla), liver, white adipose, and
harderian gland in addition to the mammary gland at 48-h post-dosing,
while the lowest concentrations were found in brain and bone.
The fetal blood AUC0-last was 12% of the maternal blood AUC0-last. Fetal
and associated tissue concentrations were generally much lower than
maternal blood, except for amnion, placenta, and brain. AUC0-last ratio of
placenta/maternal blood was 1.3, fetus average/amniotic fluid was 18.3,
and fetal brain/maternal brain was 2.4.

Albino/non-pigmented (SD rat):
• Mostly similar distribution in male and female rats.
• At 5 h post-dosing, the highest concentrations were found in adipose
white, liver, brown adipose, and mammary gland region.
• At 8 h post-dosing, lowest concentrations were found in eye wall, brain,
and bone.
• Greater amounts of radioactivity were found in the reproductive organs
of females (1.715 μg-equiv/g in ovary and 0.692 μg-equiv/g in uterus)
relative to males (0.143 μg-equiv/g in testis) at 5 h post-dosing.
• Blood to plasma ratios determined for each time point ranged from 0.58
to 0.79 suggesting greater portioning to plasma.
Pigmented rat (Long Evans rat):
• Concentrations of radioactivity in the tissues and blood was similar to
that in non-pigmented rat.
• Concentration of radioactivity at 35-days post-dosing remained elevated
in the eye uvea (0.019 μg-equiv/g) but was below detection in
pigmented skin. Findings in the eye are similar to that in study R-13624.

PK Studies: Excretion
Study Title & Design
R-13623

Rat (oral) @ 10 mg/kg
In intact rats and bile duct
cannulated rats

Study findings
In intact rats:
• Major route of elimination was found to be via the feces (94.2%) within
168 h post-dosing.
• Urinary elimination was minor (0.9%).
• 76.5% of the dose was recovered within 24 h of dosing, remaining
dose was eliminated relatively slowly [total recovery: 96.6%].
In bile duct-cannulated rats:
• Major route of elimination was via the bile (61.1%).
• Fecal and urinary excretion accounted for means of 29.5% and 0.9%
of the dose respectively.
• Considering the radioactivity recovered in bile, urine, and the residual
carcass (minus the gastrointestinal tract), at least 66.1% of the dose
was absorbed by these animals.
Also refer to study R-13716 summarized above.

In-vitro Pharmacokinetic Drug Interaction Studies
Effects of elinzanetant and metabolites on cytochrome P450 isoforms (CYP)
• Data from human liver microsomes with selective CYP inhibitors and from
recombinant human CYP enzymes indicated that CYP3A4 is the primary CYP
isoform involved in the oxidative metabolism of elinzanetant [study R-13657,
PH42629]. Inhibition of CYP2E1 could not be determined [R-13658].
• Induction potential of elinzanetant and its metabolites M27, M30/34, and M18/21
towards human CYP isoforms was assessed at both mRNA and enzyme activity
level, as summarized in Table 24 and Table 25 [Summary from study R-13656
and B003095].

Effects of Elinzanetant and Its Metabolites on Transporters
The interaction of elinzanetant with various transporters was investigated in in-vitro
studies.
Elinzanetant as a transporter substrate:
o Elinzanetant is classified as a substrate of P-glycoprotein (P-gp), a
transporter that removes substances from cells. IV coadministration of
elinzanetant with elacridar (GF120918A) [a non-specific inhibitor of P-gp
efflux transporters] to rats increased by ~5X the elinzanetant brain:blood
ratio and by ~2.5X the systemic exposure to elinzanetant [study R-13621].
o Elinzanetant is not a substrate of the bidirectional transporter breast
cancer resistance protein (BCRP), the uptake transporters hOATP1A2
and hOATP2B1, and the MRP4 efflux transporters.
o Elinzanetant is not a substrate of the OATP1B1, OATP1B3, OATP1A2
and OATP2B1 uptake transporters.
Elinzanetant and its metabolites as transporter inhibitors:
o Elinzanetant inhibited MATE1-, BSEP-, and OCT1-mediated metformin
transport as well as OAT3-, OATP1B1-, OATP1B3-mediated transport.
Elinzanetant is an an inhibitor of BCRP with an IC50 value of 7.4 μM [study
R-13631, R-13686, B002205, R-13635].
o OATP1B1 was inhibited by elinzanetant with an IC50 value of 0.7 μM
[study R-13633].
o Elinzanetant inhibited the transport of digoxin via human P-gp in vitro with
an IC50 of 14 ± 6 μM (corresponding to 9.6 μg/mL as free base) [study R13634].

Reviewer’s comment for labelling: In Section 13.2 of the label,
under CNS subheading, the lowest doses that caused involuntary
muscle contractions in male and female rats are noted as being
equivalent to ≥4-fold the MRHD based on AUC exposures at the
time of onset. The multiple of exposure was estimated using
extrapolated AUC(0-24) values for male and female rats. AUC(0-24)
data are available only for treatment days 1 and 91, whereas the
safety signals were noted around treatment day 24 (tremors) and
day 34 (convulsions) in females and around day 31
(rigidity/spasms) and day 34 (convulsions) in males. Linear
regression of the available data for the LOAELs (20 mg/kg/day in
female rats and 50 mg/kg/day in male rats) allowed the
extrapolation of the AUCs for the days when convulsions were
noted. Additional caveat in the study was that the monitoring was
not done continuously and hence findings could have occurred
prior to day 24.
Mortality: 1 in control and 1 in 50 mg/kg/day males (difficulty breathing
noted), not considered treatment related.
Body weight: The final body weight was marginally (1-5%) lower in
treatment groups than in the respective controls, without a clear doseeffect relationship.
Hematology:
@ 180 mg/kg/day in M and 80 mg/kg/day in F: Lower hematocrit and
red cell distribution width in both sexes @ week 13 and 26, higher
mean cell hemoglobin concentrations in both sexes at Week 13 only,
low mean cell volume and low hemoglobin concentration in males only
@ week 13 and 26.
Clinical Chemistry:
• Elevated ALT at week 26 in M @ 180 mg/kg/day (2-fold). AST
increase in F @ 50, 80 mg/kg/day at week 26 (2-fold).
• Bilirubin levels increased in treatment groups in M @ both
week 13 and 26.
• Cholesterol levels decreased in M @ 120 and 180 mg/kg/day
@ week 13 and 26 (180 mg/kg/day only).
• Alterations of plasma electrolyte concentrations and markers
of glomerular filtration rate.
Urinalysis:
• Increase in protein and glucose concentration in the urine from
@ 180 mg/kg/day in M and 80 mg/kg/day in F.
• Urine volume of male rats dosed at 120 and 180 mg/kg/day
was higher than controls.
• Increased incidence of white blood cells in the urine of males
[consistent with mild kidney damage].

increased bilirubin levels, and reduced cholesterol levels. In the
absence of histopathology, the effects were considered adaptive
rather than adverse.

significant accumulation (2.4- to 3.0-fold) was observed after 26 weeks
of dosing. At the comparable dose for males and females (50
mg/kg/day), exposure in females was notably higher than in males and
this difference was more pronounced with repeated administration.

• Increase liver weight (relative to body or brain weight) in both

changes in the liver.
• In M, dose-dependent decrease in epididymis and testes
mean weight. Note# The male animals were found to have
varying degrees of sexual maturity that may have influenced
organ weight differences (i.e., 2 controls were sexually
mature, whereas all treated males were immature).
Reviewer’s comment. NK1R/NK3R inhibition in KNDy
neurons in the hypothalamus reduces the activity of
hypothalamic neurons that secrete gonadotropinreleasing hormone (GnRH). The reduced GnRH release
suppresses the release of gonadotropins (luteinizing
hormone [LH] and follicular stimulating hormone [FSH])
from the anterior pituitary gland. A reduction of the LH
and FSH levels due to elinzanetant-induced inhibition of
NK1R/NK3R could explain the dose-dependent reduction
of the mean weight of epididymis and testes.
Histopathology:
• No test article-related changes in microscopic findings.
TK:
•
•

High inter-animal variability and some overlap in exposure
between doses.
Mean exposure in M was higher than in Fs on both Days 1
and 91 @ 15 mg/kg BID whereas on Day 1 the mean
exposure in F @ 30 mg/kg BID was higher than in M.

Study findings
• There was a statistically significant decrease in mean

of variations in the affected litters, (ii) incidence of variations
in elinzanetant-exposed litters being well below the incidence
in historical controls in the same facility, and (iii) lack of dose
responsiveness. The finding could be a result of the maternal
toxicity at the high dose.

Phototoxicity
Study No & Designs

In vitro 3T3 Neutral Red Uptake

Mouse Balb/c 3T3 clone A31 cells

Study Findings
Elinzanetant is noted to absorb light in the visible part of the spectrum;
hence, an in-vitro 3T3 NRU (Neutral Red Uptake) phototoxicity assay
was performed.
Key findings
• Cytotoxicity was observed at the highest 4 concentrations of
elinzanetant analyzed (1.00 to 31.6 μg/mL) in presence of UV
irradiation, resulting in an IC50 of 0.845 μg/mL and a noobserved-effect-concentration (NOEC) of 0.316 μg/mL.
• The MPE (mean photo effect) value for the positive control,
chlorpromazine, was 0.662 and that for elinzanetant was
0.442; as the MPE value was ≥0.15, elinzanetant was
phototoxic in this assay.
• The Applicant assessed the tissue distribution of elinzanetant
in two whole-body autoradiography studies conducted in rats:
study WD2008-00842-00 (study report R-13624) and study
KINE 220019-EXT (study report R-14368).
• Detailed multiple of exposure (MOE) calculations taking into
account the exposures in eye and skin and the % unbound of
elinzanetant are noted in the appendix section.

Reviewer’s comments:
1. The Pharm/Tox review team estimated the most
conservative multiple of exposure for phototoxicity to be
approximately 7-fold.
2. Although the MOEs calculated by the Applicant and by
the Pharm/Tox review team appear reasonable, they
should be interpreted with caution because elinzanetant
concentrations in human pigmented tissues are derived
based on the distribution of elinzanetant to rat pigmented
tissues (eyes and skin) following a single treatment. No
information is available to determine the extent of tissue
accumulation in melanin-containing tissues following
repeated treatment with elinzanetant.
3. Elinzanetant has several characteristics that, per the
Guidance for Industry: S10 Photosafety Evaluation of
Pharmaceuticals (January 2015), available at
https://www.fda.gov/media/85076/download, make it a
potential phototoxicant:
• It absorbs photons in the ultraviolet (UV) spectrum
(290-700 nm).
• It distributes to and accumulates in melanin-rich
tissues (see below; Study Report R-13624; Study
Report R-14368).
• It is cytotoxic in the in-vitro Balb/c 3T3 neutral red
uptake phototoxicity assay, with an IC50 of 0.845
µg/mL and an NOEC of 0.316 µg/mL in presence of
UV-A (Study Report R-13578).
4. In the pooled safety analysis of the 4 studies (SWITCH-1,
and OASIS 1, 2 and 3), 5 women under elinzanetant 120
mg and 1 woman under placebo treatment reported
photosensitivity reaction (PTs). Of the 5, one had to
withdraw because of photosensitivity reaction (onset day
290). The other 4 cases resolved despite continued
treatment with elinzanetant 120 mg, and no actions were
taken for these events.

$ Not previously reviewed under IND 129492 [Refer to Appendix for full review].

11 Integrated Summary and Safety Evaluation
Bayer submitted NDA 219469 for elinzanetant (BAY 3427080) in soft gel capsule
dosage form for the indication to treat moderate to severe VMS associated with
menopause. The recommended oral dose of elinzanetant is 120 mg (two 60 mg
capsules) taken orally once daily at bedtime. Bayer has submitted a full nonclinical
program for elinzanetant to support their NDA under the 505 (b)(1) pathway as an NME
(New Molecular Entity).

116

Reference ID: 5623053

NDA #219469

Edna Albuquerque, Ph.D.
Pratistha Tamrakar, Ph.D.
Sarah Lee, Ph.D.

Pharmacology
Elinzanetant is an NK1R/NK3R antagonist. Inhibition of NK1R/NK3R on KNDy neurons
can decrease neuronal activity involved in thermoregulation, which is thought to
contribute to the VMS associated with menopause.
Elinzanetant has ~10-fold higher affinity to NK1R compared to NK3R, with mean pKi
values of 9.43 and 8.42 for NK1R and NK3R, respectively. Elinzanetant has three
principal metabolites M27, M30/34, and M18/21, which also act as noncompetitive
antagonists at NK1R and NK3R.
In-vitro selectivity assays/ (b) (4) screen including a wide range of receptors, ions
channels, transporters, and enzymes to identify potential off-target effects of
elinzanetant yielded only a few notable findings. Elinzanetant and its three principal
metabolites may have the potential to inhibit estrogen and progesterone receptors (ER
and PR, respectively). Radioligand binding and functional assays with elinzanetant
produced equivocal results. In study R-13674, elinzanetant had no effect on radioligand
binding to ER and PR, and in study R-14344, elinzanetant (up to 30 μM) had no effect
on the activity of recombinant human PR-B. However, in study 14343, elinzanetant
inhibited radiolabeled estradiol and progesterone binding to recombinant human ERβ
and to recombinant human PR-B, respectively; the IC50s were 22.5 μM and 0.64 μM,
respectively. The metabolites M27, M30/M34 (major metabolite), and M18/21 inhibited
radiolabeled progesterone binding to recombinant human PR-B with IC50s of 1.34 μM,
1.20 μM, and 1.69 μM, respectively.
Elinzanetant did not generate major safety signals in a complete battery of safety
pharmacology studies (cardiovascular, respiratory, and CNS). Refer to Table 57 below.

Pharmacokinetics (PK)
Absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion of elinzanetant were assessed in
whole-body autoradiography studies rats and non-radiolabeled assays in rats, monkeys,
and dogs.
Clearance differed between species. It was low in rats with differential clearance
between male and female rats. Significant accumulation of elinzanetant was observed
over the dose range tested in female rats, but not in male rats. Bioavailability was
moderate in male and female rat (77% and 47%), and low in monkey and dog (19%).
High clearance was seen in dog, with low bioavailability (19%). Hence, monkeys (also
with low bioavailability of 19% but moderate clearance compared to dog) were chosen
as the second nonclinical species for chronic toxicity studies besides rats. No notable
accumulation in monkeys post repeat dosing was observed.
Plasma protein binding was high across all preclinical species tested (99.5 to 99.9%)
and higher in human (>99.9%) for elinzanetant as well as the principal metabolites
(M27, M30/34 and M18/21). No concentration dependence of the unbound fraction (fu)
of elinzanetant was observed.
Elinzanetant was brain penetrant in the mouse, rat and monkey with brain:blood ratios
of 0.5:1, 0.1:1 to 0.5:1 and 0.6:1 respectively. Elinzanetant distributes more into plasma
than into the blood cells resulting in a Cb/Cp [blood-to-plasma concentration ratio] range
of 0.574 to 0.663 in human blood and of 0.6-0.7 in the animals’ species.
Distribution: In rat whole-body autoradiography studies, radioactivity showed high
distribution to most tissues. Highest levels were noted in liver, kidney, adrenal gland,
abdominal and brown fat, bulbo-urethral gland, pancreas, lacrimal glands, harderian
gland and mucous gland, whereas brain had lower levels which did not change with
time (no accumulation). After 35 days, radioactivity was still present in brown fat, uveal
tract/retina, spleen and adrenal cortex.
The brain to blood ratio of elinzanetant is 0.1 to 0.5:1 in rats and 0.6:1 in monkeys.
In pregnant rats, the organ distribution was similar to non-pregnant rats. Fetal and
associated tissue concentrations were generally much lower than maternal blood,
except for amnion, placenta, and brain. AUC(0-tlast) ratio of placenta/maternal blood was
1.3, fetus average/amniotic fluid was 18.3 and fetal brain/maternal brain was 2.4.
Metabolism: Elinzanetant is metabolized primarily by oxidation at the methyl-phenyl
moiety as well as at the morpholine ring leading mainly to metabolites M27, M30/34,
and M18/21. Based on clinical data, M30/34 (~11%) is considered as the major human
metabolite. Exposure to all three principal metabolites were investigated in toxicological
studies. Dedicated studies, including chronic repeat dose studies, were also conducted
with M27 as it was considered disproportionate in rat.

119

Reference ID: 5623053

NDA #219469

Edna Albuquerque, Ph.D.
Pratistha Tamrakar, Ph.D.
Sarah Lee, Ph.D.

Excretion: Major route of elimination was via feces and bile in both rat and monkeys.
Similarly in humans, metabolic profiling in plasma, feces and urine demonstrated ~40%
elinzanetant in plasma, ~90% of the administered dose was excreted via feces (about
50% unchanged and ~40% was metabolites) and negligible amount in urine (<0.5%).
Radioactivity was secreted into the milk of lactating SD rats to a moderate extent (6.1%
of dose within 48 h post administration).

Reproductive and developmental toxicity
A full package of reproductive and developmental toxicity studies was conducted in rats
and rabbits. In reproductive and developmental toxicity studies, elinzanetant
administration prior to or during pregnancy caused fetal harm in rats in the form of preand post-implantation loss, reduced litter size or total litter loss, decrease in fetal body
weight, and decrease in neonatal pup viability. No teratogenicity was observed in the
reproductive and developmental studies with elinzanetant in rats or rabbits.
Key findings from the studies along with the safety margins / multiples of exposure are
summarized in the table below and is also summarized as a finding of safety concern
based on nonclinical finding below.

Integrated Summary of Potential Safety Concern based on Nonclinical Findings
The main clinically relevant nonclinical safety signals are discussed in the next sections
and include: (i) central nervous system (CNS)-related signals, including tremors and
convulsions, (ii) skeletal muscle degeneration, (iii) malignant adenocarcinoma of the
uterus, the combination of malignant and benign endometrial tumors and squamous cell
carcinoma of the uterus, and lymphomas of the hematolymphoid system, (iv) phototoxic
signals, (v) gastrointestinal (GI)-related signals, and (vi) reproductive and
developmental toxicity signals. The potential for hepatotoxicity with elinzanetant, based
on the integrated assessment of liver-related signals detected in the nonclinical studies
and a comparative quantitative structure-activity relationship analysis of elinzanetant
and the NK3R inhibitor fezolinetant are also discussed below.

CNS-related safety signals
Convulsions were noted in two nonclinical studies – a 2-year carcinogenicity study

origins.

In the 13-week repeat-dose toxicity study R-13628, male SD:Hsd rats (Netherlands)
were treated with oral elinzanetant (free base) doses of 0, 25, 60, or 150 mg/kg (highest
dose reduced to 87.5 after day 9), BID (twice daily), and female SD:Hsd rats
(Netherlands) were treated with doses of 0, 10, 25, or 50 mg/kg, BID. Treatments were
delivered by oral gavage for 13 weeks. Muscle spasms (lasting up to 3 min) and tremors
were noted around day 24 after start of treatment and were followed by convulsions
(starting around treatment day 34) in 2 out of 16 females at 20 mg/kg/day, 3 out of 16
females at 50 mg/kg/day, and 3 out of 21 females at 100 mg/kg/day. Likewise, 1 out of
16 males in the groups that received the low and mid doses (50 and 120 mg/kg/day,
respectively) had tremors, whole-body rigidity, spasm (lasting up to 1-3 min), stiff tail,
and involuntary muscle contractions (convulsions). In male rats, rigidity and spasms
were first noted on treatment day 31 and convulsions were first noted on treatment day
34. Male rats treated with the highest tested dose (300/175 mg/kg/day) died
prematurely after presenting with reduced activity, hunched posture, abnormal gait,
piloerection, and prostration.

measured on treatment days 1 and 91. Using the linear regression of the timedependent increase in AUC(0-24)s (Figure 16), the AUC(0-24) generated in female rats

In the 2-year carcinogenicity study, female SD:Hsd rats (U.S.) were treated with oral

100 mg/kg. The substrain of SD rats from Charles River is referred to as SD:Crl. In the
26-week study R-13894, SD:Hsd rats were from Envigo (UK); in this study, female rats
were treated twice daily with the oral dose of 0, 10, 25, or 40 mg/kg, and male rats were
treated twice daily (BID) with the oral dose of 0, 25, 60, or 90 mg/kg. In both studies, the
treatments were delivered by oral gavage.

On treatment day 1, systemic exposures of female rats treated BID with 20 mg/kg/day
were comparable between the 13-week repeat-dose toxicity study in which rats
developed convulsions (R-13628) and the 26-week repeat-dose toxicity study in which
rats were also treated twice daily with elinzanetant but did not develop convulsions (R13894) (
Figure 17). As reported in other studies conducted by the Applicant, elinzanetant
accumulated with the repeated daily treatment in the studies discussed here (
Figure 17). However, throughout the treatment duration, systemic exposures measured
in the 13-week study R-13628 became slightly higher than those measured in the 26week study R-13894 (
Figure 17).
As discussed in previous paragraphs, on treatment day 34, when convulsions were first
noted in female rats treated with the dose of 20 mg/kg/day in the 13-week study R13628, systemic exposure was estimated to be approximately 35111 μg•h/L. At the
same dose (20 mg/kg/day), in the 26-week study R-13894, systemic exposure was
estimated to approximate 35111 μg•h/L on treatment day 50 and was as high as 59840
μg•h/L on the last treatment day (day 182). However, convulsions were not observed
throughout the treatment of female rats with the dose of 20 mg/kg/day in the 26-week
study R-13894.
Likewise, on treatment day 106, when convulsions were first noted in female rats
treated with the dose of 80 mg/kg/day in the 2-year carcinogenicity study, systemic
exposure was estimated to be 150076 μg•h/L. At the same dose (80 mg/kg/day), in the
26-week study R-13894, systemic exposure was estimated to approximate 150076
μg•h/L on treatment day 42 and was as high as 311000 μg•h/L on the last treatment
day. Yet, convulsions were not observed throughout the treatment of female rats with
the dose of 80 mg/kg/day in the 26-week study R-13894. Therefore, the apparently
inconsistent CNS effects between studies could not be fully accounted for by insufficient
systemic exposures.
It is unclear why convulsions were inconsistently observed across the different studies
or why convulsions were associated with higher exposures in elinzanetant-treated
female rats in the 2-year carcinogenicity study than in the 13-week study R-13628. It is
possible that the differential seizure susceptibility of different substrains of SD rats
(SD:Crl vs SD:Hsd) and of SD:Hsd rats from different sources (UK, Netherlands, and
U.S.) could have accounted for, or contributed to, the discrepant findings from the
toxicity studies in SD rats treated with elinzanetant. According to a study published by
Langer and collaborators6, SD:Crl rats are less susceptible than SD:Hsd rats to
developing seizures in response to electrical stimulation of the basolateral amygdala

6

Langer M, Brandt C, Löscher W. Marked strain and substrain differences in induction of status epilepticus and subsequent
development of neurodegeneration, epilepsy, and behavioral alterations in rats: Strain and substrain differences in an epilepsy
model in rats. Epilepsy Res. 2011 Oct;96(3):207-224.

(BLA). In addition, SD:Hsd rats from the Netherlands are less susceptible than SD:Hsd

Biological Plausibility of Elinzanetant-Induced Seizures in Rats
Considering the current knowledge that NK1R/NK3R activation increases neuronal
excitability7,8 and the Applicant’s finding that, in acute habenula slices from guinea pigs,
elinzanetant inhibited neuronal firing induced by the NK3R agonist NKB (Study R13877), it is unlikely that elinzanetant-induced inhibition of NK1R/NK3R would lead to
the development of convulsions.
The Applicant has reported that, at 10 μM, the elinzanetant metabolite BAY 3462933
(M30/34) inhibits [3H]tert-butylbicycloorthobenzoate ([3H]TBOB) binding to gammaamino butyric acid type A (GABAA) receptors in Wistar rat brain membrane preparations
by ~55% (R-14018). GABAA receptor antagonists (e.g., picrotoxin and bicuculline) are
well known for their proconvulsant effects.9 Considering that, in female rats treated with
the elinzanetant dose of 60 mg/kg/day, Cmax and AUC0-24h of BAY 3462933 (M30/34)
were 2.09 μM and 46.8 μM•h, respectively, on treatment day 358, BAY 3462933
(M30/34)-induced inhibition of GABAA receptors could have contributed to the
proconvulsant effects of elinzanetant in rats.
Additionally, BAY 3462933 (M30/34) inhibits [3H]progesterone binding to PR-B with a Ki
of 0.96 μM. Two other metabolites of elinzanetant – BAY 3462932 (M27) and BAY
346934 (M18/21) – also inhibit PR-B with Kis of 1.08 μM and 1.35 μM, respectively.
According to binding studies, interactions of elinzanetant with PR-B are equivocal (see
Secondary Pharmacology above). However, in one study, elinzanetant inhibited binding
of [3H]progesterone to PR-B ectopically expressed in insect Sf9 cells with an IC50 of
0.64 μM. PR-B inhibition by the elinzanetant metabolites (and, possibly, elinzanetant
itself) may contribute to the proconvulsant properties of elinzanetant because PR
antagonists and null mutations of the genes that encode PR-A and PR-B reportedly
suppress the anticonvulsant effects of progesterone.10,11

the CNS-related safety signal of convulsions and whether it

The Neurotoxicology Subcommittee indicated that it is rather
common to not see histopathological changes even when
there is evidence of seizures in animals. Seizures of
prolonged duration may be accompanied by histopathological
changes, but shorter seizures may not.
The Neurotoxicology Subcommittee considered it acceptable
to set NOAELs based on convulsions and prodromal signs,
including spasms and tremors. The margins would be to the
highest dose with no observed clinical CNS signs.
The Neurotoxicology Subcommittee considered that additional
nonclinical studies may not help better define the safety
margins for the safety signal of convulsions.
Finally, the Neurotoxicology Subcommittee agreed that
describing the nonclinical findings of convulsions in the
subsection (13.2) in section 13 of the drug product labeling is
appropriate. The Neurotoxicology Subcommittee further
recommended that, if human findings warrant the addition of
the potential for elinzanetant to increase the incidence of
seizures to the “Warnings and Precautions” section of the
labeling, they should be linked to the nonclinical findings
described in section 13.

Summary and conclusion
Based on the totality of evidence, the CNS-related findings in the rat were determined to
be related to elinzanetant treatment. The mechanism of the CNS-related findings in
elinzanetant-treated rats has not been determined; however, as discussed above, PR-B
inhibition by the elinzanetant metabolites (and, possibly, elinzanetant itself) and GABA A
receptor inhibition by the metabolite BAY 3462933 could contribute to the convulsions
observed in elinzanetant-treated rats. These findings were discussed with internal
neurotoxicology experts (PTCC Neurotoxicology Assessment Subcommittee), and it
was determined that, at the time of this review, additional nonclinical studies were not
needed to better define safety margins for this safety signal.
Skeletal muscle degeneration
In the 13-week repeat-dose toxicity study (R-13628 [RH17GJ]) conducted in SD:Hsd
rats (Envigo, Netherlands), male rats (11/11) and female rats (3/10) that died
prematurely following treatment with the highest test doses of elinzanetant (300
mg/kg/day and 100 mg/kg/day, respectively) presented with moderate to severe
degeneration and necrosis of the skeletal muscles in the leg, tongue, and/or larynx

Skeletal muscle degeneration/necrosis correlated with increased transaminases, lactate
dehydrogenase, and creatine kinase and was considered the primary cause of death or
early termination of rats treated with the highest test doses of elinzanetant. Three
additional female rats died prematurely following treatment with the highest test dose
(100 mg/kg/day); however, the cause of death was undetermined for these 3 female
rats, which presented no remarkable histopathological findings. As a note, rats with the
skeletal muscle degeneration findings were different from the rats that had CNS-related
findings (as described above).
The finding of skeletal muscle degeneration was not observed in other repeat-dose
toxicity studies conducted in rats and other animal species. In addition, the finding was
not reproduced in a separate study that the Applicant designed and conducted
specifically to investigate the mechanistic basis of the finding.
Summary and conclusion
Biological plausibility of elinzanetant to cause skeletal muscle degeneration/necrosis is
unclear. A mechanistic study that the Applicant conducted in male rats (R-13644) to
mimic the effects recorded in the 13-week repeat-dose toxicity study (R-13628
[RH17GJ]) failed to reproduce the severe skeletal muscle degeneration. The most
conservative multiple of exposure for this finding derived from the 13-week repeat-dose
study at 100 mg/kg/day in female rats is 16X the human therapeutic exposure on an
AUC basis. The clinical relevance of this skeletal muscle finding is unknown.
Genotoxicity and Carcinogenicity
In-vitro and in-vivo genotoxicity studies with elinzanetant and its three main metabolites
(M27, M30/34, and M18/21) showed negative results.
There were no neoplastic findings in the 26-week transgenic mouse study (B003184).

Positive carcinogenicity findings were present in the 2-year rat study (B003186). Female
rats were treated orally with elinzanetant doses ranging from 7 to 80 mg/kg/day
compared to vehicle for 104 weeks. Elinzanetant dose dependently reduced body
weight gain (body weights were 9%, 9%,17%, and 19% lower at 7, 20, 60, 80
mg/kg/day, respectively, compared to control at terminal sacrifice), but had no effect on
overall survival. Elinzanetant treatment resulted in neoplastic findings in the uterus and
the hematolymphoid system as described in Table 64 below, along with safety margins
based on clinical exposure.

Biological Plausibility of Elinzanetant-Induced Endometrial Carcinomas in Rats
The main metabolites of elinzanetant – BAY 3462932 (M27), BAY 3462933 (M30/34),
and BAY 346934 (M18/21) – inhibit [3H]progesterone binding to PR-B with Kis of 1.08
μM, 0.96 μM, and 1.35 μM, respectively. Considering that Cmax and AUC0-24h of BAY
3462933 (M30/34) were 2.09 μM and 46.8 μM•h, respectively, in female rats treated
with the elinzanetant dose of 60 mg/kg/day, it is possible that inhibition of PR-B by BAY
3462933 (M30/34) contributes to the increased incidence of endometrial cancers in rats
treated with elinzanetant doses ≥60 mg/kg/day.

As mentioned in the subsections “Secondary Pharmacology” and “CNS-related signals”
above, elinzanetant produced equivocal signals in binding studies assessing its
interactions with PRs. In one study, elinzanetant inhibited [3H]progesterone binding to
PR-B in a concentration dependent manner, with an IC50 of ~0.64 μM. It is, therefore,
plausible that inhibition of PR-B by the parent drug may also contribute to the increased
incidence of endometrial cancers in elinzanetant-treated rats.
According to nonclinical pharmacological studies conducted by the Applicant (see
Section 4.2 Secondary Pharmacology), the elinzanetant metabolite BAY 3462933
(M30/34) at 10 μM inhibited by ~50-60% binding of [3H]estradiol to human estrogen
receptor α (ERα) ectopically expressed in Sf9 cells, an ovarian cell line. The Applicant
did not conduct studies to determine how the metabolite regulates ERα activity in
different organs. As described in the literature, selective estrogen receptor modulators
can act as ER agonists or antagonists depending on their tissue-selective interaction
with the receptor. For instance, while tamoxifen acts as an ER antagonist in the breast,
it acts as an ER agonist in the uterus.12 An agonistic action of BAY 3462933 (M30/34)
on ERα in the uterus could contribute to the increased incidence of uterine
adenocarcinomas in female rats treated with elinzanetant doses ≥60 mg/kg/day. On the
other hand, an antagonistic action of BAY 3462933 (M30/34) on ERα in breast, pituitary,
and thyroid tissues could contribute to the apparent reduction in the incidence of
mammary gland neoplasms and hyperplasia, pituitary adenomas, and thyroid C-cell
adenomas in female rats treated with elinzanetant doses ≥60 mg/kg/day for 2 years.
Although not statistically significant, the incidence of these tumors in elinzanetanttreated female rats was >50% lower than in vehicle-treated female rats.
The primary mechanism of action of elinzanetant may also be an important factor
contributing to its carcinogenic potential, particularly when treatment spans ages when
sex hormones are regularly cycling as it did in the 2-year carcinogenicity in female rats.
In this study, twice daily treatment of female rats with elinzanetant started at
adolescence (~2 months of age) and continued through adulthood and reproductive
senescence. As discussed earlier in this review, inhibition of NK1R/NK3Rs in the
hypothalamus can reduce the activity of KNDy neurons, which are known to synapse
onto GnRH-releasing neurons (see Figure 1). Reduced KNDy neuron activity can lead
to reduced activity of GnRH-releasing neurons and, thereby, contribute to suppression
of the activity of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis (see Figure 1). As
discussed below, findings consistent with suppression of the HPG axis were reported in
healthy premenopausal women treated with elinzanetant in a randomized, singleblinded, placebo-controlled clinical study.13

In the clinical study published by Pawsey et al.,13 33 healthy premenopausal women
were examined during two consecutive menstrual cycles and received a 21-day
treatment with elinzanetant (40 mg, 80 mg, or 120 mg, oral) during the second cycle.
The authors reported that treatment with elinzanetant caused a dose-dependent
reduction of LH levels during the second menstrual cycle compared to the first (though
the finding did not reach statistical significance). The largest reduction in serum LH
levels was noted at the elinzanetant oral dose of 120 mg/day and was accompanied by
a significant reduction of estradiol and progesterone levels during the second menstrual
cycle compared to the first. Reduced levels of estradiol remained within the therapeutic
window of 30 to 50 pg/mL thought to be important to minimize vasomotor symptoms
and bone loss.13 However, levels of progesterone were sufficiently reduced to increase
the duration of the luteal phase of the cycle and prolong bleeding during the menstrual
cycle.13 Thus, treatment of premenopausal women with elinzanetant resulted in a
hormonal imbalance with relative estrogen dominance.
Considering the findings of the clinical study by Pawsey et al.,13 it is possible that, in the
2-year carcinogenicity study, the life-long elinzanetant treatment covering ages when
sex hormones were regularly cycling in the female rats caused a hormonal imbalance
with relative estrogen dominance that could, in turn, have contributed to a reduction of
the potential protective effect of progesterone against development of sex hormonesensitive tumors such as endometrial adenocarcinomas.
Summary and conclusion
In the 2-year carcinogenicity study in female rats, the highest noncarcinogenic dose of
elinzanetant was 20 mg/kg/day (7.5X the human therapeutic exposure on an AUC
basis) and the lowest dose found to be carcinogenic was 60 mg/kg/day (~29X the
human therapeutic exposure on an AUC basis). The neoplastic findings were observed
in the uterus and the hematolymphoid system of the female rat.
Phototoxicity
Elinzanetant has several characteristics that, per the Guidance for Industry: S10
Photosafety Evaluation of Pharmaceuticals (January 2015)14, make it a potential
phototoxicant.
• Elinzanetant absorbs photons in the ultraviolet (UV) spectrum (290-700 nm).
o One peak was detected at 321.4 nm with a calculated molar extinction
coefficient (MEC) of 3762.3 L•mol-1, which exceeds the threshold of 1000
L•mol-1 for phototoxicity (Study Report R-13578).
• Elinzanetant distributes to and accumulates in melanin-rich tissues (Study Report
R-13624; Study Report R-14368).
• Elinzanetant is cytotoxic in the in-vitro Balb/c 3T3 neutral red uptake phototoxicity
assay, with an IC50 of 0.845 µg/mL in presence of UV-A (Study Report R-13578).

Summary and conclusion
Based on the in-vitro phototoxicity assay, the most conservative MOE for phototoxicity
was approximately 7-fold. Refer to full review in the appendix for details on the
calculations. The MOE should be interpreted with caution because elinzanetant
concentrations in human pigmented tissues are derived based on the distribution of
elinzanetant to rat pigmented tissues (eyes and skin) after a single dose and no
additional in-vivo animal photosensitivity studies have been conducted.
GI-related signals
GI-related signals were noted with elinzanetant treatment in repeat-dose toxicity studies
in rats and monkeys.
In rats treated orally with elinzanetant for 7 days [study R-13586], histopathological
findings of mucosa degeneration along with regeneration of the gastric mucosa, isthmus
regenerative hypertrophy, and/or hyperplasia of the isthmus epithelium were observed
at 300 mg/kg/day in both male and female rats. Minimal multifocal degeneration/
regeneration was also noted at 100 mg/kg/day in female rats. In a 13-week repeat-dose
toxicity study with 4-week recovery (study R-13628), rats with decreased food
consumption died prematurely [3 males at 300 mg/kg/day and 2 females at 100
mg/kg/day] and had alterations in the large intestine consisting of distended colon or
cecum and/or hard content in the colon.
In monkeys, GI-related adverse effects consisted of findings of loose feces, decreased
food consumption, and excessive salivation starting at 60 mg/kg/day (10-fold the human
therapeutic exposure on an AUC basis) in a 7-day oral repeat dose study [study R13627]. Ulceration in the pyloric region of the stomach was seen in females at 100
mg/kg/day (2.4-fold the human therapeutic exposure on an AUC basis). In a 4-week oral
repeat-dose toxicity study [study R-13639], 2 monkeys (1 male and 1 female) that were
prematurely sacrificed treated with 60 mg/kg/day (4-fold the human therapeutic
exposure on an AUC basis) had abnormal fecal consistency (loose/watery) and
reduction in food intake along with histopathological findings of hemorrhage in the
adventitia and in mucosa of multiple regions in the GI tract.
Similar findings were noted in the 13-week studies [R-13629 and R-13612] and the 39week study [study R-13895], with abnormal feces (liquid/soft) and/or diarrhea observed
in many animals across all dose groups (highest dose tested was 80 mg/kg/day) at
various points throughout the study. In the 13-week study, monkeys treated with once
daily oral elinzanetant doses ≥20 mg/kg/day (≥0.5-fold the human therapeutic exposure
on an AUC basis) presented with increased incidence of thin appearance and
dehydration; these findings are indicative of GI disturbances. In the 13-week study,
monkeys treated with twice daily oral elinzanetant doses ≥30 mg/kg/day (≥0.2-fold the
human therapeutic exposure on an AUC basis) presented with diarrhea and doses ≥80
mg/kg/day (≥2.3-fold the human therapeutic exposure on an AUC basis) presented with
thin appearance. In the 39-week study, 2 female monkeys treated twice daily with oral
doses ≥60 mg/kg/day (2-fold the human therapeutic exposure on an AUC basis) and

male monkeys treated twice daily with oral doses ≥30 mg/kg/day (0.7-fold the human

Summary and conclusion
The multiples of exposure for the GI effects in monkeys is low, with observed findings
starting at the oral elinzanetant doses equivalent to 0.2-fold the human therapeutic
exposure at the MRHD.
Reproductive and developmental toxicity
In reproductive and developmental toxicity studies, elinzanetant administration prior to
or during pregnancy caused fetal harm in rats in the form of pre- and post-implantation
loss, reduced litter size or total litter loss, decrease in fetal body weight, and decrease in
neonatal pup viability. No teratogenicity was observed in any of the conducted studies.
In a fertility and early embryonic development study in rats, there was an increase in the
percentage of pre- and post-implantation embryo loss and decrease in fetal body
weights at 40-fold the human therapeutic exposure when rat dams were treated orally
prior to mating and through the early embryonic period.
In a pre- and postnatal developmental study in rats, a higher incidence of still born pups,
an increase in total litter loss, a decrease in pup viability between postnatal days 0 and
4, and an increase in the number of neonatal pups without milk in the stomach were
observed in the mid- and high-dose groups, with maternal systemic exposures that were
within the range of human therapeutic exposure. Decreased maternal care was also a
clinical observation in these treatment groups. Whether the neonatal effects were due to
decreased maternal care or other potential elinzanetant-related effects on the offspring
could not be definitively concluded from this study.
In an embryofetal development study in rabbits, maternal toxicity was noted in the form
of marked body weight loss and decreased food consumption at systemic exposures
that were within the range of human therapeutic exposure.
No teratogenicity was observed in the reproductive and developmental studies with
elinzanetant in rats or rabbits.
Biological Plausibility of Pregnancy Losses and Stillbirths in Rats Exposed to
Elinzanetant During Gestation
The pregnancy losses and stillbirths noted in rats exposed to elinzanetant during
gestation may be related, at least in part, to NK1R/NK3R inhibition. The inhibition of
NK1Rs and NK3Rs can reduce the activity of GnRH-releasing neurons in the
hypothalamus and, consequently, suppress the HPG axis leading to an adverse
imbalance of the hormones needed to sustain pregnancy. In rats, drugs that act as
GnRH receptor inhibitors (e.g., relugolix) are known to cause pregnancy loss and

138

Reference ID: 5623053

NDA #219469

Edna Albuquerque, Ph.D.
Pratistha Tamrakar, Ph.D.
Sarah Lee, Ph.D.

stillbirth.15 However, studies have not been conducted to examine this mechanistic
relationship resulting in hormonal imbalance in the rat or rabbit after elinzanetant
treatment.
Summary and conclusion
Based on findings from animal reproduction studies, elinzanetant may cause pregnancy
loss or stillbirth when administered during pregnancy. Fetal malformations were not
observed in these animal studies.
Potential for liver toxicity
In the pivotal chronic toxicity studies conducted by the Applicant, including a 26-week
study in Sprague-Dawley rats (R-13894) and a 39-week study in monkeys (R-13895),
elinzanetant increased levels of the liver-associated enzymes ALT, AST, and ALP.
Specifically, in male rats treated orally with the dose of 180 mg/kg/day (90 mg/kg, BID),
ALT increased by ~2 fold, and in female rats treated orally with ≥50 mg/kg/day (≥25
mg/kg, BID), AST increased by ~2 fold. In male and female monkeys treated orally with
the dose of 40 and 30 mg/kg, BID, respectively, ALT increased by ~1.8 fold (male
monkeys) to ~3.6 fold (female monkeys). In these studies, the increased enzyme
activity was not associated with histopathological findings that are typically indicative of
adverse liver tissue damage.
Liver damage was reported in non-pivotal short-term studies in rats and monkeys.
Specifically, following a 7-day oral treatment with elinzanetant tosylate doses of 100 and
300 mg/kg/day, SD rats presented with hepatocellular necrosis and lobular
hepatocellular hypertrophy (Study 13586). In addition, following a 4-day oral treatment
with the elinzanetant dose of 300 mg/kg/day, monkeys (n = 2; 1 male and 1 female)
presented with hepatocellular vacuolation and/or single-cell necrosis (Study 13580).
The discrepancy in the liver-associated histopathology findings between the chronic and
short-term studies is unclear. However, upregulation of certain cytochrome P450 (CYP)
enzymes is thought to contribute to drug-induced liver injury (Jaeschke et al. 200216),
and the Applicant reports that elinzanetant and its metabolites are CYP inducers. Thus,
the initial injury that develops following short-term treatment with elinzanetant could
result at least in part from upregulation of CYPs and could be subsequently resolved by
adaptative responses. In this context, hepatic adaptation to an initial drug-induced liver
injury has been reported with other drugs (Eakins et al. 201517).
Following a consult request from the OND/Drug-Induced Liver Injury (DILI) team, the
CDER Computational Toxicology Consultation Service (CTCS) team conducted a

Hypothetical hepatotoxicity predictions for elinzanetant considering findings from
fezolinetant
Fezolinetant is an NK3R antagonist approved under the brand name VEOZAH [NDA
216578; approval date: 5/12/2023] for the treatment of moderate to severe VMS due to
menopause (). In the pre-approval clinical trial database, elevations of hepatic enzymes
were seen with fezolinetant but there were no cases meeting Hy’s law criteria or with
elevated bilirubin levels. The approved fezolinetant labeling thus included a warning for
its potential to elevate liver enzymes, and FDA recommended monitoring and follow-up
of hepatic function and injury in patients taking fezolinetant. After receiving postmarketing reports of serious hepatotoxicity in patients taking fezolinetant, FDA revised
labeling in 2024 to add a Boxed Warning for serious hepatotoxicity that occurred within
40 days of starting treatment and recommended monthly testing of hepatic function for
the first three months of treatment and additional follow up testing at 6 and 9 months
after initiation of treatment.
In February 2025, Nuthi et al.18 published an article reporting that a reactive carbene
metabolite could contribute to the hepatotoxicity of fezolinetant. The authors
hypothesized that the high electrophilicity of a carbene metabolite that can be generated
from the fezolinetant metabolite referred to as fezo-acid, as illustrated in Figure 18, is
likely to favor the carbene reaction with thiol groups in the liver to produce thiol adducts
that can be hepatotoxic.
Figure 18: Generation of the fezo-carbene metabolite by decarboxylation of the
fezolinetant metabolite fezo-acid

structure and the neutral carbon atom with a valence of two and two unshared valence electrons in the fezo-carbene structure.
18 Nuthi A, Mishra G, Dixit VA. Carbene reactive metabolite explains the hepatotoxicity of the hot flashes drug fezolinetant: A

DFT investigation. Bioorg Chem. 2025 Apr;157:108291.

The Nonclinical Team consulted with the CTCS team to determine if the mechanism
hypothesized in this paper could help further inform the (Q)SAR assessment to predict
the hepatotoxic potential for elinzanetant and its metabolites. The CTCS team’s overall
conclusion indicated that elinzanetant is unlikely to be converted into a carbene
metabolite and is not predicted to have a hepatotoxic potential comparable to that of
fezolinetant. The following is a summary of the CTCS assessment:
1. The elinzanetant acid metabolite M10 could hypothetically undergo
decarboxylation to form a carbene metabolite (Figure 19). However, per Nuthi
et al., in part due to stabilization of charges by resonance, decarboxylation
would be more likely for heteroaromatic rings (as the thiadiazole ring that has
the -COOH group in fezo-acid) than for a benzene ring (as the ring that has
the -COOH group in the elinzanetant metabolite M10). Without empirical
evidence, it is difficult to predict whether decarboxylation of the benzene
group in the M10 metabolite can happen in vivo.
Figure 19. Hypothetical carbene metabolite generated by decarboxylation of the
elinzanetant metabolite M10 [Reviewer-generated figure].

The red circles highlight the carboxylic acid group in the elinzanetant M10 metabolite and the neutral carbon atom with a valence
of two and two unshared valence electrons in the hypothetical carbene metabolite.

2. Both elinzanetant and fezolinetant have bi-aryl structural alerts (Figure 20).
However, in part because the dissimilar aromatic ring types between the two
compounds cause the alerts to be weighed differently for each molecule, the
(Q)SAR models predict elinzanetant to be negative and fezolinetant to be
positive for liver enzyme abnormalities.
3. The presence of a methyl substituent (that could undergo enzymatic oxidative
hydrolysis) in the bi-aryl alert is not a requirement for a bi-aryl substructure to
be identified as an alert by the hepatotox (Q)SAR models. Thus, the
possibility of carbene generation is not a requirement for bi-aryl substructures
to be identified as structural alerts for hepatotoxicity.

Figure 20: (Q)SAR-identified structural alerts in fezolinetant and elinzanetant

The blue circles highlight the bi-aryl substructures in the structural alerts (substructures
in red font) in fezolinetant and elinzanetant. The stars mark the methyl groups that could
undergo enzymatic oxidative hydrolysis to carboxylic acids.
4. Additional (Q)SAR analysis on M10 or any other metabolites is unlikely to
yield additional useful information because the liver tox model training sets
are largely populated with drug substances with information from post-market
reporting and do not include many metabolites or impurities.
Summary and conclusion
There were no histopathological findings indicating hepatotoxicity in the pivotal, longterm repeat-dose toxicity studies in rats and monkeys. The findings of hepatocellular
necrosis and lobular hepatocellular hypertrophy, hepatocellular vacuolation, and/or
single-cell necrosis seen in short-term toxicity studies at high doses have multiples of
exposure of 21X (average of males and females) in rats, 13X in male monkeys, and
2.7X in female monkeys as compared to the human therapeutic exposure on an AUC
basis. Considering the comparative (Q)SAR analysis by the CTCS team, the likelihood
of generation of a reactive carbene metabolite that can form hepatotoxic thiol adducts is
low for elinzanetant compared to fezolinetant due to their dissimilar structures.
Therefore, from the nonclinical perspective, the potential for hepatotoxicity with the
maximal recommended human dose of elinzanetant is lower than with fezolinetant.
Conclusion
Elinzanetant is an NK1R/NK3R antagonist, and inhibition of NK1R/NK3R activity in
hypothalamic KNDy neurons is proposed to contribute to the suppression of hot flashes
experienced by women with VMS during menopause. The complete package of
nonclinical studies submitted to support this application are adequate and PharmTox
supports the approval of this application.

assessed by the Applicant, its effects are not long lasting.

NOAEL and Multiples of exposure
• The Applicant sets the NOAEL for maternal toxicity, F1 maturation, and F1
reproductive function for this study at the highest dose tested or 15 mg/kg/day
(BAY 3427080 Cmax of 2940 μg/L and AUC0-tlast of 36200 μg*h/L), which provides
a safety margin of 4.2-fold on an AUC basis [based on AUC0-24h of 8572
ng•h/mL (Elinzanetant) obtained from clinical study B002427].
Reviewer’s comment: This reviewer agrees with the NOAEL set at 15
mg/kg/day for F1 maturation and reproductive function. However,
based on maternal findings of body weight loss, clinical signs of not
attending to offspring, and general poor health observed in 3 F0
dams at 5 mg/kg/day and 3 F0 dams at 15 mg/kg/day, the maternal
toxicity NOAEL should be set at the low dose of 1.5 mg/kg/day.
•

The Applicant set the NOAEL for developmental toxicity at the low dose or 1.5
mg/kg/day (corresponding to maternal BAY 3427080 Cmax of 134 μg/L and
AUC(0-24h) of 2000 μg*h/L on GD 20), based on the increase in litter loss and
clinical observation of missing milk bands.
Reviewer’s comment:
1) This Reviewer agrees with a NOAEL for developmental toxicity of
1.5 mg/kg/day.
2) At the NOAEL of 1.5 mg/kg/day for developmental toxicity there is
no safety margin (0.23 X) based on AUC0-24h of 8572 ng•h/mL
(Elinzanetant) obtained from clinical study B002427.
3) Metabolite coverage in F0 rats: Based on AUC0-24h of 2496
ng•h/mL (M27), 4570 ng•h/mL (M30/34), 2326 ng•h/mL (M18/21),
obtained from clinical study B002427, there is no coverage for
any of the metabolites in the dams.

Key Study Findings
• Sprague Dawley rats were administered a daily via oral gavage of 0 (vehicle: 1%
aqueous methylcellulose), 5, 25 and 100 mg/kg/day (once daily; QD) and 50
mg/kg BID of BAY 3427080 from implantation (GD 6) to lactation day 4.
• Mortality occurred at 100 mg/kg/day once daily and 50 mg/kg/day (twice daily)
groups. Clinical observations of dystocia (e.g., piloerection, rough pelage,
hunched posture, and decreased activity), decreased body weight and body
weight gain (-16% to -34%), and decreased food consumption (up to -47% on
GD18 to 21).
• Other toxicities included increased gestation length (23.5 or 23.6 days compared
to 23 days in control) and post implantation loss (up to ~49%), decreased
number of liveborn pups delivered (~7 compared to ~11 in control), decreased
number of litters remaining on lactation day 4 (% viability as low as 5% compared
to 94% in control), decreased pup body weights (up to 27%), and pups found
with no milk in stomach (with 33, 15, 2, and 11 pups affected in groups
administered 5, 25, or 100 mg/kg/day or 50 mg/kg/dose BID).
• Increase in total litter loss and decreased pup viability (by PND 5) in all
elinzanetant treated groups: 3 in 5 mg/kg/day, 2 in 25 mg/kg/day, and 5 in 100
mg/kg/day. Additionally, decrease in activity, slow respiration and cool to touch
were noted in groups starting at 5 mg/kg/day.
• Applicant set the maternal NOAEL at 25 mg/kg/day once daily (BAY 3427080
Cmax of 3630 μg/L and AUC(0-tlast) of 57200 μg*h/L on GD 17).
• NOAEL for developmental toxicity was not established due to litter loss in all
treatment groups.

In vitro Phototoxicity

Key Study Findings
• NT-814 was assayed for phototoxicity to Balb/c 3T3 fibroblast cells using the
Neutral Red Uptake assay.
• NT-814 was phototoxic in this in vitro test system when tested up to the limit of
solubility in culture medium.
• The multiples of exposure based on IC50 for plasma exposure, eye exposure and
skin exposure are 198-fold, 99-fold and ~40-fold, respectively based on the
human Cmax data obtained from PK modeling study [B002427]

survival, in the absence of UV-A light. In the presence of UV-A light,
cytotoxicity, as indicated by a decrease in Neutral Red uptake, was observed
at the highest four concentrations of NT-814 analyzed (1.00 to 31.6 μg/mL).

calculated.

Mean Photo Effect (MPE) was used for evaluation. An MPE value of 0.442 was
calculated for NT-814 and as this MPE value was ≥0.15, the test article was
considered to be phototoxic in this assay. [Note# The MPE is based on

Tissue Distribution
The Applicant assessed the tissue distribution of elinzanetant in two whole-body
autoradiography studies conducted in rats: study WD2008-00842-00 (study report R13624) and study KINE 220019-EXT (study report R-14368).
In study WD2008-00842-00, male Lister Hooded pigmented rats were treated with
radiolabeled elinzanetant tosylate (in 1% Methylcellulose (w/v)-containing sterile water)
via the oral or IV route of administration and euthanized at various times for
measurements of radioactivity concentrations in tissues. The oral dose delivered to the
rats was 10 mg/kg.
Radioactivity concentrations in blood, pigmented skin, and uveal tract/retina peaked
between 2 and 8 h (Table 74). At 35 days following the oral treatment, radioactivity was
still quantifiable in about half of the tissues, with highest concentrations generally
present in brown fat, uveal tract (choroids, ciliary body and iris)/retina, spleen, and
adrenal cortex. The extent of the persistence of radioactive drug-related material in the
uveal tract/retina following either route of administration suggested some long-term
association of drug-related material with melanin.

Although as mentioned above, the Applicant questions the relevance of study WD200800842-00 for this NDA, the Applicant appears to have derived potential multiples of
exposure (MOEs) for phototoxicity using: (i) the accumulation of elinzanetant in
pigmented tissue estimated on the basis of study WD2008-00842-00 (2x in the eyes
and 5x in the skin), (ii) the IC50 for elinzanetant to induce cytotoxicity in-vitro in the
presence of UV-A (0.845 µg/mL), and (iii) the NOEC (0.316 µg/mL).
Calculation of MOEs [using estimated eye and skin accumulations from Study
WD2008-00842-00 (2x for eyes and 5x for skin)]:
• IC50 in presence of UV-A = 0.845 µg/mL
• NOEC in the presence of UV-A = 0.316 µg/mL
• Cmax in clinical study = 1423 µg/L or 1.423 µg/mL (Clinical Report B002427,
Table 21.3.1, Pg 521)
• Considering the unbound fraction of elinzanetant (~0.3% in human based on
study#), the Cmax exposure = 0.3% of 1.423 µg/mL= 0.00426 µg/mL.
• The distribution data in the quantitative whole-body autoradiography study
(melanin binding) indicate that elinzanetant concentrations in the eye can be up
to 2-fold higher and pigmented skin concentrations can be up to 5-fold higher
than in blood.
• Hence, in the eyes, concentration = 2 x 0.00426 µg/mL= 0.00852 and in the skin,
concentration = 5 X 0.00426 µg/mL= 0.0213
MOEs (IC50/Cmax):
• Based on plasma exposure= 0.845/0.00426 = 198-fold
• Based on eye exposure = 0.845/0.00852 = 99-fold
